title: Designing Against Deskilling: Metacognitive Feedback Reduces Cognitive Offloading to LLM Assistants
content: Cognitive offloading to AI can reduce opportunities to practice skills, creating risks of deskilling. However, it remains unclear how to prevent deskilling without restricting access to AI. Here, we design two interventions to reduce offloading decisions: (1) metacognitive feedback that makes the implications of offloading for users explicit, and (2) an effort-based reward that incentivizes less extensive LLM assistance. We test both in a preregistered online experiment ($N = 704$) with a 2$\times$2 design and a no-AI control. The task was to practice fraction arithmetic with an LLM-based assistant that provided solutions only on explicit request, followed by an unaided test. Metacognitive feedback reduced answer offloading (OR $= 0.47$) and improved test performance (OR $= 1.51$). We found no evidence that the reward affected either outcome. Our results identify metacognitive feedback as a promising design choice to reduce cognitive offloading.

title: How to get digital copies of your UAE government documents on your smartphone for free
content: Dubai: If you’re a Dubai resident, you know that paperless transactions and communications are the way to go. That’s why the emirate has made getting digital copies of all official documents a simple process.Here’s how you can get digital versions of all your government-issued documents, right from your smartphone.Why do I need digital copies of documents?The shift to digital document management, rather than reliance on physical hard copies, is inevitable in a visionary city like Dubai.The government of Dubai has been taking proactive steps to create a fully paperless government for years. Launched in 2018, the Dubai Paperless Strategy eliminated more than 336 million sheets of paper used for government transactions every year, saving time, resources and the environment.Digital Dubai, the government entity that’s tasked with digitalising all aspects of life in Dubai, is leading the emirate’s shift toward a fully integrated, smart government.In April this year, His Highness Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence of the UAE, and Chairman of The Executive Council of Dubai, directed all government entities in the emirate to integrate services for individuals and businesses into a unified digital ecosystem within one year, with Digital Dubai overseeing its implementation.As part of these initiatives, ensuring government-issued documents are available to all residents without the need for paper, is a key aspect of the city’s vision. What kind of documents can I request, as digital copies?According to Digital Dubai, your UAE PASS permits you access to a host of documents available in official digital formats. Here are just a few examples of documents you can own digitally:Emirates IDPassport for UAE citizensDriving licenceVehicle registration card (Mulkiya)Attested academic certificates and recordsPeople of determination card (Sanad)How do I request digital copies? You will require your UAE PASS, which is your national digital identity, to request a digital copy of a government-issued document. Follow these steps to make your request:Download the UAE PASS app through the Google Play Store or Apple App Store. Log in with your biometric information.At the bottom of the home screen, tap on ‘Documents’ in the menu bar. Tap on ‘Request a document’.You will now be able to view a list of all official documents that can be requested, such as driver’s licence or academic qualifications equivalency certificate. Find your required document and click ‘Request’.Your Emirates ID card information will be used to request the document. Select ‘Confirm request’. Wait for the process to complete.Once the process is complete, you will receive a notification via the app. Click on ‘View document’. You will be to see the digital version on your app.Click on the three dots beside the document to be able to view more details and access other facilities, such as saving the document as a PDF, seeing the date issued, and removing the document. Fee: The service is free of charge.

title: المطبخ المصري يستعيد تراثه بأكلات العصور القديمة
content:
يتميز المطبخ المصري بمكوناته وأكلاته ووصفاته التي تحمل أبعاداً تراثية بعضها يعود للعصور القديمة. وقد نظمت فعاليات وأنشطة حول الطعام المصري بما يمثله من خصوصية تثري الأبعاد السياحية، خصوصاً في مجال السياحة الثقافية بالتركيز على ثقافة الطعام.
وفي هذا الإطار نظمت جمعية الحفاظ على السياحة الثقافية، الأحد، فعاليات مسابقة «المطبخ المصري تراث وهوية» بين طلاب كليات ومعاهد السياحة والفنادق في مختلف أنحاء مصر، بهدف الحفاظ على الموروث الغذائي المصري، والتعريف بالمطبخ المصري بوصفه جزءاً أصيلاً من الهوية والتراث والثقافة المصرية.
وقدم الطلاب مجموعة متنوعة من الأطباق المصرية المتميزة، التي عكست ثراء وتنوع المطبخ المصري، واختلاف البيئات والثقافات التي شكلت هويته على مر العصور.
و«تنوعت الأطباق المشاركة بين وصفات مستوحاة من التراث المصري القديم، وأطباق من المطبخ البدوي، إلى جانب عدد من أشهر الأكلات التي ارتبطت بالمائدة المصرية، ومن بينها (أم علي)، و(المندي)، و(الفتة المصرية)، و(المسقعة)، و(محشي الكرنب)، و(البامية باللحمة)، وغيرها من الأطباق التراثية»، وفق بيان لجمعية الحفاظ على السياحة الثقافية.
وضمت لجنة التحكيم نخبة من المتخصصين في مجال الطهي والضيافة، من بينهم الشيف حسام سليمان، رئيس مجلس إدارة جمعية الطهاة المصريين.
وحضر الفعاليات التي أقيمت في المعهد العالي للدراسات النوعية بميدان الحجاز، الدكتور خالد سعد، الخبير الأثري والمشرف على الطبق الفرعوني، وعدد من قيادات وأعضاء جمعية الحفاظ على السياحة الثقافية، من بينهم محمد الحسانين، رئيس مجلس الإدارة، ومحمد المنتصر، الأمين العام.
وأكدت الجمعية أن «المسابقة تأتي في إطار رؤيتها للحفاظ على عناصر التراث المصري، وإعادة تقديمها للأجيال الجديدة، مع ربط الموروث الغذائي بصناعة السياحة، كون الطعام أحد المكونات المهمة للهوية الثقافية، وأحد عناصر التجربة السياحية».
واستهدفت المسابقة «منح طلاب السياحة والفنادق فرصة عملية للتعرف على قيمة الأكلات المصرية التراثية، وتشجيعهم على تطوير طرق تقديمها والحفاظ على وصفاتها وذاكرتها المرتبطة بالبيئات والمناطق المختلفة في مصر»، وفق البيان.
وتتضمن الفعاليات التي تمتد إلى يوم 24 سبتمبر (أيلول) الحالي جلسة حوارية تتناول أهمية التراث المصري والحفاظ عليه، ودور المطبخ المصري بصفته أحد عناصر التراث والهوية، وكيفية توظيف هذا التراث في دعم السياحة والثقافة المصرية.
ويأتي مشروع «المطبخ المصري تراث وهوية» ضمن جهود جمعية الحفاظ على السياحة الثقافية لتوثيق الموروث الغذائي المصري والتعريف بأكلاته من مختلف مناطق مصر، وربط هذا التراث بصناعة السياحة والثقافة والهوية المصرية، بما يسهم في تقديم المطبخ المصري كأحد عناصر التجربة السياحية المصرية.
وتحرص مصر على تقديم أنماط متنوعة من السياحة، من بينها السياحة الثقافية والترفيهية والبيئية والعلاجية والرياضية وسياحة السفاري والمؤتمرات، وأطلقت وزارة السياحة والآثار برنامجاً ترويجياً في هذا الإطار بعنوان «مصر... تنوع لا يُضاهى».
وكان المتحف القومي للحضارة المصرية قد استضاف من قبل فعاليات حول الأكلات المصرية الشعبية والتراثية ضمن مبادرة «طبلية مصر»، وتقدمت مصر بملف لـ«اليونيسكو» لتسجيل الكشري المصري ضمن الأكلات المصرية الأصيلة، وبالفعل تم تسجيل «الكشري المصري» على القائمة التمثيلية للتراث الثقافي غير المادي بـ«اليونيسكو» عام 2025.

title: QMC launches ‘Nahj’ to promote responsible digital content
content:
Qatar Media Corporation (QMC) Wednesday launched the “Nahj” initiative to elevate digital content creation, reinforce national values and identity, and encourage responsible use of social media platforms.
The programme, unveiled under the slogan “Committed to Our Values,” is being implemented in partnership with Qatar University, various ministries, educational institutions and other relevant entities. It targets school and university students, content creators and the general public through meetings, seminars, workshops and digital platforms over three months.
Mohammed bin Sal’an al-Marri, supervisor of the Nahj initiative, said the corporation launched the programme out of its sense of responsibility towards society and the digital sphere.
“The goal is to support the creation of responsible content that upholds national values and identity while promoting the conscious use of digital platforms,” he said.
He explained that the initiative rests on four core messages: taking pride in one’s identity, upholding responsibility for the spoken and written word, delivering content that adds value, and fostering national pride. “While platforms may change and evolve, the values governing one’s presence remain constant; every published word carries responsibility, and every piece of content presented can leave an impact on both the individual and society,” al-Marri noted.
He added that Nahj aims to cultivate content creators equipped with the knowledge, skills and adaptability needed to keep pace with digital transformations while producing material that befits society and the nation, content that upholds its morals, values and authentic national identity. The initiative will feature direct engagements with content creators as well as seminars and workshops aligned with its messages and objectives.
Al-Marri expressed pride in the Nahj ambassadors, academics, media professionals and content creators, who convey the initiative’s message through their expertise and influential presence. He highlighted Qatar University’s role in hosting the launch as a national academic venue that reinforces knowledge’s role in serving society. He invited the public to follow Qatar Media Corporation’s accounts for updates and materials produced by the Digital Media Office.
In a statement to reporters, he stressed that Nahj serves as a gateway to knowledge and informed engagement with digital content by promoting positive material and inviting academics, researchers and content creators to participate.
The programme seeks to raise awareness of risks in the digital sphere, enhance the ability to distinguish between positive and negative content, and support responsible interaction with platforms.
A panel discussion at the launch featured specialists who addressed key issues in digital content creation and creators’ responsibilities. Participants emphasised the importance of awareness when navigating the digital space, the ability to distinguish between positive and negative content, and the need for self-regulation among creators and users.
They also discussed the role of influencers in shaping messages based on a clear vision and positive impact that reinforces national values, identity and belonging while preserving cultural and societal privacy.
Dr Abdulrahman al-Harmi, a media personality and educational consultant, focused on the responsibility of handling digital content and the need to verify it, viewing this as a religious duty as much as a societal one.
He noted that one’s mindset forms gradually and can lead to either refinement or moral bankruptcy, depending on the path taken. “A fundamental challenge today is that minds are being shaped in the digital realm,” he said, calling for intellectual protection for the current generation and urging families and society to fulfil their roles in guiding the rising generation.
Dr Talib al-Athba, a lecturer in the Department of Mass Communication at Qatar University, emphasised that social media influencers must conduct themselves responsibly given the wide reach of their content. He called for self-regulation among both influencers and users, particularly as the digital landscape is often dominated by trends that lack inherent value.
“The decision maker in choosing content is the user himself, which requires him to choose what is useful... and to realise that the positive word is what remains,” he said, adding that responsibility extends beyond production to the messages carried and their impact.
Dr Aisha Jassim al-Kuwari, CEO of Rosa Publishing House and a media consultant, stressed the need to maintain the right approach, adhere to values and national identity, and take pride in the Arabic language and our belonging. “These are interconnected elements in creating content that expresses society and preserves its privacy,” she said.
She noted that the challenge with the Arabic language lies not in the language itself but in presenting it in ways that appeal to young people, and that the local dialect is an extension of Arabic that should be reintroduced in innovative ways.
Fidaa al-Din Yahya, one of the initiative’s ambassadors, said digital platforms make communication easier and have become a path to fame. He noted how money and audiences shape an influencer’s psychology, warning that the self can become preoccupied with financial gain. He underscored the importance of integrity in one’s words as a fundamental quality that content creators must uphold.

title: Great Mosque of Rome exhibition brings a message of dialogue to Doha
content:
An immersive exhibition on Rome’s Great Mosque opened in Doha on Monday, with Italy’s ambassador to Qatar saying architecture can bridge religious and cultural communities and strengthen dialogue during an uncertain time in the region.
Ambassador Paolo Toschi said “the whole idea” behind the exhibition is rooted in “the concept of dialogue and of bridging religious backgrounds and cultures”.
Hosted at the Museum of Islamic Art, The Great Mosque of Rome – Immersive Experience takes visitors into architect Paolo Portoghesi’s work through an immersive documentary and virtual-reality exploration.
The Embassy of Italy in Qatar promoted the project in collaboration with Qatar Museums and Qatar Foundation, with support from Sapienza University of Rome and the Islamic Cultural Centre of Italy.
For Toschi, presenting the exhibition in Doha carries particular significance. He said the city is “increasingly a capital” that welcomes people who embrace its cultural diversity, while praising “the leadership and the vision of Qatari authorities”.
“I want to acknowledge the vision of Qatar Museums and the leadership of Sheikh Al-Mayasa, Her Excellency, who hosted us at the Museum of Islamic Art,” he said.
“We’ve seen a huge amount of interest, a full house tonight,” Toschi said. “People are eager to learn about a monument of contemporary architecture in Rome that speaks to the bonds between our communities, Islam, Christianity and other religious communities that can coexist in peace.”
The exhibition also reflects Italy’s commitment to cultural diplomacy. “The Embassy of Italy is very committed to cultural diplomacy,” Toschi said, calling it “a key mission that we undertake every month and every season”.
He said cultural initiatives become meaningful “at times of uncertainty in the region”, when messages of dialogue and unity can help bring people together.
“Our aim is often to bring here the top Italian contents that can inspire,” Toschi said, pointing to the “great deal of enthusiasm and warm reception” from the public.
The immersive installation allows visitors to engage with the mosque through digital storytelling and VR, offering a closer look at its spaces and craftsmanship. The exhibition is scheduled to remain at the Museum of Islamic Art until November 21.
For Toschi, the evening’s crowded galleries offered a clear sign of the exhibition’s reception. “People were standing up and able to take a seat,” he said. “It makes me very happy, very grateful, and we will continue on this path.”

title: Iran mobilisation drive extends to children under 15
content:
Four years have passed since Zhina Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old woman who had travelled to Tehran to visit family, died after being detained by the morality police.
She could never have imagined how her name would appear on walls, streets and university campuses, or on the lips of millions of Iranians, or how three simple words, “Woman, Life, Freedom,” would become one of the most enduring slogans in Iran’s modern history.
The story of 2022 is not only the story of a slogan. It is the story of the price thousands paid to break through the wall of fear.
Zhina’s death on September 16, 2022, sparked protests across Iran. Human rights organizations documented live ammunition and pellet fire, mass arrests, torture, sexual violence and the killing of protesters. HRANA later recorded protests in all 31 provinces, 160 cities and 143 universities, and reported at least 530 people killed, including 68 children and teenagers.
Nika Shakarami and Sarina Esmailzadeh were both sixteen. Kian Pirfalak was nine, remembered for “In the name of the God of the rainbow” and the small boat he built with his own hands. Khodanour Lojei, a 27-year-old Baluch man, lives on in videos of him dancing, alongside the haunting image of him with his hands tied to a pole and water placed before him while in detention.
Their stories were different, but each became part of the collective memory of Woman, Life, Freedom.
Then came the gallows. Mohammad Mehdi Karami, a 22-year-old karate champion, was executed after being sentenced in connection with the fortieth-day commemoration for Hadis Najafi. Seyed Mohammad Hosseini, who worked at a poultry farm and taught martial arts to disadvantaged children for free, was executed the same day; human rights reports say his confessions were obtained under torture. Majidreza Rahnavard, executed only 23 days after his arrest, asked before his death that people not cry at his grave but celebrate and play happy music.
These names are reminders that behind every statistic was a family.
The repression did not end with the street protests. Students, schoolchildren, journalists, artists, athletes and activists were arrested. Families sometimes went weeks or months without news. Some detainees appeared in televised “confessions” that human rights organizations said were tainted by torture. Families seeking the truth about those killed also faced pressure. Others eventually left Iran after imprisonment, threats and persecution, carrying the cost of the uprising into exile, lost careers, interrupted education and separation from family.
And yet one of the movement’s deepest legacies is visible in an ordinary scene: a woman walking down an Iranian street without compulsory hijab.
The state responded with fines, vehicle seizures, arrests, flogging, business closures, cameras and surveillance. But women’s defiance continued. Four years after Zhina’s death, a woman without compulsory hijab is no longer the exceptional image it was in September 2022; it has become part of Iran’s social reality.
That is also where the connection to Dey 1404 (December 2025 and January 2026) becomes important.
The new protests began amid the collapse of the currency, inflation and protests by Tehran bazaar merchants, but quickly moved beyond economic demands. According to HRANA data cited in a UK government report, by January 27 at least 656 gatherings had been recorded in 201 cities across all 31 provinces, compared with 160 cities during the 1401 protests.
There are no reliable data to compare total participation, but the later uprising was documented across more cities and had a far higher reported toll. By March 2026, HRANA had recorded information on more than 7,000 people killed and more than 53,000 arrested in connection with the Dey and Bahman protests, far above the Iranian government’s figures.
HRANA described the confirmed cases as the minimum it could verify, with thousands more still awaiting review. Internet shutdowns, pressure on families and the lack of independent access inside Iran made the full scale harder to establish.
But the difference was not only scale. The society that entered January 2026 was not the same society that had existed before September 2022.
Iranians had lived through a national experience of disobedience, broken taboos, solidarity, bullets, prison, executions, migration and grief.
Abolfazl Hajizadegan’s research on “The Lives of Dey,” based on the social-media traces of 957 of those killed, found people from widely different professions and backgrounds, from baristas, repair workers and sports coaches to lawyers, professors, filmmakers and musicians.
The uprising also entered families in ways that made the breadth of the upheaval painfully visible.
Mehdi Shafiei, 44, and his 18-year-old son Mani were killed in Eslamshahr less than two hours apart. In Bushehr, 37-year-old nurse Mansoureh Heydari and her husband, Behrouz Mansouri, were both killed, leaving behind two children. Elsewhere, fathers and daughters were arrested together.
This does not mean that the 1401 and 1404 uprisings were identical, or that all protesters shared one ideology, leader or vision of Iran’s future. Their immediate triggers were different. But something had changed in society’s relationship with fear.
Repression continued, but the memory of disobedience could not simply be erased. Hajizadegan’s research suggests that those who came into the streets in 1404 did not acquire their anger overnight. Their earlier posts showed dissatisfaction and protest stretching back through previous protest waves, including the November 2019 protests and the 2022 uprising.
Dey 1404 was therefore not simply the explosion of an economic crisis. It was part of a longer accumulation of experience. Perhaps this is one of the most important legacies Woman, Life, Freedom left behind: not a single organization or leadership, but a social experience of the possibility of saying “no.”
The government’s response in Dey 1404 was severe. From January 8, the internet was almost completely shut down. Amnesty International reported widespread killings, mass arrests, enforced disappearances, torture and systematic pressure on victims’ families.
Yet behind every new number was another life: Hamid Mahdavi, Mohammad Jabbari, Mehdi and Mani, Mansoureh and Behrouz, just as Nika, Sarina, Kian and Khodanour had been lives, not statistics, four years earlier.
From September 2022 to January 2026, the names and faces changed and the sparks were different, but each chapter left something for the next: memory, wounds, language, courage and sometimes hope.
Zhina is not only the name of a young woman, and Woman, Life, Freedom is not merely the name of a few months of protest. It became part of the social and political language of a generation that paid an extraordinarily heavy price and emerged with a different understanding of choice, dignity and the possibility of standing firm.
Zhina and thousands of others killed in Iran’s protest movements are no longer with us. But something of them remains: in the hair of a woman who chooses not to cover it; in a mother who refuses to let her child’s name be erased; in a father who rejects the official account of his son’s death; in a family that dances at a loved one’s grave despite threats; and in a generation that has not abandoned its questions about freedom, dignity and the future.
Repression can empty the streets for a time, but it cannot erase what a generation has lived through.

title: Meet UAE gemologist who travels to mines, through rivers, to find precious stones
content: What Fatma Almheiri remembers most about her trip to Sri Lanka's Ratnapura region, home to some of the world's finest sapphire deposits, was not crossing a river with a powerful current, nor even the demanding work at the mine site that followed. What she remembers most is how it ended: leeches."To some people, such journeys may look like adventures," she says of her travels. "But to me, they are an essential part of understanding a gemstone. When you see for yourself the environment it comes from and the conditions in which people work to recover it, your perception of that same gemstone changes completely when you later see it displayed in the window of a luxury jewellery store."Stay up to date with the latest news. Follow KT on WhatsApp Channels.Inside the mine: Almheiri inspecting the rock face firsthand, where gemstones begin their journeyThis is what separates Almheiri from most people in her field. The Emirati field gemologist, gemstone dealer, jewellery designer, and certified trainer founded Fatma Almheiri Jewellery Art in 2009. She has trained more than 400 students and professionals, and has completed nearly 38 field trips across more than seven countries in Africa, Asia and Europe. She holds a Graduate Gemologist (G.G.) qualification alongside several professional certifications in diamond and gemstone evaluation, jewellery design, and gemstone cutting.And it all began with a drawing.At a sapphire mine in Africa, 2019A question that changed everythingUnable to find a jewellery design she had in mind, Almheiri drew it herself. The drawing led to a question, the question led to a diploma in jewellery design, then a G.G. qualification in gemology. But the laboratory was not enough. "My curiosity eventually took me from the design table into mines and fieldwork," she says. Ethiopia in 2014 was the first stop."I have always loved to introduce myself as a daughter of the desert and the granddaughter of a pearl diver," she says, which is an accurate description. Almheiri descends into mines the way her grandfather descended into the sea, guided by curiosity and the belief that what lies beneath the surface is worth the journey.At the Mahenge spinel mine, TanzaniaThe stone that money cannot valueTwelve years and nearly 38 field trips later, ask Almheiri about the most valuable stone she has ever handled and she will not name a sapphire or a diamond. She will tell you about a garnet. "It was the first gemstone I ever extracted from the earth with my own hands. Its value cannot be measured by price. It represents the moment when my knowledge changed from something I studied into something I experienced." Behind that garnet is a lesson she carries into every transaction: a parcel of rough garnet that revealed spinel after cutting proved that rough gemstones hide what the eye alone cannot see.At an aquamarine mine in Tanzania, 2024The country she carries with her, and the path she built aloneFamily has been Almheiri's most consistent source of support, but she carries a second source of belonging into every country she visits. "Wherever I travel, I proudly carry my identity as an Emirati." Encountering Emirati projects operating across several African countries affected her deeply. The Sharjah Chamber of Commerce and Industry, through the UAE Jewellers initiative, has opened local and international platforms for her and other Emirati talents. "To be Emirati today means coming from a country that has created extraordinary space for us to dream."In a field with almost no Arab predecessors, Almheiri says the absence of a role model was never an obstacle. "On the contrary, it motivated me to create my own path." The title "first Arab field gemologist" is one she uses with precision: no international body formally awards it, but her journey speaks for itself.Ruby mine, Africa 2024Five steps, one ruleFor any young woman considering this field, Almheiri is clear: education first, then practical experience, market exposure, learning from established experts, and finally fieldwork to understand the true journey of a gemstone from the earth. Her advice does not change:"Study first. In the gemstone world, knowledge is not simply an advantage. It is what protects you and builds your credibility and reputation over the long term."'Emirati women are strong': Senior citizens recall their vital role in supporting menLook: UAE woman quits job to turn Emirati heritage into handcrafted dolls'Rode to find myself': Meet the UAE woman who biked to 27 countries

title: NT Aboriginal leaders' resignations come with an explosive exit note
content:
analysis
String of NT Aboriginal leaders resign, claiming CLP government policies are 'dividing' Territorians
After resigning from her position as the boss of Aboriginal Housing Northern Territory this week, Leeanne Caton came out swinging.
Her target: the NT's Country Liberal Party (CLP) government, which was elected in a landslide in 2024 on a mandate to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour.
Since the CLP's election, it has overhauled laws on bail, youth criminal responsibility and child protection, and given police a range of new powers.
NT Police say the territory has been recording lower crime rates following the changes.
But Ms Caton said she believed this was all done without listening to Aboriginal leadership.
"The reason why I'm leaving is basically every piece of legislation that gets put through has a negative impact directly on Aboriginal people," the Kalkadoon-Waanyi woman told ABC Radio Darwin.
"It's killing my spirit.
"I just can't stand to see what's happening to Aboriginal Territorians in this environment at the moment."
The straw that broke the camel's back for Ms Caton was the handling of the future of a Darwin homeless shelter, which is being shifted to the regional town of Batchelor.
The departure of the peak body boss is the latest in a string of resignations by Aboriginal leaders and organisations in the Territory over fraying relationships with the NT government.
Among them, the NT Children's Commissioner Shahleena Musk, independent chair of the NT Children and Families Tripartite Forum Rob McPhee, Darwin Waterfront Corporation chairman Richard Fejo, members of the NT Justice Policy Partnership and independent Arnhem Land parliamentarian, Yiŋiya Guyula.
All have made public statements about their decisions to quit and, while each has been for a different reason, they have all shared ideological opposition to the NT government's laws or policies, with most citing an inability to have their voices heard.
'Still considered flora and fauna'
Now back in the Arnhem Land bush, Mr Guyula was asked for his reaction to Ms Caton's resignation and the current relationship between Aboriginal leaders and the CLP.
"They are creating a significant divide that is harming the NT," he said.
"They are tearing us all apart by treating our people as though we are not human, as though we are … considered flora and fauna."
He described the CLP's move to relocate the homeless shelter as "about dividing people in an attempt to push our people out of Darwin".
"It just does more harm to everyone," he said.
Former NT Labor politician and long-term First Nations advocate Scott McConnell said he feared diminishing trust between Aboriginal groups and the government was damaging the jurisdiction's future prospects.
"The geography of the NT is vast [but] the community is very small," he said.
"Governments need to stop dividing us based on race and geography and remember we have one shared future.
"I am very concerned that prominent leaders I know, trust and respect are finding the current environment so difficult they are leaving the front line.
"We all need to continue to support these fighters."
CLP government denies division
The NT's Acting Chief Minister Gerard Maley has fiercely defended the government's relationship with Aboriginal people and communities following the resignations.
Mr Maley also said his government stood by its continued focus on stamping out crime.
"We are listening to Aboriginal people," he said in a press conference on Friday.
"We work with many, many Aboriginal organisations right across the NT.
"And we need to work with them because we need to make sure the Aboriginal sector continues because there are a lot of Aboriginal people here.
"We want to make sure [their] safety is also our number one priority, and we're going to work with anyone we can to make sure that happens."
Mr Maley took issue with a question about why Aboriginal people were shut out of the conversation around the homeless shelter's move to Batchelor.
"We've been working with all sorts of organisations about that," he said.
In her parting shots at the NT government, Ms Caton vehemently disagreed: “It’s [been] disrespect and a lack of courtesy all round.”
Despite the vocal criticism and walk-outs, the government continues its mission towards a safer territory; no matter who argues against the way it’s going about it.

title: 10 Public Artworks to See Across the US This Fall
content:
10 Public Artworks to See Across the US This Fall
Camille Henrot’s pack of dogs take Central Park, Wanda Raimundi-Ortiz leads a procession through Philadelphia, and Sara Genn paints the sky in Santa Fe.
The best things in life are free, as Janet Jackson and Luther Vandross once sang. While a $30 museum ticket goes against that age-old ethos, we can rejoice this fall in the wealth of free public art sprouting across New York City and beyond. Some of the artists behind these highlighted interventions seek to ground us in our environments, while others transport us to new realities altogether. Some stoke newfound appreciations for what's always been right in front of us, and others ask us to consider how and why things could be different.
Jane D. Marsching recognizes trees as historic witnesses in Boston's Hyde Park neighborhood, and Camille Henrot makes her public art debut at Central Park with "Dogs" (2026). In a major outdoor activation in St. Louis, Kite invokes Lakȟóta cosmology through geometric symbols and other signifiers. And in Philadelphia, a procession led by Wanda Raimundi-Ortiz will channel different experiences of migration from a diasporic Puerto Rican perspective. With an overarching emphasis on art for everybody, these site-specific installations, public performances, and interactive experiences infuse our daily routines with moments of curiosity, contemplation, and comedic relief.
New York City
Julien Creuzet, "Nos diables rouges, nos dérives commotions (...) danse papillon"
Midnight Moment at Times Square, Broadway from 41st to 49th Street, Theater District, Manhattan
Nov. 1–Nov. 30
In this video work, the French-Caribbean artist introduces a horned and masqueraded figure evoking the red devils that course through the streets during Fat Tuesday (Mardi Gras) — the festive peak of Martinique’s Carnival. Reflecting on how the devils’ annual appearance opens a channel to buried histories and lost worlds, Creuzet’s anonymized protagonist is juxtaposed with the tales of Saint George and the dragon, and Perseus and Andromeda, in a fluid exchange of significance and veneration.
Amol K. Patil, "The Voices Cast in Dust"
The High Line at 24th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan
Oct. 2026–Sept. 2027
Along 24th Street on the High Line, a monumental cast-bronze sculpture ensnares a quarrel between humans in a singular, hapless mass in which desperate limbs jut outwards in an effort to move upward or make a lateral escape. Finding parallels between the struggles of the working class and marginalized people of Mumbai and New York, Patil’s sculpture highlights the urban labor landscape’s contradictory dichotomy of growth through cooperative effort and a ruthless, everyone-for-themselves mentality.
Christopher Williams, "MODEL (High Line Billboard, 18th Street and 10th Avenue, New York, 10011)"
The High Line Billboard, 18th Street and 10th Avenue, Chelsea, Manhattan
September–November 2026
It is what it is, until it isn’t … Christopher Williams continues his decades-long media criticism with the word MODEL, which appears as if it’s been ripped off the headline of a heavily retouched editorial photoshoot, blown up, and pasted on the High Line’s billboard. Only, it’s not that. Williams’s rendering of the word reveals unsettling evidence of the human hand and unrefined textures that subtly contrast with the gleaming high-rises that serve as the billboard’s glamorous backdrop.
Camille Henrot, "Dogs"
Doris C. Freedman Plaza, Central Park, Manhattan
Through Aug. 29, 2027
As the artist’s first public exhibition in New York City, Dogs holds a mirror to the concrete jungle’s ballooning obsession with canine culture through a variety of sculptures that start as zany and endearing, but reveal themselves as dimensional probes into the nature of attachment, domestication, and dependency. Across a variety of hard, weather-resistant materials, Henrot’s sculptures invoke noteworthy references to dogs across history, pop culture, society, and media in a sustained exploration of the species’ traits of loyalty and sociability.
Across the US
Tom Burr, "Roses"
Counterpublic House, St. Louis, Missouri
Sept. 10–Dec. 12
Contrary to the name, there aren't any flowers in Tom Burr’s rose-named installation behind the Counterpublic Triennial’s HQ in St. Louis. Instead, the conceptual artist gestures beyond the garden bed, bringing park infrastructure, rose-tinted mirrors, and chain-link fences in dialogue with queer history-at-a-slant, drawing upon the legacy of Rose Williams, the institutionalized sister of the openly gay playwright, Tennessee Williams.
Kite, "Wíhaŋyablapi (of St. Louis)"
Tower Grove Park, St. Louis, Missouri
Sept. 10–Dec. 12
Across Lakȟóta quillwork and beadwork, intricate geometric patterns emerge in an accretive process, tapping into a deep cultural reservoir between minute human action and the cosmos. Oglála Lakȟóta artist, composer, and performer Kite renders these patterns on a massive scale with boulders and plants for this new outdoor sculpture commissioned by Counterpublic.
Jane D. Marsching, "Tree Care"
Hyde Park, Boston, Massachusetts
Sept. 10–Nov. 8
The trees of Hyde Park have seen a lot, including the training of the first all-Black army unit in the Northern states during the Civil War, the 1870s Women’s March and Vote, and tensions over school desegregation in the 1970s. As a range of environmental factors now threaten to reduce the longstanding urban canopy, Jane D. Marsching tags 1,000 trees in Boston’s southernmost neighborhood with a textile tag encouraging the public to view each tree as an indispensable community member.
Sara Genn, "Ladder to the Sky"
SITE Santa Fe, Santa Fe, New Mexico
Oct. 16–Jan.11, 2027
Sara Genn’s monochromatic gradient paintings are satisfying in the same way that a paint swatch strip at Benjamin Moore is — and in more ways, of course. Ahead of her first solo institutional exhibition, How to Build a Sky, Genn splashed an exterior wall of SITE Santa Fe with a blue gradient mural that flows seamlessly into the azure New Mexico sky.
Saif Azzuz, "Entryways"
Institute of Contemporary Art (ICA), Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
Sept. 26–Sept. 12, 2027
We often first see a museum through its windows. As part of the ICA’s Entryways series, Yurok artist Saif Azzuz paints renditions of Philadelphia’s natural environment directly on the museum’s windows, drawing upon his work based on Indigenous symbolisms and northern California plant life.
Wanda Raimundi-Ortiz, "Vámonos pa’l monte (Let’s Go to the Mountains)"
Philadelphia City Hall, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
October 17
Inspired by the migration stories that undergird the Puerto Rican diaspora, Wanda Raimundi-Ortiz leads a festive four-mile processional performance from Philadelphia’s City Hall to Norris Square Park. Like the Puerto Rican-inspired garments she adds or sheds along her route, various members of the public are expected to filter in and out throughout the celebration, reflecting the diverse paths within migration.

title: Federal government urged not to let fire ant eradication funding lapse
content:
States urge federal government to fund next tranche of fire ant eradication
In short:
Advocates are urging the federal government to commit to funding the next step of the National Fire Ant Eradication Program in the next budget.
State and federal agriculture ministers have agreed total eradication of the pests remained "technically feasible, cost beneficial and in the national interest".
What's next?
Funding for the current eradication plan expires in June 2027.
Advocates are urging state and federal treasurers to fund the next step of fire ant eradication efforts, with a funding cliff looming in June next year.
State and federal agriculture ministers met last week to discuss the National Red Imported Fire Ant Eradication Program Response Plan 2027-32.
Queensland Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrett presented the potential impacts and consequences of wider proliferation of fire ants.
Eradication of the pests was deemed to remain "technically feasible, cost beneficial and in the national interest".
Ministers "agreed to consult their respective governments on funding and come back together for a final decision" ahead of next year's budget.
Loading...'Turning of the tide'
Invasive Species Council (ISC) advocacy director Reece Pianta said the program was beginning to see a "turning of the tide" in fighting the spread of fire ants.
"We've seen 208,000 hectares, an area almost the size of the ACT, transition from the suppression zone into active eradication," Mr Pianta said.
"Fire ants removed from the Murray-Darling Basin in northern New South Wales, no new nests detected in central Queensland."
Mr Pianta said if the ants got out of control they would cause more than $2 billion in economic damage each year. ISC modelling suggests the eradication program would cost $1 billion over five years.
He said the track record of funding for the program was "pretty scary", and that the last funding gap in 2023 saw efforts move backwards.
"What that resulted in was about a 40 per cent increase in the fire ant infestation zone. It grew from around 600,000 hectares to about 850,000," he said.
He said another funding gap in the program could see governments lose the chance to eradicate the pests completely.
The ISC urged governments to ensure funding for the next "really crucial" phase of the program.
"There's a responsible program in the field now, the community is backing it," Mr Pianta said.
"We need our governments to fund it to complete its work.
"For our treasurers and finance ministers around the country, the cost-benefit analysis is clearly in favour of paying to complete eradication right now."
Mr Perrett told state parliament in June that fire ants remained "one of Australia's most significant biosecurity threats" as he announced $10.5 million in state funding for suppression efforts in 2026-27.
"Primary producers have strongly supported the suppression efforts because they understand what is at stake … sugarcane, nursery, turf and hay know that fire ants threaten their industries, and more broadly agricultural production, regional economies, and our way of life," he said.
"Noting that a new response plan is being negotiated for the nationally cost-shared program, I again call on the federal government and cost share partners to include fire ant suppression within the next response plan."
Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins has been contacted for comment.
Program aims to strangle spread
Fire ant eradication works by mixing insect growth inhibitor with corn grit, which is then carried to the queen by worker ants.
The bait stunts the growth of the queen, who then cannot produce new worker ants, and the colony collapses.
The biosecurity zone map covers Brisbane, Logan, and Ipswich, and reaches as far north as the Sunshine Coast and south into northern New South Wales, with isolated hotspots across the south-east.
Any materials such as soil or hay being moved from these areas must go through strict biosecurity measures to ensure no fire ants are onboard.
The National Fire Ant Eradication Program targets properties in a broad band known as an "eradication area" around a fire ant "suppression zone", which covers a large corner of south-east Queensland, including Brisbane.
The goal is to treat every property in the eradication area up to six times over a two-year period, before contracting the zone and targeting a new set of properties.
That band is intended to shift gradually toward Brisbane and the coast, strangling the ants' spread.
Properties not within the eradication zone will not be specifically targeted, but residents can contact the Fire Ant Suppression Taskforce and work with them to treat fire ants found on their properties.
Areas are monitored for five years following treatment to ensure fire ants do not return.

title: مصر.. 4 "قيصرية" من بين كل 5 ولادات
content:
اقتربت الولادات القيصرية في مصر من نسبة 80 بالمئة من إجمالي الولادات، في معدل مرتفع دفع وزارة الصحة إلى تكثيف تحركاتها للحد من العمليات غير المبررة طبيا، وإعادة تصميم منظومة رعاية الأم والطفل.
وقالت نائبة وزير الصحة والسكان لشؤون السكان وتنمية الأسرة عبلة الألفي، إن معدل الولادات القيصرية ارتفع من 51.8 بالمئة عام 2014 إلى 72.2 بالمئة عام 2021، ثم بلغ نحو 79 بالمئة وفق أحدث البيانات التي عرضتها عن الوضع حتى نهاية 2025.
ونقلت صحف عن الألفي قولها إن معدل القيصريات في مصر بات يدور حول 80 بالمئة، مما يعني أن نحو 4 من كل 5 ولادات تنتهي بعملية جراحية.
وتظهر الأرقام الرسمية السابقة أن الزيادة ليست طارئة، إذ قفزت نسبة الولادات القيصرية بأكثر من 20 نقطة مئوية بين عامي 2014 و2021.
ووفق نتائج المسح الصحي للأسرة المصرية لعام 2021 الذي أجراه الجهاز المركزي للتعبئة العامة والإحصاء، بلغت نسبة الولادات القيصرية 72.2 بالمئة على مستوى البلاد.
وسجل المسح تفاوتا واضحا بين المحافظات، كما كشف عن فجوة بين المنشآت الصحية الحكومية والقطاع الخاص.
لماذا تتحرك وزارة الصحة؟
أكدت الألفي أن الهدف الحكومي ليس رفض الولادة القيصرية في حد ذاتها، إذ تظل ضرورية في حالات طبية عديدة ويمكن أن تنقذ حياة الأم أو الطفل، وإنما تقليل العمليات التي تجرى من دون مبرر طبي.
وأضافت أن نحو 97 بالمئة من الولادات في مصر تتم داخل منشآت صحية، مما يجعل تغيير الممارسات داخل المستشفيات وتدريب الكوادر ومتابعة معدلات القيصرية عناصر رئيسية في خطة خفض العمليات غير الضرورية.
وتشمل التحركات الحكومية تطوير خدمات القبالة وتمريض التوليد، وتحسين الرعاية أثناء المخاض والولادة، ودعم الرضاعة الطبيعية والتلامس المباشر بين الأم والطفل عقب الولادة.
وتضع مبادرة "الألف يوم الذهبية" التابعة لوزارة الصحة، دعم الولادة الطبيعية وخفض القيصريات غير المبررة وتحسين صحة الأمهات وحديثي الولادة ضمن محاورها الأساسية.
وفيات حديثي الولادة
وأعادت تصريحات الألفي فتح النقاش بشأن صحة المواليد، بعدما قالت إن معدل وفيات حديثي الولادة ارتفع من 11 إلى 18 وفاة لكل ألف مولود، مشيرة إلى أن الوزارة تعمل على تحسين الرعاية قبل الولادة وأثناءها وبعدها.
ولا تثبت هذه الأرقام أن ارتفاع القيصريات تسبب مباشرة في زيادة وفيات المواليد، كما لم تعلن وزارة الصحة وجود علاقة سببية بين المؤشرين.
وتقول منظمة الصحة العالمية إن العملية القيصرية، عندما تكون ضرورية طبيا، يمكن أن تمنع وفيات ومضاعفات خطيرة لدى الأمهات والأطفال، لكنها مثل أي جراحة تحمل مخاطر قصيرة وطويلة الأمد، ولا توجد أدلة على فائدتها لمن لا يحتجن إليها طبيا.
ولا توصي المنظمة بنسبة موحدة للولادات القيصرية يتعين على جميع الدول أو المستشفيات تحقيقها. لكنها تشير إلى أن الدراسات السكانية رصدت انخفاضا في وفيات الأمهات والمواليد مع ارتفاع استخدام القيصرية حتى مستوى يقارب 10 بالمئة، من دون ظهور انخفاض إضافي في الوفيات عند تجاوز هذا المستوى.

title: طوق نجاة لمرضى السرطان.. عالم مصري يطور خلايا تدمر الأورام
content:
حقق عالم الفيزياء المصري أحمد الجندي، الأستاذ المشارك بقسم الفيزياء في جامعة تكساس في "إل باسو" بالولايات المتحدة، إنجازا علميا جديدا في مجال مكافحة الأورام السرطانية، بتكنولوجيا "النانو".
وحصل الجندي على ميدالية ماري كوري لعام 2026 على مساهماته في مجال لعلاج السرطان، حيث تمكن من تطوير نوع من الجسيمات النانوية المغناطيسية التي يمكن استخدامها لاستهداف الأورام الصلبة وتدميرها.
إلى أين وصلت التقنية؟
كشف أحمد الجندي عن أن البحث وصل حاليا إلى مراحل التجارب المعملية، إذ يتم دراسة الخواص الفيزيائية والكيميائية للمواد، بالإضافة إلى إجراء تجارب على الخلايا، وتطبيق التقنية على نموذجين من الحيوانات.
وأردف: "أجريت التجارب على فئران مصابة بسرطان الثدي والبروستاتا، وهناك اتجاه للتجريب على مزيد من الحيوانات المصابة بأنواع سرطان أخرى، وفي حالة نجاح التقنية بالكامل سيتم الانتقال للتجارب السريرية على البشر".
وأشار إلى إمكان استخدام تقنية النانو المغناطيسية في المستقبل إلى جانب العلاج الإشعاعي والكيماوي، وذلك بعد تعديل خصائص الجسيمات النانوية المغناطيسية، ليكون بإمكانها حمل المواد العلاجية لداخل الأورام.
وأكد على أنه في هذه الحالة سيكون بإمكان الجهات المعالجة أن تجمع بين أكثر من طريقة علاج أو "آلية دوائية"، فيكون التأثير الميكانيكي الناجم عن المجال المغناطيسي داعمًا للعلاج الكيميائي أو الإشعاعي المستخدم.
وذكر الجندي أن فريقه قام بدراسة العديد من العوامل، ومن ضمنها الخواص المغناطيسية والحرارية للجسيمات، وقوة المجال المغناطيسي وتردده، مشيرا إلى أنه بالإضافة إلى ذلك، درس الفريق القائم على الدراسة البحثية الجرعات المناسبة والتي تؤدي إلى إنتاج درجة حرارة يمكنها أن تؤثر في الخلايا السرطانية، وهو ما يعرف باسم "العلاج الحراري المغناطيسي"، عبر التقنيات النانوية.
من جانبه قال الأستاذ المساعد بقسم الأورام والاستشاري أحمد حامد، إن المختلف في التقنية الجديدة أنها تواجه الأورام الصلبة بتعريضها لمجال مغناطيسي متناوب، وهو ما يؤدي إلى تدميرها بأسلوب ترددي وجديد.
وأضاف، في تصريحات خاصة لموقع "سكاي نيوز عربية"، أن طريقة استخدام المجال المغناطيسي في استهداف الخلايا السرطانية تعد في حد ذاتها توجها عالميا وثورة في عالم الطب، عكس أسلوب تسخين الورم التقليدي.
حامد أوضح أنه وفقا لما تداولته المجلات العلمية حتى الآن- تعمل التقنية الجديدة من خلال خلق مجال مغناطيسي "ميكانيكي" لا يعتمد على توليد الحرارة داخل الورم، وبالتالي فإن المجال الترددي هو المسيطر.
وتابع: "المجال المغناطيسي يخلق قوة أو حركة ميكانيكية لجسيمات نانوية يتم وضعها داخل الخلية السرطانية، وهذه الحركة أو القوة الميكانيكية تؤدي إلى اضطراب في غشاء الخلية السرطانية، وهو ما يؤدي إلى تدميرها".
ولفت إلى أن هذا الاتجاه يعد مخالفا لما هو متعارف عليه من إدخال جسيمات للخلايا السرطانية وصناعة مجال مغناطيسي يؤدي إلى تسخينها، لذلك فهو قادر على تحقيق نتائج إيجابية أعلى من تلك الموجودة عالميا حاليا.
متى يمكن استخدام التقنية؟
من جانبه، قال طبيب الغدد وعلاج الأورام أحمد عبدالسلام وكيل، إن تقنية النانو المغناطيسية واعدة بالفعل، ومن المنتظر أن تحقق تقدمًا سريعًا ويتم من خلالها إنقاذ الملايين من مرضى الأورام بمختلف أنواعها.
ولكنه أكد في حديثه لموقع "سكاي نيوز عربية" على أنه في المرحلة الحالية لا يمكن تحديد موعد بدء التجارب السريرية، إذ إن البحث العلمي يلزم أصحاب الدراسة بمزيد من التجارب على الحيوانات للتأكد من عدة عوامل.
ومن بين هذه العوامل بحسب وكيل، درجات السلامة وتأثير الجسيمات النانوية في الخلايا غير المصابة بالسرطان (أي الخلايا السليمة)، فمن الوارد أن يكون للجسيمات تأثير في المرض، مصحوب بأثر سلبي في الصحة العامة.
بالإضافة إلى ذلك، يجب الحصول على موافقة هيئة الغذاء والدواء الأميركية "FDA" لبدء التجارب السريرية من خلال تقديم بيانات متكاملة عن مراحل الدراسة والتجارب على الحيوانات، وكلها أمور تستغرق وقتا طويلا.

title: Western Australia is experiencing a child safety crisis. Here’s what would help
content:
One of Australia’s most resource-rich regions, South Hedland in Western Australia, sits alongside a mining industry generating enormous wealth. This is in stark contrast to persistent social and economic disadvantage affecting parts of the local community, particularly among Aboriginal residents.
Much of this disadvantage has made headlines recently. Multiple media outlets are reporting a child safety crisis has emerged in the area.
Reports have focused on local tragedies, including the deaths of three children in 2022, and revelations about a reported “hellhole house” in Frisby Court where up to 15 children have reportedly been living with no adult supervision, in squalid conditions.
But the language of crisis implies something unexpectedly sudden. It suggests we were unaware of the issues, or what was needed to address them.
Yet Aboriginal women in the Pilbara were describing the conditions placing children at risk six years ago. They also offered solutions, but the response has not matched the level of need.
Dire warnings
In 2020, Aboriginal women told us about concerns in South Hedland. Throughout the Pilbara, Aboriginal women spoke to the Australian Human Rights Commission as part of the Wiyi Yani U Thangani (Women’s Voices) project, led by former Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner June Oscar.
South Hedland women described substance abuse, family and domestic violence, mental health concerns, racism, unemployment and housing issues.
They also spoke about children’s safety being compromised at times, with girls sometimes running away and wandering the streets alone.
Women in South Hedland called for practical responses, including a holistic healing centre for men who perpetrate violence and better access to substance abuse services. They described bureaucracy and waiting periods as barriers to treatment at the point where someone was ready to seek help.
While there has been some investment in the Pilbara since 2020, services are working in an extraordinarily complex environment, often with high demand and workforce pressures. Nowhere is this more evident than in child protection.
In 2024–25, 12,529 children were the subject of child protection investigations in Western Australia. About 41% of these concerned First Nations children.
More than half of the total investigations concerned children who had previously been involved with the system. This is a pattern evident nationally.
Repeated child protection involvement indicates substantial and persistent family need. It also highlights the limits of expecting the statutory child protection system to resolve these problems alone.
Is removal the best option?
Across Australia, families coming to the attention of child protection authorities are experiencing multiple, often overlapping challenges. These include family and domestic violence, mental health concerns, substance abuse, housing instability, poverty and unemployment.
While some may believe the answer lies in more child removals, evidence shows removal can create new risks and harms. For Aboriginal children, child removal also repeats the destructive cycle of disconnection from family, culture and community.
This is not to say that removal should never occur. Rather, with appropriate and accessible support, parents can often address concerns before they escalate, while extended family can step in where additional care is needed.
Sophisticated child safety responses must go beyond child protective services. Keeping children safe requires early, targeted support alongside practical and therapeutic responses to the reasons children end up in the protection system. The earlier these supports are provided, the greater the chance of success.
There are solutions
Recent events demand scrutiny and accountability. But tragedies in child protection also create a risk of policy being driven by outrage and the court of public opinion.
Aboriginal children’s safety matters. That we can all agree on. But how we achieve that safety requires a nuanced, considered approach, consistent with evidence and local, on-the-ground expertise from people living in their communities.
If the concerns for Aboriginal children’s safety are genuine, then the response must act on Aboriginal solutions, rather than imposing solutions on families and communities.
Aboriginal community-controlled organisations have demonstrated what is possible when appropriately resourced.
The Victorian Aboriginal Child and Community Agency has trialled an Aboriginal-led initiative to safely divert families away from the child protection system. The program achieved a 78% diversion rate.
Rather than close the report and wait for the next one, families were offered support to address the issues bringing them to child protection’s attention. This success demonstrates that Aboriginal solutions work.
Family-led decision-making offers another avenue. Evidence from South Australia indicates family decision-making can reduce substantiated child maltreatment and entry into out-of-home care.
WA has already taken steps in this direction. Yet five years after the Aboriginal Family-Led Decision-Making pilot began, it remains limited to two areas and is unavailable in the Pilbara.
The WA government’s commitment of $7.2 million over four years to continue the pilot represents important progress. However, there is an opportunity to expand it across Western Australia alongside greater investment in services families need before reaching crisis point.
Keeping children safe requires governments to invest in the conditions that make safety possible. No family decision-making forum can manufacture a house that doesn’t exist, a rehabilitation bed that is unavailable, or a mental health service that cannot be accessed.
We do not need another tragedy to tell us what Aboriginal communities need. They have already told us. It’s time we started listening, and acting on it.

title: ما تأكله اليوم قد يغير نومك الليلة.. دراسة تكشف السر
content:
قد لا يكون تعديل قائمة الطعام أول ما يخطر في البال عند البحث عن نوم أفضل، لكن دراسة حديثة تشير إلى أن زيادة الألياف خلال اليوم قد ترتبط بتغيرات قابلة للقياس في النوم خلال الليلة نفسها.
ولا تعني النتائج أن طبقا من الخضراوات يضمن نوما عميقا، أو أن وجبة واحدة تستطيع علاج الأرق. لكنها تضيف دليلا جديدا إلى الأبحاث التي تربط النظام الغذائي بجودة النوم ومراحله المختلفة.
الدراسة، المنشورة في دورية "نيتشر هيلث" مؤخرا، حللت 4793 ليلة مسجلة لنحو 3600 بالغ. وسجل المشاركون وجباتهم في الوقت الفعلي، بينما تابعت أجهزة قابلة للارتداء مدة نومهم ومراحله ومعدل ضربات القلب أثناء الليل.
ماذا وجدت الدراسة؟
ربط الباحثون ارتفاع كثافة الألياف في الطعام بزيادة محدودة في نسبة الوقت الذي يقضيه المشاركون في النوم العميق ونوم حركة العين السريعة، مقابل انخفاض الوقت المسجل في النوم الخفيف.
وبالأرقام، ارتبط تناول ألياف أكثر، مقارنة بإجمالي السعرات الحرارية، بزيادة النوم العميق بمقدار 0.59 نقطة مئوية، ونوم حركة العين السريعة بمقدار 0.76 نقطة مئوية، مع انخفاض النوم الخفيف بنحو 1.35 نقطة مئوية.
كما ارتبطت كثافة الألياف الأعلى بانخفاض متوسط معدل ضربات القلب أثناء الليل بمقدار 1.14 ضربة في الدقيقة.
ورصد الباحثون نتيجة مشابهة لدى الأشخاص الذين تناولوا أنواعا أكثر تنوعا من الأغذية النباتية الكاملة.
هذه الفروق صغيرة، لكنها لافتة لأنها ظهرت عند مقارنة الطعام المستهلك خلال اليوم بالنوم في الليلة نفسها. ومع ذلك، لا تثبت النتائج أن الألياف كانت السبب المباشر وراء التحسن، لأن الدراسة لم تكن تجربة عشوائية خاضعة للرقابة.
هل يجب تناول الألياف في العشاء؟
لم تثبت الدراسة أن تناول الألياف في وجبة العشاء أكثر فائدة من تناولها في الإفطار أو الغداء. وكانت النتيجة الأساسية مرتبطة بإجمالي ما تناوله المشاركون خلال اليوم، لا بوجبة محددة.
وفحص الباحثون أيضا توقيت الوجبات، ووجدوا أن تناول نسبة أكبر من السعرات الحرارية خلال الساعات الست السابقة للنوم ارتبط بزيادة مدة النوم بنحو 7.7 دقائق، لكنه ارتبط كذلك بارتفاع طفيف في معدل ضربات القلب ليلا.
وهذا يعني أن النوم مدة أطول لا يساوي بالضرورة نوما أفضل، كما أن النتائج لا تقدم مبررا لتناول وجبة كبيرة قبل التوجه إلى الفراش.
دراسة قديمة تدعم العلاقة
تتفق النتائج الجديدة جزئيا مع دراسة أجريت عام 2016 وشملت 26 بالغا يتمتعون بصحة جيدة. ووجدت أن تناول كمية أكبر من الألياف ارتبط بوقت أطول في النوم البطيء العميق، بينما ارتبطت الدهون المشبعة بنوم عميق أقل، والسكريات بمزيد من الاستيقاظ أثناء الليل.
لكن الدراسة القديمة كانت محدودة العدد، ولم تختبر ما إذا كان تناول الألياف في العشاء تحديدا يحسن النوم.
كيف يمكن تفسير العلاقة؟
يطرح الباحثون عدة تفسيرات محتملة، منها دور الألياف في دعم استقرار سكر الدم وتغذية البكتيريا النافعة في الأمعاء. وتنتج هذه البكتيريا مركبات قد تتفاعل مع عمليات عصبية واستقلابية مرتبطة بالنوم، لكن هذه الآلية لم تحسم بصورة نهائية.
وتوجد الألياف في الخضراوات والفواكه والبقوليات والحبوب الكاملة والمكسرات والبذور. وإضافتها تدريجيا إلى الوجبات قد تدعم الصحة العامة، لكن لا ينبغي التعامل معها كعلاج للأرق.
فالنتيجة الأوضح ليست أن عشاء واحدا سيضمن نوما عميقا، بل أن نمط الطعام اليومي قد يكون جزءا من معادلة النوم، إلى جانب انتظام مواعيده والنشاط البدني وتقليل المنبهات وتهيئة غرفة مناسبة للراحة.

title: Citizen search for Nannup Four gets underway
content:
Citizen search for Nannup Four begins in tough bushland in southern WA
In short:
A renewed search to find any trace of the Nannup Four has begun in WA's South West.
Chantelle McDougall and her daughter Leela have not been seen since their disappearance in July 2007, along with her partner Simon Kadwill and friend Tony Popic.
Ms McDougall's parents are hopeful, but realistic, about the potential for the search to provide long-awaited answers.
A group of citizen searchers will begin scouring a stretch of almost impenetrable wilderness in southern Western Australia this week to find answers in one of the country's most baffling missing persons cases.
Chantelle McDougall and her five-year-old daughter Leela vanished from the outskirts of Nannup in July 2007, along with her partner Simon Kadwill and their friend Tony Popic.
They've become known as the Nannup Four.
In the days after their disappearance, Ms McDougall's family were under the impression the four had emigrated to Brazil, but reported their daughter and grandchild missing when they failed to hear from them.
Their bank accounts were untouched, and their passports hadn't been used.
Loading...Mr Kadwill, whose real name is Gary Felton, was living under a stolen identity while running an online cult in which he espoused doomsday beliefs.
He had spoken of a plan to "wander into the wilderness" and carry out a murder-suicide.
A 2017 coronial inquest failed to determine if the four were dead or alive.
ABC investigation sparks new search
Following a long-running investigation, The ABC's Expanse: The Nannup Four uncovered police error, new details of coercive control and evidence pointing to a possible burial site.
Among the podcast's audience was Matt Strickland, an exploration geologist with a hand in a number of private searches for missing people.
He contacted the McDougall family and offered his assistance.
"There's not a lot I can say, but there's a lot I can do," Mr Strickland said.
Mr Strickland is the vice-president of Find Our Lost Loved Ones (FOLLO), a missing persons search team based in Tasmania.
It began with a successful volunteer-led search to find the remains of missing Belgian hiker Celine Cremer.
The group went on to locate the remains of another missing Tasmanian, Peter Willoughby, in May this year.
"We've managed to [solve] two missing persons cases in six months with very limited resources," Mr Strickland said.
"So we know it's possible."
Months of correspondence with Chantelle McDougall's uncle Barry McIntosh followed.
A retired Victorian police detective, Mr McIntosh has continued to probe his niece's disappearance, with a fresh search effort his long-term goal.
Call for volunteers
In August, Mr Strickland put a call out on ABC radio asking for people with bush experience to volunteer their time for the two-week search in WA's South West.
More than 40 volunteers signed on over the following weeks.
"We are going to be operating on what could potentially be a crime scene," Mr Strickland said.
"So we need to be responsible; we need to have responsible people there."
Despite previous success, he concedes the Nannup Four case brings significant additional challenges.
"The searches that we've had so far, we've been searching for people who were lost and probably died of exposure, and they wanted to be found," he said.
"In the case of the Nannup Four, it appears that they didn't want to be."
Where will the search focus be?
The search will focus on bushland near the WA town of Northcliffe, about 100km south of Nannup, where the group was living, and 350km south of Perth.
In the days surrounding the disappearance, either Mr Kadwill or Mr Popic purchased two bus tickets, with Northcliffe believed to be the final destination.
Three months later, in October 2007, prisoners carrying out track clearing in bushland near the town reported finding items of clothing and a "smell of death" in the area.
Police subsequently searched the area, but have since admitted they were in the wrong location.
A team of cadaver dogs were taken to the right location in 2024, where they picked up the scent of human remains.
The near-impenetrable terrain will also increase the complexity for the search teams.
"It's all regrown, and it's quite thick, and it is formerly a logging area," Mr Strickland said.
"So the ground itself … kind of chaotic would be one way of describing it."
A LiDAR drone survey to identify ground disturbances, and the same cadaver dog team used in 2024, will help assist the search effort.
Family grateful for help
The search will run for two weeks, with the key aim of finding any evidence of the four's remains or possessions in the area.
At its centre will be Jim and Cath McDougall, Chantelle's parents, who are driving across Australia from their home in regional Victoria to assist.
"I think it's absolutely amazing," Mrs McDougall said.
"I'm so grateful to all these people helping because for years it felt like we had no-one on our side trying to help us.
"I want to be really involved. I want to help search if I can, if I'm not a nuisance, and want to be there in amongst it all."
But after years of waiting for closure, Mrs McDougall is balancing the hope of finding answers with the reality she may never get them.
"We try not to get our hopes up too much," she said.
"Because over the years, we felt that all the little leads and things we had have come to a dead end, and we sort of still don't know anything.
"I'm just hoping we get some really good results."

title: Für leistbaren Wohnraum braucht es mehr als verschärfte Regeln für Airbnb
content:
Angesichts knapper werdenden leistbaren Wohnraums ist es eine gute Nachricht: Die Stadt Wien verschärft die Regeln für Airbnb & Co und führt ab 2027 eine Registrierungspflicht ein. Mit dem Register wird sichergestellt, dass Plattformen nur korrekt angemeldete Wohnungen anbieten können. Außerdem wird damit endlich ein valider Überblick über den Markt der Kurzzeitvermietung in Wien ermöglicht.
David Krutzler
Für leistbaren Wohnraum braucht es mehr als verschärfte Regeln für Airbnb
Die Registrierungspflicht bei Kurzzeitvermietung ist ein Schritt in die richtige Richtung. Wien muss aber auch Maßnahmen für die Mobilisierung von Leerstand setzen

title: Tiere im Tiefkühler - Unfassbare Zustände: Über 75 Katzen in Wohnung
content:
Tiere im Tiefkühler
Unfassbare Zustände: Über 75 Katzen in Wohnung
Was sich in einer kleinen Pariser Sozialwohnung abspielte, schockiert selbst erfahrene Tierschützer: Mehr als 75 Katzen wurden dort unter offenbar völlig untragbaren Bedingungen entdeckt. In der Tiefkühltruhe fanden Helfer zudem tote Kätzchen.
Nach der Zwangsräumung der Wohnung im 15. Stadtbezirk baten Polizei und ein Gerichtsvollzieher den Tierschutzverein YouCare um Unterstützung, wie die Zeitung „Le Parisien“ berichtete. „In der Tiefkühltruhe wurden außerdem tote Kätzchen gefunden“, sagte Vereinsvorsitzender Thomas Moreau am Montag.
Einige Tiere in Tierklinik
Die Katzen seien unter „unerträglichen Zuständen“ gehalten worden. Einige der Tiere mussten in eine Tierklinik gebracht werden. Weil der Verein nicht alle Katzen gleichzeitig aufnehmen konnte, wurde ein Hilfeaufruf gestartet.
Rund 30 Katzen mussten zunächst in der Wohnung bleiben. Helferinnen und Helfer kümmern sich dort täglich um die Tiere.
Hinweis auf Tiersammelsucht
Nach Einschätzung des Vereinsvorsitzenden handelt es sich wahrscheinlich um einen Fall von Tiersammelsucht. In Frankreich wird dafür auch der Begriff „Noah-Syndrom“ verwendet, angelehnt an die biblische Figur Noah und seine Arche.
Bei dem psychiatrischen Krankheitsbild sammeln Menschen eine große Zahl von Haustieren auf engem Raum, ohne in der Lage zu sein, die Tiere ausreichend zu versorgen, zu füttern oder medizinisch zu betreuen.

title: Patriarchat beenden - Männergewalt: So können wir Burschen „umerziehen“!
content:
Stärke. Ehre. Besitzanspruch. Noch immer prägen solche Werte das Bild von Männlichkeit – und fördern damit patriarchale Strukturen, die im schlimmsten Fall in Gewaltexzessen münden. Eine Kehrtwende ist längst überfällig. Wie wir sie genau jetzt schaffen und Burschen ein neues Rollenbild von Männlichkeit vermitteln können, zeigt ein aktueller Bericht auf.
Das Patriarchat: Wir stehen längst vor einem gesellschaftlichen Problem, das endlich an der Wurzel angepackt werden muss. SOS-Mitmensch hat sich dieser Mammutaufgabe in einem 52-seitigen Bericht angenommen. Dafür wurden elf Expertinnen und Experten aus Bildungsarbeit, Schule sowie Burschen- und Männerarbeit befragt.
Ja, wir können etwas ändern
Ihre klare Botschaft: Es gibt konkrete Möglichkeiten, Burschen von dem klassischen männlichen Rollenbild zu lösen – unter dem viele sogar selbst leiden. Dafür muss aber an vielen Punkten arbeiten: Selbstbewusstsein, Selbstbestimmung, soziale Kompetenz, Fürsorge, Kreativität und Kooperation.
Buben, die patriarchal auftreten und sich über Besitzdenken, Ehre und Gewalt definieren, sind ein erhebliches gesellschaftliches Problem, aber kein Naturgesetz.
Alexander Pollak, Sprecher von SOS Mitmensch
Gefühle normalisieren und darüber sprechen
Ein zentraler Punkt dabei: Burschen müssen lernen, über das zu reden, was in ihnen vorgeht – und das möglichst schon im frühkindlichen Alter. Der Bericht empfiehlt deshalb, das Reden über Gefühle und Bedürfnisse stärker in den Alltag zu integrieren. Auch soziales Lernen soll nicht bloß ein gelegentliches Projekt sein, sondern fixer Bestandteil des Unterrichts werden.
Kinder sollen zudem lernen, gemeinsam Regeln zu entwickeln, Verantwortung zu übernehmen und Konflikte auszutragen. Als konkrete Beispiele nennt der Bericht etwa Klassenräte, Morgenkreise und Fächer wie „Kommunikation-Kooperation-Konfliktlösung“.
Soziales Lernen ist das Um und Auf und muss von Anfang an trainiert und geübt werden.
AHS-Lehrer Patrick Osterkorn
Auch Gender- und Gleichstellungsbildung soll einen fixen Platz bekommen. Burschen sollen sich mit Rollenbildern auseinandersetzen und so lernen, dass es weit mehr als nur die eine Art gibt, ein Mann zu sein.
Der Mann von morgen: Fürsorglich, verletzlich, kooperativ
Dabei geht es laut Bericht aber nicht darum, Burschen ihre Männlichkeit auszureden. Im Gegenteil: Sie sollen mehr Möglichkeiten bekommen, sie selbst zu gestalten. Männer, die fürsorglich, verletzlich und kooperativ sind und Gleichberechtigung selbstverständlich leben, sollen zu zentralen Vorbildern werden.
Aber auch Frauen in gesellschaftlichen Führungspositionen sollen für Burschen sichtbar sein. So sollen Jugendliche erleben, dass Eigenschaften, Berufe und gesellschaftliche Rollen nicht automatisch an das Geschlecht gebunden sind.
Es braucht Räume, in denen Männlichkeit nicht auf Härte, Dominanz & Abwertung beruht, sondern sie Verlässlichkeit, Fürsorge und Gleichberechtigung erfahren.
Shokat Walizadeh, Geschäftsführer des Vereins „Neuer Start“
Ein weiterer wichtiger Punkt ist der Umgang mit problematischem Verhalten. Demnach sollten nicht Sanktionen im Vordergrund stehen, sondern viel mehr das Verhalten selbst hinterfragt und Bewegegründe aufgearbeitet werden. Dafür brauche es konkret mehr Beziehungsarbeit, Schulsozialarbeit und schulpsychologische Betreuung.
Auch nach einem Vorfall dürfe nicht einfach zur Tagesordnung übergegangen werden. Eine konsequente und transparente Aufarbeitung von Gewalt sei ein wichtiger Teil der Prävention.
Social-Media-Verbot für Kinder gefordert
Ein besonders brisantes Kapitel des Burschen-Berichts widmet sich den sozialen Medien. Die Expertinnen und Experten sehen dort einen wachsenden Einfluss problematischer Geschlechterbilder und Online-Misogynie und sprechen sich daher großteils sogar für ein Social-Media-Verbot für Kinder aus.
Bis es noch bessere Lösungen gibt, ist ein Verbot besser als so weiterzumachen wie bisher.
Simon Hirt, Sekundarstufen-Lehrer im WUK
Allerdings wird gleichzeitig betont: Ein Verbot allein sei kein Allheilmittel. Gefordert werden ebenso mehr Medienkompetenz, Unterstützung für Eltern und ein gemeinsames Vorgehen von Schulen, Politik und Gesellschaft.
Politik am Zug
Der vielleicht wichtigste Punkt des Berichts: Prävention soll nicht erst beginnen, wenn bereits etwas passiert ist. Es werden deshalb mehr Ressourcen für Schulen und außerschulische Einrichtungen, mehr Schulsozialarbeit sowie dauerhaft finanzierte Angebote zur Geschlechtersensibilisierung und Gewaltprävention gefordert.
Die „geballte Expertise“ des Berichts könne „ein echter Gamechanger sein“, so Pollak. Dazu müsse die Politik die am Tisch liegenden Forderungen ernst nehmen und umsetzen, regt Pollak einen runden Tisch von Politik und Burschen-Experten an.
Unser Bericht zeigt, dass es klare Lösungswege gibt, um Burschen von gewaltfördernden und patriarchalen Rollenbildern zu lösen.
Ziel des Ganzen ist natürlich nicht, Burschen „umzuerziehen“, damit sie weniger männlich werden. Sie sollen vielmehr aus der Vorstellung befreit werden, dass ein Mann hart, dominant und unangreifbar sein muss – und damit keine Gefahr mehr für Frauen, die Gesellschaft – und nicht zuletzt sich selbst werden.
Liebe Leserin, lieber Leser,
die Kommentarfunktion steht Ihnen ab 6 Uhr wieder wie gewohnt zur Verfügung.
Mit freundlichen Grüßen
das krone.at-Team

title: Zimtschnecken und Co. - Worldskills: Steirerin bäckt gegen 22 Nationen an
content:
Zwölf junge Steirer kämpfen als Teil des 48 Köpfe starken, rot-weiß-roten Teams aktuell in Shanghai um die Medaillen der Berufsweltmeisterschaften Worldskills. Am ersten Tag herrschte Kampfgeist – und es flossen Tränen.
In der Halle 4.1 des National Exhibition and Convention Center riecht es süß nach Plundergebäck und nicht nach Veranstaltungszentrum. Jennifer Lueger knetet, mehlt den Teig und rollt ihn aus. Schnellen Schrittes schiebt sie das Gebäck ins Rohr, die Kappe verdeckt ihr Gesicht. So will die 21-Jährige sich voll und ganz auf den Wettkampf fokussieren.
„Sie ist sehr konzentriert“, sagt ihre Mutter Manuela, die durch die Plexiglaswand zuschaut. #teamjenny steht auf den Ärmeln der T-Shirts, die Papa Jakob, Schwester Lara und Schwager Markus aus St. Jakob im Walde extra anfertigen haben lassen, um Jennifer in Shanghai zu unterstützen. „Ich habe eigentlich ein bisschen Flugangst“, sagt Jakob Lueger. „Aber jetzt, wo ich hier bin, würde ich es echt bereuen, zu Hause geblieben zu sein.“
„Bei den Broten ist sie super“
Normalerweise steht die 21-Jährige in der Backstube in Miesenbach bei Birkfeld. 8500 Kilometer Luftlinie entfernt bäckt sie gegen 22 Nationen an, von Kasachstan bis Mexiko, auf einer Fläche, die 20-mal so groß ist wie die Grazer Messe. Nach den Zimtschnecken mit Apfelchutney am Mittwochvormittag war die Anspannung zur Mittagspause groß, erzählt Mama Manuela, die Jennifer einen Burger vorbeibrachte. Es flossen ein paar Tränen. „Bei den Broten ist sie super. Die sind perfekt geworden.“
Bei den Bäckern herrscht Schichtbetrieb, deswegen wird Jennifer Lueger schon am Donnerstag fertig und kann dann ihre Teamkameraden anfeuern. Etwa Logistiker Paul Zadravec aus Leitring. Er sitzt insgesamt vier Tage lang mit dicken Kopfhörern vor dem Computer, mit Oreo-Keksen und Cola am Tisch, und löst Probleme mit Lieferketten, telefoniert mit Firmen, nimmt Aufträge an.
Medaillenvergabe am Sonntag
Zwölf Steirer sind insgesamt beim Wettbewerb dabei, Österreich stellt das größte Team aus Europa und hat traditionell in den Handwerksberufen gute Chancen. 2024 in Lyon ging eine Goldene an Fliesenleger Florian Gruber aus Aigen im Ennstal. Am Sonntagabend wird feststehen, wer die heiß begehrten Medaillen mit nach Hause nehmen kann.
Ob Edelmetall oder nicht: „Als Mama ist man auch bei Rückschlägen da“, sagt Manuela Lueger. Sie und Papa Jakob sind schon jetzt „gewaltig stolz“ auf ihre Tochter.

title: Jenni Scharingers letzter Weg: Abschied einer Vielgeliebten
content: Unmenschliches hat die Familie Scharinger in den vergangenen acht Jahren durchgestanden. Auf der Suche nach ihrer Tochter, ihrer Schwester, die seit 22. Jänner 2018 spurlos verschwunden war. Und deren Ex-Partner im vergangenen August zu lebenslanger Haft plus Unterbringung in einem forensisch-therapeutischen Zentrum verurteilt wurde; nicht rechtskräftig.Doch diese Tage sind die Schlimmsten. Am kommenden Wochenende wird das Begräbnis von Jenni Scharinger in Hanfthal, Bezirk Mistelbach, stattfinden. In der Pfarrkirche jenes kleinen Ortes, in dem Jenni aufgewachsen ist. „Vor dem Begräbnis habe ich Angst“, sagt Mutter Brigitta. Denn dann ist der Abschied von ihrer jüngsten Tochter endgültig. Jeden Tag, so beschreibt es die Mutter, gönne sie es sich, „ein paar Mal zu plärren“.All die Jahre zuvor hatte sie ihre gesamte Energie in die Suche nach Jenni gesteckt. Indizien gegen den Ex-Freund gab es viele. Doch Beweise oder ein Geständnis fehlten. Also fing die Mutter mit Unterstützern selbst an, zu ermitteln. Die Suche nach der Leiche ihres Kindes führte sie auch in die Wälder, in denen sie mit dem Spaten unzählige Gruben aushob, um endlich Jennis sterbliche Überreste zu finden. Zuletzt war es eine List, die Jennis Mörder überführte. Ein anonymes Gespräch über eine Dating-Plattform, in dem der Mann darüber sprach, wie er eine Leiche am besten verschwinden lassen würde.Später legte der 33-jährige bei der Polizei ein Geständnis ab, führte die Ermittler zu Jennis sterblichen Überresten auf dem Truppenübungsplatz Allentsteig.Den Prozess verfolgte Jennis Mutter nicht. Sie wollte mit Clemens T. nicht im selben Raum sein. Jennis Schwester vertrat die Familie, viele Freundinnen der damals 21-Jährigen waren anwesend. „Jetzt kann er niemandem mehr etwas antun“, sagt die Mutter.Schon in der Vorwoche nahm sie am „Gehen gegen Gewalt“ teil. „Weil das aufhören muss. Es darf nicht so weitergehen!“Es soll ein würdiger Abschied von ihrer Tochter werden, wünscht sie sich. Auch die Sängerin Oska wird ihren Teil dazu beitragen. Die Amadeus-Preisträgerin wird unter anderem „You are my Sunshine“ singen. „Weil Jenni unser Sonnenschein war.“

title: Nach drei Generationen: Blumen Doll schließt endgültig
content:
Das Firmengelände in Nonntal wurde schon vor einiger Zeit an eine Investorengruppe verkauft. Dort soll bald ein Neubau entstehen. Noch ist Blumen Doll an der Nonntaler Hauptstraße geöffnet. Zu beiden Seiten der Straße erinnern die Glashäuser an eine lange Salzburger Gärtnertradition. Doch viele Regale sind bereits leer, nur noch wenige Kunden kommen vorbei.
Lob der Kundschaften in höchsten Tönen
Entsprechend wehmütig fällt der Abschied aus. Die Gastronomin Evelyn Brandstätter sagt, ihr blute das Herz: „Es geht eine Institution verloren. Und wer soll diese Lücke ausfüllen?“ Die Pongauer Spitzenköchin Johanna Maier betont, sie sei traurig: „Traurig, traurig, sehr traurig ich wurde hier seit meinen Jugendzeiten immer bestens beraten.“ Anna Breser ist pensionierte Sozialarbeiterin: „Es ist das beste Geschäft in Salzburg.“
Noch neun Tage geöffnet
Bis zum endgültigen Aus bleiben nur noch neun Verkaufstage. Danach endet für Eigentümer Jörg Doll ein Familienunternehmen, das über drei Generationen geführt wurde: „Es wird mir nun immer bewusst, eine emotionale Achterbahnfahrt. Es ist schon auch traurig.“
Ganz verschwindet Doll aus Salzburg allerdings nicht. Zuletzt gab es neben dem Stammsitz in Nonntal noch zwei Filialen: im Borromäuspoint in Parsch und im Europark. Die Doll-Schilder sind dort zwar bereits abmontiert. Beide Blumengeschäfte werden jedoch weitergeführt.
Einiges „lebt“ weiter in neuen „Tochterfirmen“
Auch für die Grabpflege gebe es eine Nachfolgelösung, so Doll: „Wir sind stolz, dass drei Mitarbeiterinnen eigene Unternehmen gegründet haben. So nehmen sie den Esprit mit, den sie bei uns gelernt haben.“ Für die Mitarbeiterinnen bedeutet das, dass zumindest ein Teil ihrer bisherigen Arbeit weitergeht.
Was von Blumen Doll bleibt
Für Jörg Doll selbst endet mit der Schließung nicht nur ein Geschäft, sondern ein Stück Familiengeschichte. Was nach drei Generationen und vielen Jahrzehnten Kunstgärtnerei bleibt, fasst er so zusammen: „Ein volles Herz bleibt – und viel Dankbarkeit und Demut. Wenn ich in die Zukunft schaue, dann bin ich froh, dass ich den Segen und das Glück hatte, in der richtigen Zeit tätig sein zu dürfen.“
Am 30. September ist endgültig Schluss. Dann endet die Geschichte der Salzburger Blumen- und Gärtnerdynastie Doll nach drei Generationen – und wenig später werden auch die alten Glashäuser im Stadtteil Nonntal verschwinden.
