title: The site of India’s maiden gold: Between a bench and baseball cage
content:
Stay updated with the latest sports news across Cricket, Football, Chess, and more. Catch all the action with real-time live cricket score updates and in-depth coverage of ongoing matches.
There is a toilet, a bench and a baseball cage, the only permanent structures. And then there is the cricket pitch — the latest addition.
Korogi Athletic Park is almost too open, too green, too tranquil to be an international sporting venue. Even Harmanpreet Kaur, the India captain, knew this was a nation hardly associated with cricket. “But knowing Japan, we knew they would manage something,” she said.
They had managed something that looked quite a lot like a quaint English county ground.
On Tuesday afternoon, in this unlikely setting in the middle of a public park in Nisshin, on the outskirts of Nagoya, India won the first gold medal of its Asian Games campaign. They beat Sri Lanka by 147 runs, so comprehensively that the suspense had disappeared long before the celebrations.
When the celebrations finally came, Radha Yadav and Renuka Thakur started sprinting towards the middle with the Indian flag. Then they slowed to a walk, almost as if they had realised there was no need to hurry. The final had been so one-sided that even the celebration seemed to have time to spare.
But the people watching did not seem to mind.
Click here to read our Asian Games full coverage
A Sri Lankan family had driven for a couple of hours from Nara to be here. There were Indians from England, on holiday in Seoul, who had made their way to Nisshin to watch India play.
And then there were the Japanese. For many of them, this was their first cricket match. “I have come to watch because my daughter has married a Sri Lankan man,” said one spectator. An elderly couple, Naofumi and Chisato, had seen children practice baseball hits here, and came for cricket just out of curiosity. “We know nothing about it,” Naofumi said.
They had been handed a beginner’s guide in Japanese explaining the rules and were repeatedly looking down at them, then back at the field, trying to make sense of what had just happened. A wicket, a boundary, a change of bowler — moments that require no explanation to a cricket audience were being learnt in real time.
Mimi Hirayama, the public announcer, was helping them along. “Mainly rules, because the Japanese audience is not familiar with this sport,” Hirayama said. “But they are very familiar with baseball. So I’ll keep giving them my hints to understand what’s going on.” So a six became a home run. “And when the batter hits four, it’s like a three-base hit or something like that,” Hirayama said.
It was an ingenious way of introducing cricket to an audience that already understood another bat-and-ball sport.
Hirayama could make the comparisons because she had spent many years in England and was familiar with cricket. Before the Games, she also watched matches involving India and other countries to learn more about the sport.
For a few hours, then, Korogi contained several different versions of cricket fandom at once: Indians celebrating, Sri Lankans supporting their team, an overseas diaspora making an unexpected detour, and Japanese spectators discovering the game through baseball.
It was an unusual scene for a ground that, until recently, was not a cricket ground at all.
Korogi is a public ground that has facilities for baseball, tennis and football, which is where the teams trained, too. When cricket was added to the Asian Games programme at the last minute, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha said she helped finalise this geound as the venue. And so, the baseball ground was converted for the Games between September last year and March 2026. The 305 million yen (approximately Rs 18 crore) project involved relaying 14,984 square metres of grass, installing practice nets and building an equipment store. It hosted six matches of the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup East Asia-Pacific Qualifier in May as its first major test.
Now it has hosted an Asian Games final — and India’s first gold of these Games.
Harmanpreet said the only adjustment the team had to make was playing on the hybrid pitches. “But we knew how the pitch would behave because recently in England, we played on hybrid pitches too. The other facilities weren’t of top level but they managed it pretty well, she added.
Once the flags come down, Nisshin mayor Hiroki Kondo said the cricket will continue. “This is the second ground in Japan after Sano. After the Asian Games we will continue playing cricket here along with baseball,” Kondo said.
How often?
“About 18 days.”
A month?
“No. This is Japan — 18 days a year.”
It might not be much, but Hirayama hopes it will be just enough to keep the link with the sport alive. “I hope many people here in Japan, who have found this sport exciting and think they will enjoy it enough to play,” Hirayama said. “So I hope this ground will also be used for cricket in the future.”
Soon, Jasprit Bumrah and India’s men will walk out onto the same strip. And, somewhere between the baseball cage and the toilet, cricket has found a place to stay.

title: 'Today, a Khan and a Singh won a medal for India': Satnam on Asian Games bronze
content:
NEW DELHI: Satnam Singh and
Salman Khan won India's first-ever Asian Games medal in men's double sculls on Thursday, with the Indian pair claiming bronze at the Nagaragawa International Regatta Course.
But for Satnam, the medal meant much more than a place on the podium.
"Today, a Khan and a Singh won a medal for India. I want people to remember that. Long after we are gone, this fact will live on. Salman is like a brother to me. There are things we hear and read about, and that disturbs us. I want our people to stop fighting on religious lines," Satnam told HT.
The pair clocked 6:13.25 to finish third. China's Yi Xudi and Nie Yide won gold in 6:09.77, while Uzbekistan's Mekhrojbek Mamatkulov and Pavel Sorin took silver in 6:10.49. Satnam and Salman were second at the 1,500m mark but slipped to third in the final 500m.
A medal that brought two journeys together
Satnam and Salman had originally been selected for the quadruple sculls team along with Jakar Khan and Balraj Panwar. However, after a change in the team combinations, the duo was moved to the double sculls event in place of Navdeep Singh and Kulwinder Singh.
Satnam admitted the change did affect them, but the two decided to focus on giving their best.
"I won't say we were not affected by it, but we decided to give our best. It helped that me and Salman have been training together for seven months for quadruple sculls, so we had good understanding," Satnam said.
He also felt the conditions helped them.
"The tailwind helped us today and the waters were still. We were the lightest finalists, which helped us go faster. Both of us weigh about 85kgs each while the rest of the rowers were in 90-95kg range."
Satnam's road to the podium
For Satnam, the bronze also helped erase the disappointment of the previous Asian Games. China and Uzbekistan had won gold and silver in the event at the previous edition, although with different rowers. Satnam, who had competed with Parminder Singh, had finished last among six pairs in Hangzhou.
"The failure in Hangzhou had haunted me all these years and I was waiting for this Asiad to redeem myself. I was also part of the quadruple team that won a bronze there. We were on course for a silver in 2023 but I was exhausted and passed out which had cost us a second-place result. So all that weighed heavy on me coming into the competition," Satnam said.
The 26-year-old comes from Fatta Maluka village in Punjab's Mansa district and is employed in the Indian Navy as a Chief Petty Officer. A former national-level handball player, Satnam also played volleyball before taking up rowing. He was inspired by London Olympian Swarn Singh Virk, who also comes from Mansa.
"I was into multiple sports at school, and once my PT teacher invited Swarn Singh to our school to have a word with kids. Swarn comes from Mansa as well, so he was an instant inspiration," Satnam recalled.
Swarn encouraged him to take up rowing, and Satnam joined the Punjab Institute of Sports in Ropar, where he began training under Virjender Singh Cheema.
Satnam joined the Navy in 2019 through the sports quota and later trained at SAI centres in Odisha and Alleppey.
A promise to his mother
Satnam grew up in a family with limited means. His father, Amrik Singh, grew cotton on their farm, while his mother Harjeet Kaur tailored clothes to support the family. His brother Gurpiar Singh, a soldier with the 28 Punjab Regiment based in Jammu, supported his early training. Satnam later joined the Army Rowing Node in Pune in 2022.
"I am happy to have given them something to cheer about after all these years. I had promised my mom that I'll make up for that Hangzhou heartbreak. I am happy to have done that," he said.
Satnam is also proud of his roots and the athletes who have come from Mansa.
"There is something about Mansa that it produces strong people. Swarn Singh and double Asiad medallist rower Sukhmeet Singh are also from here. A lot of our boys join the army," he said.
Late Punjabi singer Siddhu Moosewala was another of Satnam's heroes.
"He remains an absolute star. I listen to his songs while warming-up," he said.
From driving an Uber to an Asian Games medal
Salman's journey to the Asian Games podium has also been shaped by struggle. Born in Pure Dhingai in Uttar Pradesh's Amethi, Salman is the eldest of four brothers and two sisters. His father, Mohd Kasim Khan, worked in a truck-body construction company in Tauru, Haryana, where Salman completed his schooling.
His life changed when his father died of dengue when Salman was 18. He then drove an Uber in Delhi to support his family before joining the Bombay Engineering Group of the Indian Army in 2018.
It was there that Salman discovered rowing. His 6'4" frame and raw power caught the attention of coaches, and he began training at the Army Rowing Node under senior coach Kudrat Ali and Training Officer Major Nagendra Hooda.
"It feels like a dream come true. I was expecting to win a medal at the Asian Games, and I am delighted that I could fulfil that expectation. But this is only the beginning; my next target is the Los Angeles Olympics," Salman, a Naib Subedar in the Army, said.
"I know what struggle means in life, but I never lost hope. I kept working hard and continued to believe in myself."

title: Minister calls MBG focus on disadvantaged regions as priority
content:
Indonesia's Ministry of Villages and Development of Disadvantaged Regions has urged the National Nutrition Agency (BGN) to prioritize the Free Nutritious Meals (MBG) program for residents in frontier, underdeveloped, and outermost (3T) areas.
Director General for the Acceleration of Disadvantaged Regions Development Samsul Widodo said the ministry had been communicating with BGN to direct the flagship program toward regions with the greatest needs.
"We are now drafting a letter from the Minister to the BGN chief to emphasize the importance of prioritizing disadvantaged regions," he said during the "Strategy for Accelerating the MBG Program in 3T Regions" forum, which was monitored online from Jakarta on Wednesday.
He noted that 30 districts across Indonesia remain classified as disadvantaged regions, stressing that they warrant special attention in the implementation of the nutrition program.
As an example, Widodo pointed to the insufficient number of MBG kitchens in Central Sumba District, East Nusa Tenggara Province, and several other regions.
Against that backdrop, he reiterated the urgency of expanding the MBG program while taking into account the specific conditions and needs of underserved communities.
BGN earlier announced that it had removed 1,653 educational institutions from the list of MBG recipients, redirecting resources to communities with greater needs, including those in 3T regions.
The BGN Chief, Sudaryono, said the delisted institutions comprised international schools and elite private schools.
He noted that the schools did not rely on operational assistance funds offered by the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education.
Meanwhile, Coordinating Minister for Food Affairs Zulkifli Hasan said the government is prioritizing the activation of 111 MBG kitchens across 3T regions in nine provinces, including six Papuan provinces.

title: Phillip Island removed foxes; little penguin colony grew from 12,000 to 40,000
content:
Phillip Island’s little penguins once faced a crisis that threatened to erase much of their presence from the island. By the 1980s, nine of its 10 penguin colonies had disappeared, while the final colony on the Summerland Peninsula was also under pressure from introduced predators, habitat loss and human activity. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, a long-running conservation effort combining fox control, habitat restoration, scientific research and land rehabilitation helped reverse that decline. The surviving little-penguin population grew from about 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today. The story, detailed in the organisation’s pest-control, research and history records, shows how protecting wildlife often requires more than removing a single threat—it demands sustained cooperation between scientists, governments, local communities and visitors. Read on to know more:
A predator that changed the island
Phillip Island, also known as Milawul, is famous for the nightly arrival of little penguins at the Penguin Parade. Yet the sight that attracts visitors today was once at risk of disappearing.
Red foxes were introduced to Phillip Island in the early 1900s. Over time, they became one of the most serious threats to the island’s wildlife. Little penguins are especially vulnerable because they spend much of their lives at sea but return to land to breed, moult and raise their chicks. Their nests are often located in burrows or sheltered areas close to the coast, where they can be exposed to predators.
Phillip Island Nature Parks describes foxes as the little penguins’ biggest threat on land. By the 1980s, nine of the island’s 10 penguin colonies had become extinct. The remaining colony on the Summerland Peninsula, which includes the Penguin Parade, was also under threat.
The decline was not caused by foxes alone. Research identified several other pressures, including habitat destruction, housing development, traffic near penguin colonies, fire and domestic pets. Together, these threats made it increasingly difficult for penguins to survive and breed successfully.
Warning signs from research
The island’s conservation response was shaped by research. Population studies conducted during the 1980s showed that the last remaining penguin colony could disappear by the late 1990s if existing threats continued.
That warning encouraged authorities and conservation groups to take action. The Penguin Protection Plan, announced in 1985, included scientific research, habitat management, a fox-control program and the gradual buyback of houses in the Summerland Estate.
The housing estate had been built within the penguins’ habitat. As houses, roads and associated infrastructure were removed, the land could be returned to a more natural condition. This was a major undertaking and required years of planning, funding and rehabilitation.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says the buyback and removal of the Summerland Estate continued for decades, as per reports. The final houses and infrastructure were removed in 2010, after which an ongoing rehabilitation program was established to help penguins and other wildlife thrive.
This approach recognised an important conservation principle: removing a predator is not enough if the habitat remains unsafe. Wildlife needs places to shelter, feed, breed and raise young without constant disturbance.
The campaign against foxes
Fox control began as a coordinated effort involving farmers, rangers and conservation workers. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, more than 1,000 foxes were removed over a period of 20 years.
The organisation initiated a dedicated Fox Eradication Project in 2006. Rather than relying on one method, the project used an integrated approach involving different techniques to locate and remove foxes across the island.
The goal was ambitious. Instead of simply reducing fox numbers, conservation teams aimed to remove foxes from Phillip Island altogether. This was important because even a small number of predators could threaten vulnerable colonies and prevent other species from recovering.
The campaign required persistent monitoring. Rangers and other workers had to search for signs of foxes, respond to sightings and prevent the animals from re-establishing a population. The work also formed part of wider pest management on the island, including programs targeting feral and roaming cats and rabbits.
In 2017, Phillip Island was declared fox-free after an intensive 20-year eradication program. The campaign was supported by the Victorian Government, Penguin Parade visitors, the Penguin Foundation and the Helen Macpherson Smith Trust.
Habitat restoration made a difference
The recovery of the little penguins was closely connected to the restoration of their habitat.
The Summerland Peninsula had once been transformed by housing development and human activity. Removing the houses allowed conservation teams to rebuild a landscape better suited to wildlife. The rehabilitation work helped restore vegetation, reduce disturbance and create safer areas for nesting.
The return of natural habitat also benefited species beyond little penguins. Short-tailed shearwaters and other coastal birds use the island’s protected areas, while the fox-free environment later supported the reintroduction of eastern barred bandicoots.
In 2017, the same year Phillip Island was declared fox-free, researchers released eastern barred bandicoots onto the Summerland Peninsula. The area had been rehabilitated from a former housing estate into a natural environment that supported a thriving little-penguin colony and migratory short-tailed shearwaters.
This illustrates how conservation gains can extend across an ecosystem. Protecting one habitat can create opportunities for several threatened species, especially when predators are controlled and human disturbance is reduced.
From 12,000 to 40,000 penguins
Phillip Island Nature Parks reports that extensive conservation work helped increase the number of little penguins from approximately 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today.
The figures represent more than a simple population increase. They reflect the combined effect of predator control, habitat restoration, reduced development pressure, scientific monitoring and community involvement.
The Penguin Parade also provides a useful way to monitor changes. Guides count the number of penguins crossing the beach each night, and annual averages can offer insight into population trends. These counts do not represent every penguin on the island, but they help researchers track changes in the colony over time.
Conservation teams also monitor breeding success by studying the number of chicks fledged per breeding pair at selected sites. This helps researchers understand not only how many penguins return to land, but also whether they are successfully reproducing.
Such long-term monitoring is essential because wildlife populations can change in response to food availability, disease, weather, marine conditions, human activity and other factors. Regular data collection allows managers to identify problems early and adjust conservation strategies.
Research continues on land and sea
Although the fox eradication campaign was a major achievement, the work of protecting little penguins has not ended.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says its researchers study penguins in both terrestrial and marine environments. This is necessary because little penguins spend around 80 per cent of their time at sea, even though they depend on land for breeding.
Researchers use GPS trackers and other devices to study where penguins travel for food. Tracking has shown that many penguins feed within 50 kilometres of the island’s colony, while some individuals travel farther during winter, including towards Portland in Victoria and Port Phillip Bay near Melbourne.
Understanding these movements helps scientists identify potential threats in the marine environment. Changes in ocean temperature, prey availability, pollution and human activity can all affect the penguins’ ability to find food.
Research projects also examine feeding hotspots by combining information about where penguins go, how much they eat and what prey they consume. This evidence can help guide future conservation decisions as marine ecosystems respond to environmental change.
A model for community-led conservation
Phillip Island’s recovery story shows that successful conservation rarely happens through one dramatic action. It is usually built through many years of practical work.
The fox eradication program required rangers, farmers, scientists, government agencies, conservation organisations and local residents to work towards the same goal. Visitors also contributed through tourism, with Phillip Island Nature Parks stating that visits help fund research and wildlife conservation.
The island’s history also highlights the importance of acknowledging the Bunurong people, the Traditional Owners of Milawul. Phillip Island Nature Parks recognises the continuing connection of the Bunurong to the landscape and describes its role in healing Country and supporting Traditional Owner involvement in decisions about Country.
The little penguins’ recovery is therefore not only a story about numbers. It is a story about restoring a damaged landscape, learning from scientific evidence and changing the way people share space with wildlife.
What the future depends on
The increase from 12,000 to 40,000 little penguins is encouraging, but it does not mean the species is permanently secure on Phillip Island. Conservation gains must be maintained.
Foxes must remain absent. Other introduced predators, including feral and roaming cats, require continued management. Roads, pets, fires, rubbish, human disturbance and habitat damage can still affect wildlife.
The penguins’ time at sea also creates challenges that cannot be solved entirely on land. Their food supply may be influenced by changing ocean conditions, climate change and human activity. That is why Phillip Island’s conservation program combines population counts, breeding studies, tracking and marine research.
The lesson from Phillip Island is clear: wildlife recovery becomes possible when threats are identified early and addressed consistently. A colony that once appeared destined to vanish has grown substantially because people chose to protect its habitat, remove its predators and continue monitoring its future.
For the little penguins returning to shore each evening, that long-term commitment has made the difference between disappearance and survival.

title: Malaysia’s ‘elephant whisperer’ fights to save Borneo’s endangered giants
content:
The downed elephant is one of only around 1,000 Bornean elephants left in the wild, and the team that darted her is working to protect the endangered species by minimising growing conflict between the animals and local communities.
Once the herd has been chased off, conservationist Farina Othman and her team move in to attach a tracking collar to the animal.
The collar allows them to alert villagers if the elephant strays too near.
It is also key to a programme Farina is designing to create “corridors” for elephants roaming a fragmented landscape of virgin forest patches, hemmed in by vast oil palm plantations and villages.
Farina has studied these elephants for years, earning her the nickname “Borneo’s elephant whisperer” as well as the prestigious Whitley Award for conservationists.
“It’s Pigtail,” she whispered, stroking the tranquilised elephant’s trunk and nodding to the distinctive tail that prompted its nickname.
The team works fast — the dart’s sedative effects last only half an hour, and the herd can still be heard nearby. Overhead, there are flashes of lightning as a tropical thunderstorm approaches.
As soon as the collar is securely fastened and blood samples are taken, the team, accompanied by AFP journalists, retreat into the forest before Pigtail rouses.
‘Conflict inevitable’
For the past 40 years, Bornean elephants have lost more than 60% of their habitat in Sabah to logging and, later, oil palm expansion, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which listed the animal as endangered in 2024.
Lower Kinabatangan, a floodplain in eastern Sabah of around 400sq km, is home to around 160 elephants.
But “only half of that is now a space left for the elephants,” said Farina, a Malaysian academic who heads local conservation group Seratu Aatai, or “Solidarity” in the local Sungai language.
When the animals venture into private property or nearby villages, “conflict is inevitable”, she told AFP.
In a recent incident, a herd of 20 elephants stomped into palm oil smallholdings and three villages, terrifying residents.
No one was injured, but the incident prompted calls for stronger deterrents, including upgraded electric fencing.
“People don’t feel safe around elephants, and that’s when conflict happens,” Farina said.
The animosity worsens when the animals, especially adventurous bulls, which can weigh up to five tonnes, cleverly bypass electric fencing to feast on palm trees or saplings.
That is why Farina and her team of 17 conservationists prioritise coexistence.
“We’re working to increase people’s tolerance, to increase connectivity space for elephants and to find a long-term solution,” she said.
Based in Sukau, a hamlet on the crocodile-infested banks of the Kinabatangan river, Seratu Aatai runs an outreach programme in plantation schools, distributes information pamphlets and has designated “community wildlife guardians” who help usher away elephants that have wandered into human habitation.
“Before, we didn’t know how to manage living near them,” said homestay owner Firah Kazenn, 21, who recently encountered elephants behind her home in Sukau.
“The elephants were unmonitored, and many were lost to conflict. Now, with the Seratu Aatai unit, they are protected, and the community is actively involved too,” Firah told AFP.
“We’ve learnt safe ways to guide the elephants away when they come too close to our homes, without harming them,” she added.
‘Win-win situation’
Farina believes the best way to protect the animals is by creating “elephant corridors” — pathways through plantations connecting patches of habitat.
She is hoping to convince seven plantations in the area that elephants are “an ecological reality, rather than an occasional disturbance”.
But it will be a challenge.
Fierce competition driven by tight, volatile margins means many producers are not keen to sacrifice land for corridors, said Muhammad Al Shafieq bin Mustafa, a former plantation manager in Sukau and now a palm oil industry specialist.
“Those plantations that do commit and are willing to work with people like Farina often do not get the recognition that they deserve or the financial support that they need, especially from Western palm oil buyers,” he told AFP.
Industry-funded conservation associations say plantations have made progress in becoming sustainable palm oil producers but face difficult economic realities.
“It needs to be a win-win situation between the planters and also the wildlife,” said Daniel Pamin, conservation and sustainability executive at the Malaysian Palm Oil Green Conservation Foundation.
Farina believes change will come.
Before, locals used the Malay word “halau”, meaning “chase away” or “banish”, when talking about elephants.
“Now, we are working to get people to say… ‘walking’ or ‘escorting’ out the elephant.”

title: Perhaps Malaysians are a lot kinder than we think
content:
A middle-aged Chinese woman from an NGO walked into the newsroom, seeking help.
A journalist of Indian descent was assigned to write the story — that of a young Malay girl who urgently needed medical attention.
This story, recounted by FMT executive chairman Nelson Fernandez at a forum recently, would have just been another account of how Malaysians help each other.
But this was different. People of all races came together to answer a call for help by a Chinese, disseminated by an Indian to help a Malay.
Within hours of FMT publishing the story, up to RM150,000 had been pledged, taking little Diya Amanda on her first step towards a normal childhood.
But for Fernandez, it was just another day at the office.
The Malaysia we keep saying we want is already here.
Nobody ever needed a campaign or matching T-shirts to foster unity. Nobody asked who prayed where or what box they ticked on a form.
This was simply a child who needed help.
And people came forward.
Back in 1982, Paul McCartney and Stevie Wonder sang a lovely song about “Ebony and Ivory” living together in perfect harmony. If black and white piano keys could exist in harmony, surely human beings could figure it out too.
More than forty years later, humanity is still working on it.
We, Malaysians, have spent decades talking about unity. We have slogans, campaigns and speeches about it. We have probably printed enough banners about togetherness to wrap around the country several times over.
Yet one of the best demonstrations of Malaysian unity happened without anybody needing to announce it.
Just like the song, maybe harmony doesn’t require every key to sound the same.
I don’t think Malaysia suffers from an absence of harmony. Perhaps we suffer from not seeing enough of it.
That matters because the stories we repeatedly hear about one another influence the nation we are a part of.
If Malaysians constantly encounter one another through anger, suspicion and confrontation, eventually it becomes easy to believe we are fundamentally divided.
This is why Fernandez’s argument about journalism matters beyond journalism.
He wasn’t suggesting difficult stories shouldn’t be told. Nor should they be.
He was asking for something harder: that conflict does not become the only lens through which Malaysians see one another.
We should be able to disagree fiercely without dehumanising others. We should be able to defend what we believe without humiliating someone who believes differently.
And when we report what divides Malaysia, we should not forget the stories that reveal what still holds us together.
That responsibility isn’t just journalists’ anymore.
Every one of us carries a tiny newsroom in our pockets. We decide what gets shared, forwarded and viral-ed.
Fernandez said something else at the New Muslim Community Conference in Kuala Lumpur, that stayed with me:
“Everyone talks about religion, but no one talks about love, compassion and kindness.”
Love. Compassion. Kindness.
Three words that might seem soft beside politics, race, religion and power.
But as I wrote in my previous article, we have grossly misunderstood softness and strength.
It is easy to be kind to people who agree with us and who are similar and familiar. It takes something stronger to extend that kindness to someone who isn’t.
Perhaps Malaysians do not need to agree on everything and maybe agreement was never the point.
Harmony isn’t everyone singing the same note. That’s unison.
Harmony requires difference.
Ebony and ivory don’t create music because they overcame their differences. Their differences are the point.
Malaysia isn’t so different. A unique colourful country like ours was never going to be one note.
I believe we should stop trying to make everyone sound the same and become better at hearing one another instead.
That’s where harmony begins.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

title: The human hands that keep this iconic clock ticking
content:
More than a timepiece, it has become a familiar witness to the city’s history, its chimes accompanying generations of Malaysians through moments both ordinary and momentous.
Today, the task of keeping it running falls to three men who continue the work of custodians before them.
Muhammad Kamarul Azman, L Kumarasamy and Roshdihisham Hassan, from the survey and mapping department, check, clean, wind and lubricate the century-old mechanism throughout the year.
“Every evening after office hours, we come here to wind the clock and make sure the time is accurate,” Kamarul told FMT.
Inside the narrow, sweltering tower, the trio take turns working the giant weights that keep the Gillett & Johnston clock ticking.
The task requires patience. According to Kamarul, the crank cannot be turned too quickly, as doing so could disrupt the pulley system. “That is why we rely on our own physical strength,” he said.
Their responsibility does not always end when the day’s checks are done. On one occasion, Kamarul had already returned home when a call came through informing him that the clock had stopped.
“I had already reached home when the building management called. So we had to come back at midnight to inspect it,” he recalled.
Their work takes on added meaning on the eve of Merdeka celebrations, when the clock becomes part of a national moment.
As crowds gather outside and the countdown begins, Kamarul, Kumarasamy and Roshdihisham stay inside the tower, watching closely to make sure the clock reaches midnight precisely as it should.
“At midnight, we really feel nervous. When we hear the people outside counting down, we feel proud from inside the tower,” Kamarul said.
It is a moment that turns an otherwise unseen job into something deeply personal: while thousands celebrate below, the men inside know the clock’s familiar chime depends, in part, on their hands.
Learning from those before them
For Kamarul, the role began almost by chance. When a senior colleague introduced him to the clock, seeing its century-old machinery at work sparked a fascination he had not expected.
“When you watch all the gears and machinery moving, you become very interested in learning how it all works. That is what has kept us here until today.”
There was no handbook to guide them; instead, much of what they know was learnt through experience and from those who cared for the clock before them.
And this knowledge matters because keeping the mechanism alive is not as simple as replacing a broken part.
“If any component is damaged, a replacement has to be specially made according to the original specifications because the parts are no longer available on the market,” Kamarul noted.
And so, year after year, the clock in this iconic building continues to tick – not only because of the machinery inside it, but because of the people who keep watch over it.

title: NIA assures sufficient water supply as strong El Niño draws near
content:
NIA assures sufficient water supply as strong El Niño draws near
The National Irrigation Authority (NIA) said on Sunday that adequate irrigation water is available as a strong El Niño approaches, adding that it will maintain a double dry cropping calendar to maximize the dry season.
In an interview with Super Radyo dzBB, NIA Administrator Eduardo Guillen said the agency actually prefers sunny weather, which is why it is implementing double dry cropping.
“Sa pagsasaka po, sa pagtatanim natin, mas gusto nga po ng NIA ‘yung maaraw, kaya nga po binabago ng NIA ‘yung ating cropping calendar, ginagawa po naming… double dry cropping,” Guillen said.
(When it comes to farming, NIA actually prefers sunny weather. That is why NIA is shifting our cropping calendar and implementing… double dry cropping.)
“... Ang ginagawa po ng NIA ngayon, dinadala natin ‘yung ating cropping sa parteng October, aani tayo ng January, tanim ulit tayo ng March [at] aani ulit tayo ng June. So ‘yan po ‘yung tinatawag [na] double dry cropping,” he added.
(What NIA is doing now is shifting our cropping schedule to around October so we can harvest in January, then plant again in March and harvest in June. So that is what we call double dry cropping.)
Guillen pointed out that this system differs from the previous wet and dry cropping calendar, where planting started in November or December, harvest took place in March, and replanting occurred in July.
He explained that sunny weather yields higher crop output through photosynthesis, which relies on sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. However, he emphasized that a sufficient water supply remains crucial to sustain crop growth.
Citing PAGASA, Guillen said the effects of the strong El Niño are projected to be felt in the last quarter of the year, between October and December, and will persist until the second quarter of 2027.
NIA stated that storing water is one of the key ways the agency prepares, making high dams like Magat Dam in Isabela vital to operations.
Guillen said the Magat Dam is almost full and is expected to supply irrigation to 90,000 hectares of farmland.
Meanwhile, Pantabangan Dam in Nueva Ecija, which supplies water to five areas in Luzon, is also nearly full and capable of irrigating around 120,000 hectares.
High-value crops
As part of its preparations, NIA highlighted the importance of coordination with the Department of Agriculture (DA) to jointly identify areas likely to face water shortages.
“Doon sa mga irrigated areas natin alam po ng NIA kung ilan ‘yung kaya niyang patubigan, na tataniman po natin ng palay. Kasi yung palay matakaw po sa tubig ‘yan,” Guillen said.
(In our irrigated areas, NIA knows how many hectares can be supplied with water for rice production, which requires a substantial amount of water.)
“Now, kaya po sinusulong… ‘yung masusing koordinasyon namin ng Department of Agriculture, dahil po pag na-identify namin ‘yung mga areas na kukulangin po ng patubig, marami naman po tayong pwedeng itanim na high-value crops diyan,” he added.
(That is why we are pushing for close coordination with the Department of Agriculture. Once we identify areas that will lack irrigation, we can plant various high-value crops there instead.)
Among the high-value crops he mentioned were corn and mung beans (munggo).
Guillen clarified that a lack of full irrigation does not mean fields must remain unplanted, emphasizing the critical role of interagency coordination.
NIA also urged collaboration with other government agencies, including the Department of Labor and Employment and the Department of Social Welfare and Development, to provide additional intervention measures once El Niño hits.
Farming along irrigation canals
NIA assured the public that irrigation shortages will not cause food prices to increase.
The agency highlighted its program promoting vegetable planting along irrigation canals.
“Pagkahaba-haba po ng ilang, daang libong kilometro po ang ating irrigation sa buong Pilipinas, eh kung magsipag lang yung ating mga farmers, yung ating mga irrigators association at magtanim po sa mga gilid ng irrigation natin ay malaking bagay po yan,” Guillen said.
(We have hundreds of thousands of kilometers of irrigation canals across the Philippines. If our farmers and irrigators' associations actively plant along the banks of these canals, it will be a huge help.)
Guillen said that from 2023 to 2025, vegetable farming along irrigation canals generated P1.6 billion in extra income for farmers nationwide. —RF, GMA News

title: How modern tech aids Philippines disaster preparedness
content:
How modern tech aids Philippines disaster preparedness
MANILA, Philippines — Modern technology is increasingly aiding disaster preparedness in the Philippines, with the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) advancing artificial intelligence (AI) and other technologies to help save lives even before disasters strike.
AI is powering the government’s central monitoring platform, the Handa Integrated Platform for Preparedness and Response, which was launched in March to provide information on disaster preparedness across different hazards.
“It’s like the ChatGPT of disaster preparedness,” Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) director Teresito Bacolcol said at the Cagayan Valley Regional Science, Technology and Innovation Week press conference.
“You can type in what the different active faults are in Region 2 or any part of the country, and it will provide you with answers,” he added.
Bacolcol said the Handa platform has “simplified the assessment of hazards.”
The public can access the platform at handa.georisk.gov.ph.
Anyone can submit an incident report, which will be verified by the Office of Civil Defense and local government units with accounts provided by PHIVOLCS.
AI is also being used to improve weather forecasting by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration.
“PAGASA’s data are so big, so we need to use AI to improve forecasts; our target is five days to 14 days,” DOST Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. said. “The computing time to process the data would be every three hours. We are experimenting with the use of AI to shorten it to 15 minutes so that the forecasts are more up-to-date.”
PAGASA recently released its National Hydro-Met Observing Network, or PANaHON app, which provides near-real-time information from weather stations across the country.
DOST has also turned over a unit of the Mobile Command and Control Vehicle (MoCCoV) to the Tuguegarao local government.
The MoCCoV is a mobile command center that can be set up in remote areas in just 20 minutes.
It has three air-conditioned rooms that can serve as a command room, conference room, rescue or medical triage room, kitchen or independent bathroom.
It is also equipped with solar panels and a backup generator that can run for up to 32 hours.
In a speech to policymakers and disaster responders, Solidum said DOST is committed to investing in scientific research, hazard monitoring, early warning systems, geospatial technologies, impact-based forecasting and AI to allow the public to act with greater knowledge and lead time.
“But our responsibility at the DOST goes beyond producing information,” Solidum said. “Science must enter the decisions that shape people’s lives … Science and the information it provides must guide policies and influence investment.”
“The public expects information to move and decisions to be made. They expect resources to reach the people who need them. And they expect us to be ready before the emergency begins; that’s why convergence should produce a connected and operationally ready disaster risk reduction and management system,” he added.

title: Chinese and Thai Poets Celebrate Mid-Autumn Festival
content:
Chinese Embassy and Writers’ Association of Thailand Host Chinese–Thai Poets Dialogue to Celebrate Thai–Chinese Relations and Mid-Autumn Festival
On Monday, September 21, 2026, the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China in Thailand, the China Cultural Center in Bangkok, and the Writers’ Association of Thailand jointly organized the “Chinese–Thai Poets Dialogue: Rejoicing in the Full Moon Across the World” at the China Cultural Center in Bangkok. The event celebrated the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Thailand and the People’s Republic of China, which was marked in 2025, as well as the 2026 Mid-Autumn Festival, drawing a large turnout of participants.
The event began with a cultural performance by the ASEAN Cultural Promotion Council, followed by welcoming remarks and an introduction to the event by Zhang Ruoyu, Director of the China Cultural Center in Bangkok, and Juthamas Na Songkhla, Secretary-General of the Writers’ Association of Thailand. The event was officially opened by Yang Xiaolong, Cultural Counsellor of the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China in Thailand.
Yang Xiaolong, Cultural Counsellor of the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China in Thailand, said that the China–Thailand comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership is currently operating at a high level, while the concept that “China and Thailand are one family” has become deeply rooted in the hearts of the people. Using poetry as a medium, he said, represents a gentle yet powerful expression of this shared understanding.
Literary exchanges between China and Thailand have a long history and have now expanded into diverse forms across multiple levels and fields. Poetry requires genuine emotion and feeling, and poets from both countries should listen attentively to one another through dialogue and exchange. He expressed hope that the dialogue would create more opportunities for mutual translation and collaborative creation, breathing new life into the poetry of both countries.
Juthamas Na Songkhla, Secretary-General of the Writers’ Association of Thailand, said that the friendship between China and Thailand is founded not only on 50 years of diplomatic relations, but also on a long tradition of cultural and literary exchange. Although poetry may be written in different languages, it can transcend borders and convey emotions shared by all humanity. She expressed hope that this exchange among Chinese and Thai poets, writers, and scholars would deepen mutual understanding and cooperation between the literary communities of the two countries, with literature and poetry serving as bridges of friendship and further advancing people-to-people and cultural exchanges between China and Thailand.
Zhang Ruoyu, Director of the China Cultural Center in Bangkok, said that the Mid-Autumn Festival is an important traditional Chinese festival. Bringing together poets and experts from China and Thailand in Bangkok was not only a literary exchange, but also a meeting of minds and a dialogue between civilizations. He expressed hope that the event would mark a new starting point for further exchanges and cooperation between the Chinese and Thai literary communities.
The event brought together nine poets, writers, and literary experts from China and Thailand as guest speakers for in-depth exchanges and discussions on poetry and literature.
The morning session featured an exchange of perspectives and poetry readings under the theme “When Poetry Meets: Thai–Chinese Poetic Voices Across the Frontiers of Language.” Representing Thailand were Chamaiporn Bangkombang, National Artist in Literature; Saksiri Meesomsueb, National Artist in Literature and S.E.A. Write Award-winning poet; and Chiranan Pitpreecha, S.E.A. Write Award-winning poet. They were joined by Chinese poets Liu Liu, Cheng Yong, and Zhang Huijun.
Poets from China and Thailand exchanged views on the development of poetry, distinctive approaches to poetic creation, and literary expression in both countries. They also shared their experiences and perspectives on their own creative processes and selected some of their favorite poems to read together. Through poetry readings and the exchange of ideas, the session highlighted the differences, similarities, and common ground between Chinese and Thai poetic cultures.
In the afternoon, the dialogue continued with a panel discussion titled “Poetic Voices Across Mountains and Seas: Connecting China and Thailand.” The Thai speakers included Assistant Professor Dr. Dhanate Vespada, independent scholar and former President of the Thai Language and Literature Association of Thailand under Royal Patronage; Chokchai Bundit, S.E.A. Write Award-winning poet; and Sunee Leelapornpinit, lecturer in the Academic Affairs Division at the Chinese International College, Dhurakij Pundit University. Chinese poets Liu Liu, Cheng Yong, and Zhang Huijun also participated in the discussion.
The panelists shared their views on a range of topics, including how poetry can move beyond literary circles and reach a wider public, the preservation and continuation of poetic traditions, the coexistence of artificial intelligence (AI) and poetry, and the future of Chinese–Thai literary exchanges. They also discussed the forms of expression and shared values found in the poetry of both countries within their different cultural contexts.
Chamaiporn Bangkombang, National Artist in Literature and a representative of Thai poets, said, “I am very pleased to be part of today’s event, as poetry is profound in nature. Learning about the history and connections between Thai and Chinese poetry has given me a clearer understanding of the poetic traditions of both countries, as well as a deeper appreciation of the human bonds we share. Hearing poetry recited in both Thai and Chinese, with each word carefully chosen to convey meaning and beauty, was truly impressive and deeply moving.”
Assistant Professor Dr. Dhanate Vespada, independent scholar and former President of the Thai Language and Literature Association of Thailand under Royal Patronage, representing Thai academics, said, “I am delighted to be part of today’s event, which has such a beautiful name. I believe that translation plays an important role in strengthening the connection between our two cultures. I have had the opportunity to learn about Chinese poetry since childhood and have always admired it. Thai poetry, however, has not yet been widely translated into Chinese, although there are some notable works, such as Lilit Phra Lo, which was translated from Thai into Chinese by Pei Xiaorui. I hope that relevant organizations will work together to support the continued creation of both Thai and Chinese poetry. I also place great hope in the new generation of poets. Today’s event is an excellent starting point for continued collaboration and for further strengthening the Thai–Chinese poetry community.”
Liu Liu, representing the Chinese poets, said, “Many events of this kind are held in China, but this is my first visit to Thailand to participate in a poetry festival like this. I feel deeply honored to be here and hope that, in the future, there will be more platforms and opportunities for exchanges between China and Thailand, as well as among poets from both countries, allowing us to learn from one another and read each other’s poetry.
“In China, poetry is shared and promoted in many different ways. At the community level, for example, there are numerous poetry groups and clubs that bring together people who share a passion for writing poetry. They provide opportunities for poetry lovers to meet, discuss, and exchange knowledge and ideas about poetry. Large-scale events such as this one, however, generally require support from local governments or relevant organizations in order to be organized on a larger scale.
“At the same time, poetry exchanges can take many forms and are highly accessible. Even in a small town or district, if just three to five people share a passion for writing poetry, they can regularly find time and a place to meet, learn from one another, and exchange ideas.
“On the occasion of my visit to Thailand, I would like to extend my best wishes to all our Thai friends, as well as members of the Chinese community in Thailand. I wish everyone good health and ever-growing prosperity. Thank you,” Liu Liu said.
The poetry gathering, “Chinese–Thai Poets Dialogue: Rejoicing in the Full Moon Across the World,” marked a day of meaningful encounters and exchanges among poets, writers, and scholars from Thailand and the People’s Republic of China. The event reflected the cultural ties connecting the peoples of the two countries through poetry—a form of expression that does not require people to speak the same language, yet has the power to bring their hearts closer together. It also offered participants an opportunity to experience the beauty of words from two cultures through poetry that transcends borders and embodies the spirit of enduring friendship.

title: Over 20,000 bird traps dismantled in Vietnam’s Ha Tinh
content:
Over 20,000 bird traps dismantled in Vietnam’s Ha Tinh
Authorities in Ha Tinh Province, north-central Vietnam have destroyed more than 20,000 traps set to capture migratory birds, releasing dozens of live decoys back into the wild as part of a campaign to protect wildlife during the migration season.
The provincial Forest Protection Department reported that 20,109 tools and devices used for hunting and trapping wild birds were confiscated and destroyed.
Officials also released 110 live decoy birds and those caught in traps back into their natural habitat, while one violator was fined VND3 million (US$115).
September marks the start of the annual migration season for many wild birds, when flocks stop to rest and feed in coastal fields and forests, making them vulnerable to traps set by hunters.
Since early September, forest rangers in Ha Tinh have worked with police and local authorities to patrol rural areas, dismantle traps, and raise public awareness about protecting migratory species.
The campaign follows an August directive from the Ha Tinh administration calling for stronger measures to safeguard wild and migratory birds.

title: Singapore cannot let its guard down and be complacent about peace and security: PM Wong
content:
Singapore cannot let its guard down and be complacent about peace and security: PM Wong
- PM Lawrence Wong warns Singapore against complacency in security, citing recent close calls with self-radicalised individuals planning attacks.
- SGSecure's 10th anniversary highlights the importance of public vigilance, community trust, and preparedness to maintain safety and counter extremist threats.
- New initiatives include an AI chatbot to enhance public awareness and response across schools, workplaces, and communities.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – The many years of peace and security in Singapore may result in people letting their guard down, but this is a form of complacency the Republic cannot afford, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Sept 23.
In a speech to mark SGSecure’s 10th anniversary, PM Wong said an ordinary day in Singapore is nothing dramatic, but this sense of safety should not be taken for granted.
He noted reports of close calls, with the authorities stopping potential lone-wolf attacks just weeks before they were due to be carried out.
The self-radicalised individuals include a 17-year-old whom the Internal Security Department (ISD) detained in 2024 while he was planning an attack at a neighbourhood centre near Tampines West Community Club.
“We managed to intervene in time before anyone was hurt. But things could have turned out very differently.
“So I ask myself: Can we keep catching every case in time? What if one day, despite our best efforts, something gets through? No security system can give us a 100 per cent guarantee.
“That is why we cannot become complacent about safety and security in Singapore,” said PM Wong, adding that the country has been fortunate so far.
He noted that the security agencies have worked tirelessly behind the scenes, detecting individuals who posed a danger, disrupting plots and intervening before anyone was harmed.
“As prime minister, whenever I am briefed about such a case, my first reaction is relief,” said PM Wong, at the event held at Our Tampines Hub.
He said Singaporeans go about their daily lives and attend religious services, take public transport, go for a walk at night in their neighbourhood and watch their children go to school without constantly worrying about danger.
They are used to their country being safe, he said, adding: “These things feel normal to us. But look around the world, and you realise that what we regard as normal in Singapore is actually quite exceptional.
“What we have today is possible only because we have all worked hard to keep Singapore safe – through our security agencies, and by building preparedness and trust across our society.”
He said SGSecure was launched 10 years ago to get Singaporeans to stay alert to threats and know what to do if something were to happen, and, in the event of an attack, to stay calm, help one another and not allow fear or hatred to divide society.
PM Wong said Singaporeans need to speak up when they see behaviour that is not right, and not walk away.
This includes not assuming someone else will deal with an unattended bag spotted in a public place, or ignoring a friend or family member who is drawn to extremist material online.
“To be clear, we do not want Singaporeans to live in fear, or be suspicious of everyone around them. We want to continue going about our lives with confidence and peace of mind.
“But we can only do so if we are alert and prepared, and take sensible action when something does not seem right,” he said, adding that SGSecure remains important for this reason.
PM Wong lauded the progress made so far, noting that more Singaporeans now know what to do in a crisis, including how to help someone in distress and protect those around them.
Neighbourhoods, workplaces, schools, religious and community organisations are now better prepared to deal with emergencies, he said.
“And we have built stronger bonds of trust across our society. These bonds become especially important if an attack is motivated by race or religion,” PM Wong added.
He pointed out that after ISD detained the 17-year-old, the Tampines GRC Community Response Roundtable quickly brought religious leaders together.
“They stood together and sent a clear message: such violent extremist ideologies represent none of our communities, and would not divide us.
“That is the resilience we need,” he added.
Terrorism threat
PM Wong’s remarks come amid the release of an annual threat assessment report by ISD, which showed that the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East are contributing to the high terrorism threat facing Singapore.
The report on Sept 10 noted that the conflicts have contributed to growing hostilities between communities, and anti-Semitism has surged in many parts of the world. Anti-Muslim rhetoric and Islamophobia have also intensified.
ISD said youth radicalisation is also a pressing concern, with the number of cases involving young people in the past five years almost quadrupling from four between 2017 and 2021 to 15 cases since 2022.
At the event, PM Wong attended an exhibition showcasing how Singaporeans can stay alert and keep the Republic safe.
The exhibits, which will be held at Our Tampines Hub from Sept 23 to 27, include a series of giant inflatables showing Singapore icons, collectively dubbed as the “SGSecure Kakis”, with each representing a specific role.
The event was also attended by Edwin Tong, Minister for Law and Second Minister for Home Affairs, and Sim Ann, Second Minister for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs.
In a release on Sept 23, the Ministry of Home Affairs announced that it is trialling an artificial intelligence-powered WhatsApp chatbot to help SGSecure advocates, volunteers and front-line officers access resources, guidance and test their knowledge while they engage with the public.
Other upcoming initiatives include expanding the SGSecure Advocate Programme, which trains community members to share messages on recognising threats, staying safe and reporting signs of radicalisation.
Piloted at institutes of higher learning in 2024, the programme is being extended to schools, workplaces, religious and other community organisations.
The SGSecure movement was launched by then Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong to help Singaporeans understand the evolving security landscape and new threats, as well as equip them with skills to respond during an attack.
The movement has actively engaged the community, with more than 716,000 households participating since 2016.

title: Mural of rapper Macklemore painted in Gaza after Ed Sheeran tour furore
content:
Mural of rapper Macklemore painted in Gaza after Ed Sheeran tour furore
- Artists in Gaza painted a mural of rapper Macklemore wrapped in a Palestinian flag to thank him for supporting Palestine after he was removed from Ed Sheeran's tour.
- Macklemore donated US$1 million from the tour to Gaza aid groups, sparking matching pledges from other celebrities and highlighting the need for sustained support.
- Gaza remains devastated with stalled reconstruction and ongoing humanitarian needs, as locals value celebrity solidarity for raising awareness and pushing for peace.
AI generated
GAZA/JERUSALEM – Artists in Gaza have painted a mural of Macklemore wrapped in a Palestinian flag on a huge slab of concrete in the ruins of Gaza City, after the US rapper was kicked off Ed Sheeran’s upcoming tour for calling for a “Free Palestine”.
The mural, on a slab that leans against ruined buildings surrounded by rubble, depicts the “Thrift Shop” rapper raising a fist in the air.
“Thank you for using your voice for Palestine,” it reads.
“We wanted to send a message to thank rapper Macklemore in this simple way,” said Anne Redwan, 26, who designed and painted the mural with fellow artist Qusai al-Helo.
“As an artist living under siege here in Gaza, we are waiting for support from anyone who can see (the) persecution we live under,” she said. “We can paint murals bigger than this to express our feelings.”
Macklemore, who has long supported Palestinian causes, was cut from British pop star Sheeran’s musical line-up over remarks on stage criticising Israel’s military assault in Gaza, which was launched after Hamas-led fighters attacked Israel in October 2023.
Sheeran said he was unable to keep Macklemore on the tour after stadium owners refused to let him appear. US billionaire Robert Kraft, owner of Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts where his New England Patriots American football team plays, said he had barred Macklemore from appearing there for anti-Semitism, which the rapper denies.
Nearly a year after a ceasefire ended major fighting in Gaza, reconstruction has yet to begin. Most buildings have been destroyed and more than two million residents are confined to around a third of the enclave’s territory, mostly in tents or crowded rooms in damaged buildings among the ruins.
A US-brokered plan to end the war has stalled, with negotiators failing to agree to conditions for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.
The furore over Sheeran’s tour has led to a series of pledges from those involved to send money. Macklemore said on Sept 16 he would donate his US$1 million (S$1.3 million) in net earnings from the tour to six aid groups supporting Gaza.
Kraft, in turn, said Sheeran had told him he would donate US$2 million for aid in the region and had asked him to match the pledge. Sheeran has not commented on any donations. Macklemore’s donation drew a matching US$1 million pledge from Ms Rachel, a popular children’s TV personality.
Aid agency officials said the boost in celebrity attention could help bring more support to Gaza, where nearly all residents rely on aid for food, water, medical care and shelter.
“But what’s really most important is that people who have been so generous keep fighting over a sustained time,” said Toby Fricker, a local official with UNICEF. “That’s why we really call for sustained support, not one-off peaks, but sustained.”
Hussein Murtaja, who runs a Gaza humanitarian group that provides mental health support to children, said Macklemore’s solidarity matters more than the money he donated.
“When artistes of this stature, with this many followers or fans, all come to know more about the cause, and support reaching a political solution, support achieving peace for the people of Gaza... That means a great deal to us.” REUTERS

title: Thailand weighs minimum delivery rider pay, platform pushes back
content:
Thailand weighs minimum delivery rider pay, platform pushes back
Thailand is moving towards a minimum compensation framework for app-based delivery riders, with officials looking beyond an ongoing dispute involving Lalamove to develop rules that could eventually apply more broadly across digital platforms.
Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said the ministry is collecting information on rider costs and payment rates to develop a minimum-rate formula.
Rather than relying only on data from Lalamove and its riders, officials plan to expand the study to other platforms and groups of workers before deciding what an appropriate benchmark should look like.
The work could eventually feed into legislation covering platform workers, a group that currently does not have a specific law directly regulating compensation in this area.
Chaichanok said discussions with the Electronic Transactions Development Agency (ETDA) and the Labour Ministry have included the possibility of separating platform workers from a broader independent-worker bill and developing dedicated legislation because their work arrangements and operating costs differ from those of other self-employed workers.
That means the current disagreement over Lalamove rates may have implications beyond one company.
A pay dispute with bigger implications
The ministry is using talks between Lalamove and rider representatives as part of the process of determining what costs should be included when calculating a minimum rate. However, Chaichanok stressed that the government does not currently have the power to simply order an individual platform to increase its payments.
Instead, officials want to establish a broader standard that could later be supported by law.
The latest three-way talks between the ministry, ETDA, Lalamove and rider representatives took place on September 17. ETDA said the parties agreed in principle on the types of factors that should be considered when calculating minimum compensation, although the figures to be inserted into that formula remain unresolved.
What should riders earn?
One of the biggest disagreements is how much riders actually need to earn per kilometre.
Rider representatives are seeking a rate of 10 baht per kilometre. Their own calculation puts operating costs at 6.69 baht per kilometre, taking into account factors including fuel, vehicle wear, life insurance and other expenses, with a 400-baht minimum wage used as part of the calculation.
Lalamove disputes that methodology, arguing that the minimum wage is not an appropriate basis for calculating rider costs. The company has not agreed to the proposed 10-baht rate and is still considering its payment structure.
There is also a significant disagreement over how common very low-paying jobs are.
Rider representatives claim around 80% of jobs pay less than 3.70 baht per kilometre. Lalamove says its own data shows the figure is closer to 3%, down from around 5% cited previously.
Chaichanok said the company’s underlying operational data had not yet been submitted to the ministry for examination, meaning the competing figures have not been independently resolved.
Lalamove has indicated that it is prepared to provide information to officials, although the minister noted that companies are not currently compelled to disclose commercially sensitive data.
The ministry has also asked Lalamove to consider adjusting its rate structure so that no rider receives less than 3 baht per kilometre. The company has not agreed to that proposal and remains in the process of reviewing its rates.
Some other rider complaints have already resulted in changes. According to Chaichanok, Lalamove reduced a suspension imposed for refusing jobs from three days to one, established a hub for complaints and appeals, and introduced a choice between 5-kilometre and 10-kilometre job-radius settings.
What this could mean for other platforms
For riders working on other apps, however, the more important development is what happens next with the minimum-rate study.
Chaichanok said officials need information from a wider range of platforms and workers so that any eventual formula is not based on conditions at a single company. The ministry intends to use that broader dataset to determine which costs should count and how a minimum compensation level could be applied within a future legal framework.
The independent-worker bill had already progressed through the Council of State before the change of government, according to Matichon, but is expected to undergo further consultation and review. Discussions are now considering whether platform workers should instead be covered by separate legislation.
No minimum rate has yet been agreed, and there is no guarantee that the figures being discussed in the Lalamove talks would become the standard for other platforms.
Further discussions are expected after Chaichanok returns from the United Nations General Assembly, with the minister planning to hear separately from rider representatives and Lalamove while officials continue gathering data from elsewhere in the platform economy.

title: Wedding, funeral music not allowed before 6am, after 10pm in Vietnam
content:
Deputy Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Trinh Thi Thuy on Monday signed a consolidated document bringing together regulations on civilized practices at weddings, funerals and festivals.
The regulations require individuals and organizations to ensure that weddings, funerals and festivals do not violate traditional cultural values or involve superstitious practices.
Such events must not be used to cause divisions within communities, clans or families, or affect traffic safety and public order.
Gambling in any form is also prohibited.
Officials and organizations are also not allowed to use working hours or official vehicles to attend weddings or festivals, except when doing so as part of their duties. Public funds cannot be used to buy wedding gifts or gifts for bereaved families.
Wedding ceremonies should be formal but economical, joyful and healthy.
Traditional practices such as family introductions, engagement ceremonies and the bride’s procession may be observed, but they should not be elaborate or involve excessive demands for gifts.
Decorations should be simple, while the bride and groom should wear appropriate and culturally respectful clothing.
Wedding music should be wholesome and cheerful, with sound levels kept within permitted limits.
Couples and their families are also encouraged to lay flowers at monuments, cemeteries honoring fallen soldiers and historical and cultural sites, plant commemorative trees and wear traditional clothing or attire representing their ethnic group on their wedding day.
For funerals, if a deceased person has no family or relatives to organize the funeral, local authorities are responsible for coordinating with mass organizations to arrange the funeral and burial in accordance with traditional customs.
Funerals should be conducted respectfully and solemnly, while avoiding unnecessary expense and reflecting national cultural traditions and the family’s circumstances.
Local authorities are responsible for facilitating funeral arrangements and encouraging families to abandon outdated customs and superstitious practices.
Funeral attire and flags should follow local, ethnic or religious traditions, with funeral flags displayed only at the funeral venue.
The sound levels of funeral music must remain within permitted limits. If the deceased belonged to a particular religion or ethnic minority, music associated with that religion or ethnic group may be used.
The regulations prohibit scattering Vietnamese or foreign currency along funeral processions.
Burials must take place in cemeteries or in accordance with local land-use plans.

title: How Megan Khung’s case could have unfolded differently if MSF’s new unit had been in place
content:
How Megan Khung’s case could have unfolded differently if MSF’s new unit had been in place
- Megan Khung’s 2020 death highlights how scattered information across agencies can delay action in child abuse cases.
- Singapore’s new SAFER unit, launched in September, connects data from multiple agencies to identify at-risk children earlier.
- Since June, SAFER flagged 70 cases, prompting timely reviews and interventions to better protect vulnerable children like Megan.
AI generated
SINGAPORE - Warning signs can be missed when information about a child’s safety and his or her family is scattered across different agencies. Connecting the dots – and taking timely action – can make a crucial difference for the vulnerable children involved.
For four-year-old Megan Khung, who died in 2020 after prolonged abuse at the hands of her mother and the woman’s boyfriend, fragmented information about her circumstances played a part in the tragedy.
A new government unit officially launched on Sept 22 aims to strengthen the child protection system so that cases like Megan’s are less likely to fall through the cracks.
SAFER, which stands for Sensemaking Alerts for Frontline Engagement and Response, collates and analyses information from the police, Central Narcotics Bureau and other agencies, and alerts protective services more promptly to the child’s risks.
Had the new unit been in place then, Megan’s case would have been flagged for review about five months before her death, said the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF).
The unit started in June. In its first two months of operations, it has flagged 70 cases to the ministry’s Protective Service and specialised agencies that manage child abuse cases.
Most of them were existing cases with notable developments, such as a parent’s arrest. One case was previously unknown to MSF or other agencies.
Here is how Megan’s case could have unfolded differently if SAFER had existed at the time, and how the new unit has intervened in three other ongoing cases.
1) How Megan’s case could have been different
Among other information, SAFER would have known about the pre-school’s report about Megan’s injuries and the police report made by the girl’s grandmother when she went missing, and could have flagged it to the authorities.
2) Discovering an unknown case
The authorities were not aware of this family until SAFER picked up a police report filed by a family member and, in June, alerted the relevant agencies, which discovered there was more than met the eye.
3) Assessing an existing case
When a mother asked to increase the frequency of access to her child in June, SAFER picked up crucial facts that helped the case worker make an informed decision.
4) Escalating an existing case
These parents kept mum about their arrest for suspected drug offences, but it was uncovered by SAFER in time and the family’s case was escalated to the authorities in August.
