title: What's making it harder for American family farms to survive
content: By — Judy Woodruff Judy Woodruff By — Sarah Clune Hartman Sarah Clune Hartman Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/whats-making-it-harder-for-american-family-farms-to-survive Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Transcript Audio For generations, the family farm has been central to the American story. But these days, farmers are struggling with sharply higher costs and crushing debt on top of the same economic pressures the rest of the country feels. Judy Woodruff reports on what it takes to keep a farm going and who will carry on the tradition. It's part of her series, Crossroads: America at 250. Read the Full Transcript Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors. Amna Nawaz: For generations, the family farm has been central to the American story. But, these days, farmers are struggling with sharply higher costs and crushing debt, on top of the same economic pressures the rest of the country feels.Judy Woodruff reports from Western Kansas on what it takes to keep a farm going and who will carry on the tradition. It's part of her series Crossroads: America at 250. Cole Carpenter, Triple C Farms: This corn should be six feet tall. Judy Woodruff: There's no corn harvest for Cole Carpenter this fall after a severe drought this summer stunted its growth. Cole Carpenter: It's tough, no matter which way you look at it. Judy Woodruff: For generations of Americans, farming was a way of life, work the land, make a living, and pass it on. At the nation's founding, nine in 10 Americans were farmers. Today, fewer than 2 percent are.Sarah Mock, Author, "Farm (and Other F Words): The Rise and Fall of the Small Family Farm": To Thomas Jefferson, America was always an agricultural experiment. We were always going to be the agricultural powerhouse of the world, and that was going to be the bedrock of our nation. Judy Woodruff: We met agricultural journalist Sarah Mock at Old Town Farm in Albuquerque, New Mexico, a former horse farm turned into a cafe and event space. Sarah Mock: Jefferson crafted this, like, yeoman idea of people who are close to the land and therefore have this, like, sense of community and loyalty and patriotism that had really not been seen by Europeans in like hundreds of years. Cole Carpenter: Yes, farming is a gamble. Judy Woodruff: I first met Cole Carpenter at his farm near Leoti, Kansas, 20 years ago, when I was reporting for a documentary about millennials. Cole's grandfather, Dale Appl, had been farming for decades. The land had been in his family since the late 1800s. But even in 2006, there were doubts about whether farming could support the next generation. Dale Appl, Farmer: And I told him he ought to have another profession. He could still farm on the side. And he might have to yet. I don't know. It's pretty tough. Judy Woodruff: Twenty years later, the Carpenters are still farming. They have expanded it 10,000 acres, added cattle, and a crop spraying business. But margins are slim. Two years ago, Cole and his wife, Bridget, sold 800 acres to put capital back into the operation.Was that a tough decision? Cole Carpenter: Oh, yes, 100 percent, yes, yes. I mean, that -- it doesn't go easily. But at the same time, the less debt, the less stress was an easier decision there. Judy Woodruff: Around them, larger operations bought up smaller farms, mirroring a national trend. The number of farms in the U.S. declined 10 percent between 2012 and 2022 to about 1.9 million. At the same time, the average size grew by 5 percent. Cole Carpenter: And it felt like we were on an island. Like, land is being gobbled. Judy Woodruff: All around you. Cole Carpenter: Around you. One of my grandpa's biggest thing was, he always said, don't worry about what the neighbors are doing or what's going on around you. Take care of what you have, keep working, and you will be fine. Judy Woodruff: Now just 4 percent of farms, the largest family operations, account for more than half of all agricultural sales. And Carpenter says the challenge isn't just producing more. It's paying for everything it takes to do it. Cole Carpenter: All the technology, all the seed we have, we're able to grow more, but it also comes with a cost. Judy Woodruff: But even with all the latest technology, those who work the land still face risks they can't control. Cole Carpenter: You can stick your hand in. Judy Woodruff: Weather, commodity prices, land costs, politics, and tariffs. Cole Carpenter: At the end of the day, we don't really have any control over what the price of wheat is today or the price of corn is. I think the American farmer and rancher is kind of caught in a wicked loophole. You know what I mean? We're just trying to survive. Sarah Mock: Jefferson's idea of how farms were going to work lasted well into the late 1800s. We really thought it's going to be fine, there's always going to be land, anyone who wants it and who has the right effort and the grit is going to have their chance. Judy Woodruff: That idea at our founding depended on one thing: There was always more land to take. But by the late 1800s, that was changing.Still, that classic image of the farmer has endured, independent, self-sufficient, and deeply rooted to the land, as seen in Grant Wood's iconic American Gothic, a painting of a stoic farmer and his daughter in 1930. Narrator: In the Wheat Belt, farmers face ruin. Judy Woodruff: But the reality has always been more complicated. The Dust Bowl and the Great Depression devastated farming, forcing many farmers off their land. The federal government stepped in and fundamentally reshaped farming into a larger, more mechanized industry. Sarah Mock: And that is basically the road we have been on since then. Farms have continued to get bigger. We have seen a huge drop-off in the total number of farmers. Judy Woodruff: And if you don't inherit land, Mock says, it is nearly impossible to make it. It's a story she explores in her book "Farm (and Other F Words): The Rise and Fall of the Small Family Farm." Sarah Mock: So I started out doing research for this book thinking, what can I learn about conventional agriculture and teach to first-generation farmers? What's the secret sauce? How do you make a farm last?And not spoil it, but it's money. Tim Peterson, Cedar Crest Farms: This is a used one. Judy Woodruff: It's a reality 71-year-old farmer Tim Peterson of Monument, Kansas, knows all too well. Tim Peterson: We have this mythical sense of what farmers are and what they do, and I think there's just -- people don't quite understand how financially and business-orientated it is nowadays. It's -- I don't know if you need quite an MBA to run a farm, but it's getting close. Judy Woodruff: He and his wife, Rebecca are facing the once unthinkable, the possibility of selling family land to pay down about $800,000 of debt. Tim Peterson: It's really hard, actually, because you give up opportunities. You give up an opportunity into the future. You will not be able to ever buy that land back. Some of the land we would sell, oh, my, well, it's been in the family certainly since the 1920s, so over 100 years, easy. Judy Woodruff: For his daughter Lydia, who works in Topeka, this land is part of her family's legacy.Lydia Peterson, Daughter of Tim Peterson: I think it's inspiring to think about all of the blood, sweat and tears my great grandparents have put into the land, and then my grandparents, several generations of hard work that the land represents. Judy Woodruff: Last fall, Lydia tried to buy back a piece of family land at an auction, but instead of the expected $350,000 price tag, it sold for $540,000. Tim says the economics of farming have become increasingly unpredictable. Tim Peterson: We will be up maybe $130,000 and then we're down $60,000 the next. Judy Woodruff: It's that volatile? Tim Peterson: Yes, it's quite volatile, and because of the crop prices and the yield. We're all -- we're really dependent on yields. Judy Woodruff: The costs of staying in business can be enormous. Nationwide, farm debt has risen sharply, up an estimated 70 percent from 10 years ago. Tim Peterson: What really kind of scares me in terms of American farming is the fact that -- the consolidation of the industry. That troubles me a lot. If you have got a farm that has 120,000 acres versus a farm that has 1,800 acres, all of a sudden you lose that diversity and the decision-making. Cole Carpenter: I mean, this obviously has withstood. Judy Woodruff: And yet the next generation hasn't given up. Cole Carpenter's sons, Huck, age 15 and Chase, 18, are still in high school, but say they want a farm. They would be the sixth generation to work on this land. Huck Carpenter: The big corporations around us are always trying to expand and take over more territory. So keeping our ground and being financially stable, it's going to be difficult. Chase Carpenter: From my grandpa to my great-grandpa, it's always been how proud this family farm was, and how we have always rolled through punches and just always came out on the end. Judy Woodruff: But their dad, just like his grandpa 20 years ago, wants them to have a choice. Cole Carpenter: I want them to be happy in whatever they do, whatever way they want to go. I hope it's coming back here. But at the same time, if it's not, that's fine, because I think life's too short to be trying to do something that you don't want to do to make somebody else happy. Judy Woodruff: And for Sarah Mock, there's something even deeper at stake, the connection that comes from knowing a particular piece of land. Sarah Mock: Being close to land and not just owning it by having the deed, but owning a place by knowing it, by being able to say, like, oh, I know where that turn in the river is. Nothing makes you more patriotic than knowing the land. Judy Woodruff: For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Judy Woodruff in Leoti, Kansas. She has covered politics and other news for five decades at NBC, CNN and PBS. @judywoodruff By — Sarah Clune Hartman Sarah Clune Hartman

title: Zelensky meets with young people from Carpathian Eight countries
content:
Zelensky meets with young people from Carpathian Eight countries
The President of Ukraine announced this on Facebook, Ukrinform reports.
“Today, I met with young people from the countries of the Carpathian Eight. They are currently in Ukraine, in our Ivano-Frankivsk region. This is very important because the Carpathian Initiative is about the future and development, and that means young people above all. And we are designing our integration projects, including the C8, with the future of young Ukrainians in mind,” he said.
At the meeting, participants discussed Ukraine’s relations with the countries of the Carpathian macro-region and the importance of unity, as well as conditions for people to return home from abroad and housing support programs.
“I expect the Cabinet of Ministers to step up communication about all the government programs that offer favorable terms for buying a home. We need to fight to keep our young people in Ukraine while encouraging people from other countries to come here and help us rebuild and create,” Zelensky stressed.
According to the Office of the President, about 250 representatives of active youth from the Carpathian regions of Ukraine, Romania, Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia, Poland and Austria took part in the event.
During the discussion, the President spoke about Ukraine’s relations with its neighbors, particularly Poland and Hungary. He stressed that Ukraine and Poland are friends because, first and foremost, they share common values.
According to Zelensky, the development of joint production, mutual investment and participation in Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction will bring the two countries even closer. The President said it was important to build as many bridges as possible with Hungary to bring the two countries closer both politically and at the people-to-people level.
The participants also discussed national communities – an issue relevant to all countries of the Carpathian region. The President believes that people should be proud that their countries are home to many different communities, each of which contributes culturally, historically and linguistically.
“We need to work to ensure that there are no problems for national minorities in Ukraine or for Ukrainians who are minorities in other countries, in our neighboring states. Because these are the same challenges and the same issues,” Zelensky stressed.
As reported by Ukrinform, Zelensky announced the launch of a new format, the Carpathian Eight (C8), bringing together Ukraine, Romania, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia, Austria and Serbia.
During the Carpathian Economic Forum, representatives of the C8 member countries presented a joint investment portfolio of 95 projects worth about €40 billion.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

title: National Park Service director calls Yellowstone's wild bison recovery an 'incredible conservation story'
content:
A little more than a century ago, Yellowstone's bison were hanging on by a thread.
Today, thousands of them roam the park. And the conservation challenge has shifted from simply saving the herd to figuring out how to manage a thriving one.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS
During an interview with OutKick OutDoors, Jessica Bowron, acting director of the National Park Service, called the recovery an "incredible conservation story."
After millions of bison once roamed the Great Plains, the animals were nearly wiped out across their historic range. Rebuilding those populations, Bowron said, has taken decades of careful scientific work and cooperation among the Park Service and its Tribal, state, local and federal partners.
"To show up at Yellowstone today and have the experience as a visitor of seeing a wild bison in a functioning ecosystem, I don't know that we could have predicted that 100 years ago," Bowron said.
That's a pretty remarkable turnaround.
And now, Yellowstone's bison are helping build conservation herds far beyond the park itself.
Yellowstone bison are finding new homes
Through the Bison Conservation Transfer Program, Yellowstone works with Tribal partners to relocate live bison that have completed the necessary quarantine process.
Since 2019, more than 600 bison have been transferred to 29 tribes across 13 states, according to Bowron. More than 200 were transferred in 2026 alone.
"This is one of the coolest parts of this entire conservation effort," Bowron said.
Once the animals are transferred, she explained, each tribe can manage its herd according to its own priorities and sovereignty.
"It's a great example of how we're able to establish and expand conservation herds through that kind of partnership," Bowron said.
But conservation success doesn't mean the work is finished.
In some places, rebuilding the population remains the goal. At Yellowstone, Bowron said the challenge now is largely about managing the healthy herd that's already there.
"I think at Yellowstone, we're in the latter — figuring out how to successfully manage the herd that we have with all of our partners," she said.
At the same time, the Park Service continues to pursue live-transfer opportunities with tribes interested in establishing or expanding conservation herds.
A conservation problem you want to have
The Yellowstone story is also a reminder that conservation wins don't happen overnight.
Bowron said rebuilding bison populations has taken decades of scientific monitoring and cooperation among Tribal, state, local and federal partners.
WHY TED TURNER'S APPROACH TO CONSERVATION IS THE MINDSET AMERICA DESPERATELY NEEDS RIGHT NOW
And even after a species rebounds, the work changes rather than disappears.
For generations, the question was whether wild bison could survive at all in places like Yellowstone.
Now, wildlife managers are dealing with a very different question: What do you do when the comeback works?
Bison don't care where Yellowstone's boundary lines are drawn. They move across a massive landscape, meaning managing a successful herd requires cooperation among the Park Service and the many communities and agencies surrounding it.
But the fact that there is a healthy herd to manage — and enough animals to help establish conservation herds elsewhere — would have been difficult to imagine a century ago.
For anyone who's ever sat in Yellowstone traffic because a bison decided the middle of the road belonged to him, it might be easy to forget just how close America came to losing that experience entirely.
SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER
Today, seeing those animals wander through the park feels almost inevitable.
It wasn't always.
So yeah, you can definitely call it a comeback.

title: These Black Los Angeles Residents May Soon Receive Environmental Reparations
content:
This story was originally published by Capital B and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
As a child in the 1950s and ’60s, Regina Martin became so used to the oil pumpjacks near her home that she assumed every child lived beside them. Everyone was made “sick to [their] tummy” by the sulfurous, rotten-egg smell that never seemed to leave, she thought.
Only until she was grown did she begin to see a possible connection between growing up on top of the nation’s largest urban oil drilling field and her own sickness and the asthma that affected her sister.
For over a century in Los Angeles and across the nation, Black people have been disproportionately likely to live near oil wells, the machinery that draws oil from deep underground. The pollution from these drilling sites are connected to birth complications, child development issues, respiratory illnesses, and cancer.
Now, a new California state law moves to turn that lived experience into a broader public-policy question: What does a state owe communities exposed to pollution for generations? And what happens when you can’t offer support to every family that has struggled through the harm?
California lawmakers have passed AB 1661, which would steer $5 million collected from penalized oil wells in Inglewood into direct cash aid for 1,000 nearby households with qualifying respiratory or reproductive health impacts. Some of LA’s Blackest suburbs and city neighborhoods, including Inglewood, Ladera Heights, and Baldwin Hills, surround the oil field.
The legislation, introduced by Assemblymember Isaac G. Bryan, is expected to be signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom by October. It sets aside enough money for payments of up to $5,000 for 1,000 impacted households under its initial structure. The money would come from the state’s community repair and reinvestment fund for people living nearest the oil field.
For Black communities living nearest to refineries, highways, landfills, and oil wells, this fund may signal something larger than one oil field or payment. It asks whether money can begin to repair harms accumulated across generations: lives cut short by illness, household wealth drained by medical bills and depressed property values, and the anxiety of raising children amid pollution.
Bryan and other supporters are calling it environmental reparations and say it is a model that could be replicated to make industrial companies help repair the damage borne by people living closest to polluting sites.
To Tianna Shaw-Wakeman, the environmental justice program director with Black Women for Wellness in LA, the law could provide a national organizing model. “My hope has always come at the community level, at the grassroots level,” she said. “I see how grassroots organizing has created long-term change in our local communities, and I see that that can be and is being replicated all over the country.”
For Bryan, who represents the communities surrounding the Inglewood Oil Field, the cash-assistance program is part of a longer fight over the field’s legacy. Bryan, the first Black legislator to chair the California Assembly’s Natural Resources Committee, said his constituents have faced lower life expectancies and higher rates of asthma and heart conditions for decades.
“The company has essentially just been extracting from the community with no investments in the community, no care in the community and what feels like no regard at times for the broader community,” Bryan told Capital B. “The community [is] due this repair, and it’s been long overdue.”
The measure builds on Bryan’s earlier legislation, AB 2716, which Newsom signed in 2024. That law requires the Inglewood Oil Field to close by 2030 and establish a penalty structure for low-producing wells. Low-producing wells can leak methane and other harmful gases into the air and water. To push operators to curb that pollution and clean up their sites, regulators imposed a penalty on companies that keep such wells operating. Bryan said operators are charged $10,000 per well each month, with the revenue directed into a community repair fund restricted to investments within 2.5 miles of the field.
The fund could eventually support affordable housing, urban greening, park infrastructure, and other community priorities, Bryan said. He described the cash program as a pilot that could help determine whether direct payments are the form of repair residents most want. “We know people are struggling,” he said. “We know one of the biggest tools against an increasingly unaffordable society is to just put more money in people’s pockets.”
As communities nationwide press for stronger environmental protections, California’s experiment could test whether government and industry are willing to move beyond preventing future harm and toward compensating people who have already lived with its costs.
“Community members who have been deeply impacted, whose health have been deeply impacted, have never gotten restitution for that in any sort of way. We deserve more than we have been getting,” Shaw-Wakeman said. “And as we transition our city, as we transition our county, part of that story has to be addressing past harms.”
At the same time, California has passed a law that would shield reparation payments from taxation. “California is actively preparing for the implementation of reparations programs,” said state Assemblymember Tina McKinnor, who introduced the legislation. “We must ensure that recipients receive the full benefit of these efforts.”
Three dozen community groups came together in support of the environmental reparations legislation. There were no groups in public opposition.
The legislation would not close the oil field or resolve the long-running fight over drilling in Los Angeles County.
Under the proposal, eligible households within 2.5 miles of the field could seek aid if a resident has experienced respiratory or reproductive health impacts. But the program’s practical reach will depend on how Los Angeles County designs the application process, what documentation it requires, and how it handles demand if more than 1,000 households apply. There are tens of thousands more households in proximity to the oil field.
Bryan said Los Angeles County was still working through how the assistance would be delivered. It could come as a lump-sum payment, monthly payments, or another structure, he said, and county officials were evaluating which approach would best serve families.
Shaw-Wakeman said Black Women for Wellness and its allies pushed for a process that does not force residents to clear burdensome or invasive hurdles to prove harm. The organization has urged officials to consider self-attestation rather than requiring applicants to produce medical records that may be difficult or costly to obtain.
That question of access may determine whether the fund actually proves relief or is another government program that excludes the people it was intended to help. Many families, particularly low-income ones, may be living with these illnesses without formal diagnoses.
The program also lands amid a larger debate over what should happen to urban oil sites once production ends. Environmental justice advocates have argued that closing wells is only the first step. They want operators held responsible for plugging wells, cleaning contaminated land, and ensuring that redevelopment does not displace the same neighbors who lived with the pollution.
As oil wells have closed in Los Angeles in recent years, rental prices and home values have risen, threatening to displace longtime Black residents.
“We can’t replace toxic oil extraction with gentrification,” Shaw-Wakeman said. “There is still a lot more to address beyond those 1,000 households. We’re trying to address the ways in which community members are still being harmed every day.”

title: Have an Apple iPhone 15 or 16? How to file a claim for up to $95.
content:
Apple settlement offers eligible iPhone owners up to $95. Here is how to file a claim.
The claim window is now open for an Apple settlement announced earlier this year, giving certain iPhone users the chance to get up to $95.
Apple agreed to pay $250 million to settle claims that it misled customers about Siri's Apple Intelligence features. Customers who were part of the class action lawsuit said they purchased iPhones expecting certain Siri features they allegedly did not receive.
"The $250 million settlement fund represents the largest false advertising settlement in history," Ryan Clarkson, co-lead counsel on the class-action lawsuit and founder and managing partner of Clarkson Law Firm, said in an email to CBS News.
Apple declined to comment. The company has previously denied the allegations. According to the settlement agreement, the settlement shall "not be construed in any fashion as an admission of liability or wrongdoing by Apple."
Here's what to know about eligibility and how to file a claim.
How do I file a claim?
iPhone users can visit SmartphoneAISettlement.com to file a claim, according to a spokesperson for Clarkson Law Firm, a public interest law firm.
The person must input basic personal information, including their name, address and phone number. They must also enter their iPhone's serial number, which can be found in the phone's Settings section.
Once they finish inputting that information, they can select the payment method. The options are PayPal, Venmo, direct deposit or check.
As SmartphoneAISettlement.com points out, consumers are limited to "one cash payment per eligible device." If they purchased another iPhone that meets the eligibility requirements, they must complete a separate claim form.
How do I know if I am eligible?
If you bought an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you're eligible to file a claim.
According to SmartphoneAISettlement.com, the person filing a claim must be the person who originally purchased the device. The phone must also be for personal or professional use, not for resale.
If you're not sure if you're eligible, you can call 1-888-988-8945 or write to this address for information: Landsheft, et al. v. Apple Inc.; Settlement Administrator; P.O. Box 301132; Los Angeles, CA 90030-1132.
How long do I have to file a claim?
The claims window is open until Dec. 21, 2026.
How much money will I receive?
Customers who submit a valid claim form will initially get $25 per eligible device. However, that amount may be increased up to $95 or decreased depending on the "total number of valid claims submitted and other factors," the claims website says.
When will I get the payment?
A district court in San Jose, California, will hold a hearing on Feb. 24, 2027, to decide whether to approve the settlement. If there are any appeals, it could delay the payment process.
"If there is no appeal, your settlement benefit will be processed promptly," according to the claim website.

title: Lopez: We don't need AI to threaten the future of humanity. We've got Trump's climate policies
content:
We don’t need AI to threaten the future of humanity. We’ve got Trump’s climate policies
- Click here to listen to this article
- Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Trump has gutted environmental protections and scientific research, and dismantled clean energy initiatives.
- Activists of all ages are organizing events to promote sustainability, biodiversity and other environmental causes.
You need a boost, right?
We’re living under a dark cloud, with a steady downpour of graft, thuggery and baloney.
There’s the raffling of presidential pardons and the attacks on reporters for doing their jobs, the clownish trade war with Canada, the bungled disaster in Iran, the petty obsessions with the ballroom and the Kennedy Center, the hogwash about a stolen election, the attacks on immigrants and the shameless presidential profiteering while working people suffer the cost of Trump’s countless broken promises.
I could go on, and I will. But rest assured, I have not forgotten about the boost I promised.
For all the affronts, nothing strikes me as more sinister than the Trump administration’s ambitious assault on the planet. Despite nearly daily headlines about the global calamity of overheated oceans, melting glaciers, stark weather transformations and species extinction, Trump keeps shoveling more coal onto a fire that will rage long after he’s dead and gone.
He’s gutted environmental protections and scientific research and dismantled clean energy initiatives. Now his administration is rolling back limits on power plant emissions, attempting to open the California coast to more oil drilling and sabotaging the state’s ambitious goals on emission controls and electric vehicle conversion.
We don’t need AI to threaten the future of humanity. We’ve got Trump.
It’s tempting to duck under the covers and wait for the nightmare to end, but the good news is that a lot of people are standing up rather than rolling over, rebelling against the ignorance and callous disregard that threatens our most precious and fragile shared inheritance.
In August, hundreds showed up to defend California’s authority to govern its own coast at a Santa Monica hearing of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Agency, and 18,000 more people filed comments online.
Letters to the Editor: The Coastal Commission has done the right things. Trump should back off
‘It is not the job of the people of California to compensate for Trump’s financial losses,’ writes an L.A. Times reader.
The rollback of environmental safeguards is, for many, a call to arms.
“Yes, I am discouraged. … But I am not despairing,” said Bill McKibben, an author and environmental activist who is organizing a worldwide event called Sun Day for next year to promote clean energy. “We’re reacting to multiple crises, and we’re led by a pack of fools, so why would anybody not stand up?”
McKibben launched a national movement five years ago called Third Act, and tens of thousands of people 60 and older have signed on to advocate for climate action, voting rights and civic participation. Third Act now operates in about 30 states, with a robust chapter in Southern California.
Former Times reporter Zan Dubin has worked as both a volunteer and a paid communications consultant for Third Act, and I asked her what someone could expect to do if they became a member of Third Act/SoCal.
“We do it all,” Dubin said, from promoting climate-friendly candidates to running phone banks and testifying at public meetings. She said Third Act co-sponsors protests at Dodger Stadium, and she and others planned to meet at Vin Scully Avenue and Stadium Way for Sunday’s game against the San Francisco Giants. They want the Dodgers to stop doing business with Big Oil and bench their sponsorship deal with Phillips 66.
She also called out Disneyland for its exhaust-spewing Autopia attraction, along with former Times climate columnist Sammy Roth, and Disneyland responded by announcing in 2024 that it was switching to electric cars beginning in 2027.
Dubin, co-founder of National Drive Electric Week, said 170 volunteer-led events were being held nationwide over the next month to promote EVs, and she was leading one Friday in Irvine.
“Action is absolutely the antidote to despair,” Dubin said. “I find that despite the onslaught of these horrifying headlines … taking action invigorates me.”
Claremont resident Margaret Davis knows that feeling. She emailed me in 2023, prior to participating in a Third Act event, and said many retirees have time on their hands, which puts them in a powerful position.
“The climate crisis is the greatest existential threat humans have ever faced, hence we live in a time when we can make the greatest change for the better,” Davis wrote at the time.
When I called her a few days ago, Davis told me she’s now a member of Senior Stewards Acting for the Environment. She lives at Pilgrim Place — a senior community with a focus on justice, peace and environment — where residents meet regularly to study, discuss and advocate for sustainability, biodiversity and environmental causes.
As legislative session closed, Newsom pushed environmental break for donor.
“When I was in college in 1970, we had the antiwar movement and that was the first year of Earth Day,” Davis said. “At the time, I thought Earth Day was just a distraction from what was going on in the world.”
Later, she said, “I came to realize it was the biggest issue of all time.”
Like Davis, I went to college in the ‘70s, and there’s no denying that our aggressively consumptive generation played a key role in manufacturing a crisis for our children and grandchildren. We’ve got matches in our hands and smoke on the horizon, and if we’re honest with ourselves, we’d see atonement not as a hobby, but as a duty.
As for the next generation, climate activist Sim Bilal, 24, said he too shares the sense that this is both a wickedly frightening time and a moment of opportunity.
“In the last month, we’ve gotten more young people involved,” said Bilal, executive director of Youth Climate Stewards 4 Local Action. “We usually have to reach out to them, but so many people have been wanting to get involved, and they’re so eager, and that’s been affirming for me. The policies are depressing, but the fact that people are reenergized and want to fight back is really exciting.”
Bilal said faith in politics, government and corporations is not high among his peers, but he’s trying to grow a network of young people to cultivate and support future leaders.
“A mentor told me there are two kinds of power — organized people, and organized money,” said Bilal, whose activism began when his grandmother died and he began wondering if her cancer, and global warming, were connected to the oil drilling in his South L.A. neighborhood. “We don’t have the money, but a lot of the work we do is political and civic education, demystifying power, and making people understand they have agency.”
You needed a boost, right?
There you go.
Whatever your age, do not despair.
Get off the chair.
steve.lopez@latimes.com

title: Cuộc thi Lan tỏa năng lượng tích cực 2026: Gốm chữa lành
content:
Gốm chữa lành - Tác giả: THANH MIỀN - ĐỨC VĨNH
Làm gốm đang trở thành một hoạt động yêu thích của giới trẻ, giúp họ thư giãn sau những giờ học tập và làm việc căng thẳng. Việc chạm tay vào đất và tạo ra sản phẩm riêng không chỉ mang lại niềm vui mà còn tạo ra năng lượng tích cực cho tâm hồn. Đây là cách tuyệt vời để tìm thấy sự bình yên trong cuộc sống hối hả.
Từ một khối đất thô sơ, qua đôi bàn tay và sự sáng tạo của mỗi người, những sản phẩm gốm dần thành hình và mang trong mình dấu ấn riêng. Với nhiều bạn trẻ, niềm vui đôi khi đến từ những điều rất nhỏ đó là tự tay làm nên một sản phẩm, trò chuyện cùng bạn bè và tận hưởng trọn vẹn những giờ phút không màn hình điện thoại.
Không chỉ là một hoạt động trải nghiệm, những workshop làm gốm thủ công còn tạo nên một không gian để mọi người gặp gỡ, trò chuyện và cùng nhau làm nên những sản phẩm mang dấu ấn riêng cho mình.
Giữa nhịp sống nhiều áp lực, đôi khi một chút chữa lành không cần bắt đầu từ những điều quá lớn lao. Chỉ cần rời khỏi màn hình, chạm vào đất, sống chậm lại và tìm về với bản ngã của chính mình.

title: Hoạt động Đoàn ở trường có sát nhu cầu, cán bộ Đoàn có sáng tạo mới hút học sinh
content:
Chị Hồ Thị Ánh Tuyết nhấn mạnh điều này tại tổng kết hoạt động Đoàn các trường học thuộc Đoàn phường, xã, đặc khu năm học 2025 - 2026 ngày 18-9 diễn ra tại Trường Đoàn Lý Tự Trọng.
Hoạt động bám đặc thù từng trường, chủ động học mô hình hay
Đánh giá các cán bộ Đoàn trường sáng tạo, linh động, có sự kết nối và hoạt động Đoàn khu vực trường học ngày càng hiệu quả, song soi vào tỉ lệ 67,89% hiện có, chị Ánh Tuyết đặt câu hỏi: “Các bạn chưa tham gia vì chưa đủ điều kiện, hay vì chưa thấy được giá trị của tổ chức Đoàn?".
Do đó thời gian tới, theo Phó bí thư thường trực Thành Đoàn TP.HCM, công tác Đoàn ở trường học cần xác định những nhiệm vụ trọng tâm, điểm nhấn rõ ràng theo từng nhóm đối tượng, để dễ hình dung và phù hợp đặc thù từng địa bàn.
Công tác giáo dục cần tìm nét riêng và học hỏi mô hình, giải pháp hiệu quả từ trường bạn.
Việc giáo dục cần gắn liền với rèn luyện kỹ năng nghề nghiệp, tinh thần khởi nghiệp, trách nhiệm xã hội, hướng đến tạo nguồn cán bộ trẻ, đoàn viên ưu tú giới thiệu cho Đảng.
"Phải đổi mới mạnh mẽ phương thức tổ chức hoạt động, chú trọng trải nghiệm thực tiễn, đặc biệt là các hoạt động tại địa chỉ đỏ, địa danh lịch sử. Cần duy trì hiệu quả các hoạt động phối hợp theo cụm, tạo không gian để các trường chia sẻ nguồn lực, hỗ trợ cán bộ, cùng giải quyết vấn đề thực tiễn.
Mục tiêu để có được hoạt động chất lượng, phù hợp với nhu cầu, sở thích của đoàn viên, thanh niên và định hướng của Đoàn cấp trên", chị Tuyết lưu ý.
Nâng tỉ lệ đoàn viên trong học sinh lên 80%
Phó bí thư Thành Đoàn TP.HCM Nguyễn Đăng Khoa nói hoạt động Đoàn khu vực trường học ngày càng phù hợp lứa tuổi học sinh, phát huy hiệu quả công nghệ và phương thức giáo dục mới. Đã có những mô hình kết hợp công nghệ, sản phẩm truyền thống trên nền tảng số giúp học sinh sáng tạo, nâng cao niềm tự hào về lịch sử, văn hóa dân tộc.
Phong trào “Học sinh 3 tốt”, hoạt động tình nguyện tạo môi trường để học sinh rèn luyện, thể hiện trách nhiệm với cộng đồng.
Tuy nhiên tỉ lệ đoàn viên tại các trường THPT mới đạt hơn 54%, trong khi mục tiêu hướng đến phải là 80%.
Cùng với đó, chất lượng cán bộ Đoàn chưa đồng đều cũng như sự phối hợp giữa Đoàn trường với địa phương chưa thường xuyên, ứng dụng chuyển đổi số trong hoạt động Đoàn cũng chưa "ngon".
Thành Đoàn TP.HCM lưu ý năm học mới chú trọng các điểm nhấn như: chiến dịch Xuân tình nguyện, Hoa phượng đỏ, mỗi trường có ít nhất 1 công trình thanh niên gắn với nhiệm vụ giảng dạy hoặc chăm lo học sinh, tỉ lệ đoàn viên trên tổng số học sinh đạt 80%...

title: More young people are getting involved with South Texas civil rights group amid Trump’s immigration crackdown
content:
Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state.
PHARR — Kimberly Trujillo became a card-carrying member of La Unión del Pueblo Entero only two months ago. But already, she’s stepped into a leadership position for one of the organization’s most important events.
The 24-year-old Brownsville native served as a delegate for LUPE’s biennial Cumbre de Miembros, a convention held in August that gathers LUPE members to determine which issues the group will mobilize around and how they will prioritize them.
As a delegate, Trujillo made the case to the rest of the membership for immigration as a top priority for them. It was the issue that motivated her to join LUPE, a community nonprofit, in the first place.
“I was really inspired by the work they were doing,” Trujillo said. “Seeing a campaign so dedicated to letting people know what their rights are, especially now amongst really harsh immigration enforcement, was important to me.”
Not surprisingly, the members voted immigration as its top priority at the organization’s convention this year.
Trujillo, like many her age, became involved with LUPE as immigrant communities across the nation face increased arrests and enforcement actions under President Donald Trump.
Participation in LUPE’s cumbre nearly doubled from 99 people in 2024 — the time it was held previously — to 197 in 2026, driven largely by an increase in members under the age of 45.
Getting involved
Trujillo first got involved by volunteering with LUPE in February after learning about a Know-Your-Rights campaign that the organization had launched in December.
The campaign, called “Valle Fuerte, Valle Libre,” consisted of distributing kits to the public that contained information about their rights in case they encountered officers with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
The Valle Fuerte campaign helped usher a shift in its membership, motivating younger people like Trujillo to get involved, said Tania Chavez Camacho, executive director of LUPE.
“We’ve actually seen a change,” Chavez Camacho said. “We’ve seen a lot of young people … and that has been surprising for us.”
This year, members under 45 years old made up the largest share of cumbre participants at 35%. Members between 45 and 64 years old made up 34%, while those 65 and older 32%.
Going by raw numbers alone, the membership participation in the cumbre of those under 45 years old also saw a significant increase, adding 36 to those who participated in this year’s cumbre. The 45 to 64 age group and the 65 and over each grew by 31 member participants.
The growth in participation this year prompted the group to shift its cumbre convention from its headquarters in San Juan, Texas, to a larger community center in Pharr. This increase in engagement comes despite fear among some in their ranks of being targeted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Involvement with the group comes despite disturbing allegations that were unearthed earlier this year against one of LUPE’s founders — Cesar Chavez. In March, the New York Times published accounts that Chavez, one of the most revered Latino civil rights leaders, sexually assaulted several girls and women, including Dolores Huerta who co-founded LUPE with Chavez.
Following the allegations, LUPE covered up a mural that pictured Chavez. The group also did not participate in any Cesar Chavez Day activities.
LUPE directors say the organization’s mission remains central to keeping its community safe.
“As an organization led by women, we knew the profound impact it would have on our community,” said a LUPE spokesperson said of news of the allegations against Chavez. “It was a moment to move intentionally, listen and learn from each other, and ground ourselves in our values of hope and justice.”
Despite the controversy that it caused, young LUPE members are still focused on the work that lies ahead.
“Their commitment lies with the issues impacting them currently, and that is leading the advocacy in the community organizing they participate in,” LUPE said. “Second to healing and facing this painful truth about Cesar Chavez, the historical preservation of the farmworker movement has been a concern for our membership, especially our movement elders who all contributed to the foundation of this work.
Taking action
As immigration enforcement increased in the Rio Grande Valley last fall, LUPE members began looking for ways to respond, said Dani Marrero Hi, deputy director of LUPE. That prompted LUPE to launch the Valle Fuerte, Valle Libre campaign, which focused on raising awareness of immigration arrests and providing residents with information about their rights.
“We wanted to give people something practical to do because there was so much anger,” she said.
It was particularly useful for people like Trujillo — those who are U.S. citizens or have some type of protected status and want to take action in support of those who are vulnerable to deportation and may not feel safe advocating for themselves.
In other places across the country, the issue of immigration has been a motivating factor for some Latinos, citing it as the most important issue for them in elections.
Outside elections, events like the cumbre provide Trujillo and others an opportunity to effectuate change in her community. And the organization is not just focused on immigration.
The members voted the economy as their second-highest priority, followed by health. Their other top issues, in order of priority, include civic participation, infrastructure, LGBTQ issues, youth education and unity and solidarity.
“It’s a testament to what’s a concern to the broader membership,” Chavez Camacho said.
During the event, the issues were presented in the form of resolutions that were formulated over months by working groups in the lead-up to the cumbre.
As the head of the immigration delegation, Trujillo and her group brainstormed actions they could take to address issues undocumented immigrants currently face.
Their goals include increasing transparency between public officials and the community and electing people who will value their members. They’re increasing awareness of constitutional rights among the public as much as possible.
“Our drive for this is that we think no one is free until we are all free, and so that really drove a lot of the components of our resolution,” Trujillo said.
Another change to the cumbre this year was that after the vote on the resolutions, the working groups broke off into groups to make definitive plans to decide what direction to take on their priorities.
The civic engagement team, for example, is tasked with coming up with a guided direction on which legislation they will engage with state lawmakers on during the 2027 legislative session.
Navigating current events
Given the increase of immigration enforcement, LUPE members and event attendees now ask before events whether ICE agents could be there.
Marrero said the organization couldn’t guarantee that agents won’t show up, but said LUPE’s events attract large numbers of people and doesn’t expect ICE to target one of its events.
“Ultimately, people have to make that personal decision of, ‘Well, I’m already living in so much fear, what else do I have left than to fight? What else do I have left than to fight for my family?” Marrero said. “I think that’s why we’re seeing so much member engagement.”
Organizing under the heightened attention and targeting of people who are undocumented has not been easy for the group, said Chavez Camacho, LUPE’s executive director. But, organizing has always had its challenges, she said, and addressing these issues is part of the reason LUPE exists in the first place.
“We are here to help advance the issues of the community through power building, and who has the power? The people,” she said.
Reporting in the Rio Grande Valley is supported in part by the Methodist Healthcare Ministries of South Texas, Inc.

title: Bổ sung chế độ bảo vệ người thân của thẩm phán
content:
Bổ sung chế độ bảo vệ người thân của thẩm phán
Ủy ban Thường vụ Quốc hội thông qua nguyên tắc nghị quyết về chế độ bảo vệ thẩm phán với nhiều nội dung quan trọng liên quan vợ chồng và người thân.
Sáng 24/9, Ủy ban Thường vụ Quốc hội xem xét, thông qua dự thảo Nghị quyết quy định về chế độ bảo vệ thẩm phán.
Nghị quyết áp dụng các quy trình, thủ tục bảo vệ thẩm phán khi thi hành công vụ hoặc trong trường hợp cần thiết. Thân nhân của thẩm phán (gồm vợ hoặc chồng, cha mẹ đẻ, cha mẹ vợ hoặc chồng, cha mẹ nuôi, con đẻ và con nuôi) được bảo vệ khi tính mạng, sức khỏe, tài sản, quyền và lợi ích hợp pháp khác bị xâm phạm hoặc đe dọa xâm phạm liên quan công việc của thẩm phán.
Người thân có thể được đưa đến nơi an toàn
Cơ quan có thẩm quyền có thể yêu cầu người vi phạm chấm dứt hành vi xâm phạm; đưa thẩm phán hoặc thân nhân đến nơi an toàn; áp dụng biện pháp ngăn chặn, không cho đối tượng liên quan tiếp cận; giữ bí mật hoặc thay đổi thông tin, dữ liệu cá nhân, nơi ở, nơi làm việc. Trong trường hợp cần thiết, lực lượng, phương tiện và công cụ có thể được bố trí để trực tiếp bảo vệ an toàn cho thẩm phán và thân nhân.
UBND các cấp được giao tiếp nhận thông tin, chủ động nắm bắt tình hình nơi thẩm phán và thân nhân cư trú; chỉ đạo công an cấp xã và các đơn vị liên quan thực hiện biện pháp phòng ngừa, ngăn chặn khi phát sinh tình huống.
Nếu tính mạng, sức khỏe của thẩm phán hoặc thân nhân bị đe dọa do công việc của thẩm phán, Chánh án có thể đề nghị cơ quan công an, đơn vị quân đội có thẩm quyền áp dụng biện pháp bảo vệ.
Chánh án TAND Tối cao Nguyễn Văn Quảng cho biết nguy cơ thẩm phán bị đe dọa, tác động, trả thù hoặc xâm hại khi thi hành công vụ là vấn đề hiện hữu. Nhiều vụ án tham nhũng, kinh tế, chức vụ, tranh chấp đất đai, khiếu kiện hành chính kéo dài hoặc có nhiều người tham gia tố tụng dễ phát sinh mâu thuẫn. Thẩm phán có thể bị tác động, can thiệp trái pháp luật, đe dọa, xúc phạm danh dự, uy tín, thậm chí xâm phạm sức khỏe, tính mạng trong quá trình thực hiện nhiệm vụ.
Các hành vi xâm phạm xảy ra dưới nhiều hình thức, từ xúc phạm, đe dọa, gây áp lực, cản trở hoạt động xét xử đến hành hung, tấn công trực tiếp. Những vụ việc này không chỉ xảy ra tại phòng xử án mà còn trong quá trình xem xét, thẩm định tại chỗ, hòa giải hoặc làm việc với đương sự.
Vì vậy, việc ban hành Nghị quyết về chế độ bảo vệ thẩm phán là cần thiết nhằm phòng ngừa, ngăn chặn hành vi xâm phạm, bảo đảm an toàn cho thẩm phán và bảo vệ tính độc lập của hoạt động xét xử.
Nghị quyết có hiệu lực từ ngày 1/1/2027.
Sơn Hà

title: Sandbondtenga/Ziga: la jeunesse mobilisée pour une opération de salubrité à la gendarmerie
content:
BURKINA-SANDBONDTENGA- SALUBRITE-GENDARMERIE-ZIGA
Sandbondtenga/Ziga: la jeunesse mobilisée pour une opération de salubrité à la gendarmerie
Ziga, 19 sept. 2026 (AIB)-Une centaine de jeunes issus de plusieurs villages de la commune de Ziga se sont mobilisés, samedi, pour une opération de salubrité au sein de la brigade territoriale de gendarmerie, en signe de solidarité avec les Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS).
Armés de machettes, de dabas, de râteaux et d’autres outils, les jeunes ont consacré plusieurs heures au nettoyage de la cour de la brigade, rendant le cadre plus propre et dégagé.
La mobilisation a également enregistré la participation d’autorités administratives coutumières locales.
Pour le premier vice-président de la Délégation spéciale de Ziga, Adama Sawadogo cette initiative marque l’engagement de la jeunesse à contribuer à l’entretien des espaces d’intérêt collectif.
Le commandant de la brigade territoriale de Ziga, l’adjudant-chef, Azad Zakaria Ouattara, a salué l’engagement des jeunes.
« Cette mobilisation montre que la jeunesse est solidaire et peut faire face à toute adversité », a-t-il affirmé, estimant que l’initiative contribue également au rapprochement entre les forces de sécurité et les populations.
Agence d’Information du Burkina

title: Cách thay đổi thói quen để cai thuốc lá
content:
Cách thay đổi thói quen để cai thuốc lá
Hạn chế rượu bia, tránh khói thuốc và thay đổi cách giải tỏa căng thẳng giúp giảm nguy cơ tái hút thuốc.
Hạn chế rượu bia
Theo Very Well Health, uống rượu bia có thể làm giảm khả năng kiểm soát hành vi, khiến người cai thuốc lá dễ hút thuốc trở lại. Nguy cơ này rõ ở người từng có thói quen vừa uống rượu bia vừa hút thuốc. Khi tham gia các bữa tiệc, bạn có thể chọn đồ uống không cồn, ngồi ở khu vực không có người hút thuốc để giảm cảm giác thèm nicotine.
Tránh đến nơi có khói thuốc lá
Khói thuốc và hình ảnh người khác hút thuốc có thể khiến người cai nhớ lại thói quen cũ. Nên hạn chế đến những nơi thường có nhiều người hút thuốc, nhất là trong thời gian đầu.
Tại nhà, nên dọn bỏ thuốc lá, bật lửa, gạt tàn và các vật dụng liên quan. Giữ không gian sống không khói thuốc giúp giảm những tác nhân dễ dẫn đến hút thuốc trở lại.
Thay đổi cách giải tỏa căng thẳng
Nhiều người hình thành thói quen hút thuốc mỗi khi áp lực, mệt mỏi hoặc bực bội. Đi bộ, vận động nhẹ, tắm nước ấm, nghe nhạc hoặc trò chuyện với người thân có thể trở thành những lựa chọn thay thế. Khi cơn thèm hút thuốc xuất hiện do căng thẳng, bạn có thể trì hoãn vài phút, uống nước, nhai kẹo cao su không đường hoặc chuyển sang một hoạt động khác cho đến khi cảm giác muốn hút giảm xuống, theo Times of India.
Xây dựng nếp sinh hoạt khoa học
Thiếu ngủ, bỏ bữa hoặc sinh hoạt thất thường có thể khiến cơ thể mệt mỏi, dễ cáu gắt và khó kiểm soát cơn thèm thuốc. Người cai thuốc lá nên ngủ đủ, ăn đúng bữa và duy trì vận động. Lịch sinh hoạt ổn định giúp hạn chế những lúc buồn chán, căng thẳng dễ dẫn đến hút thuốc.
Người cai nên xác định mục tiêu và kiên trì với quyết định của mình. Thèm thuốc, bứt rứt, khó chịu là những triệu chứng thường gặp và thường giảm dần. Nếu lỡ hút lại, không nên bỏ cuộc mà cần xác định nguyên nhân, rút kinh nghiệm và tiếp tục cai thuốc lá.
Người thân nên kiên nhẫn, tránh trách móc hoặc tạo thêm áp lực khi người cai cáu gắt, bứt rứt hay mất tập trung. Một cuộc trò chuyện hoặc lời hỏi thăm đúng lúc có thể giúp họ thêm động lực duy trì việc cai thuốc lá.
Sau khi bỏ hút thuốc, chức năng phổi và thể lực có thể dần cải thiện, đồng thời giảm nguy cơ bệnh tim mạch và đột quỵ. Cai hút thuốc cũng giúp hạn chế người thân tiếp xúc với khói thuốc thụ động, nhất là trong không gian kín.
Lê Nguyễn (Tổng hợp)

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/ Lutte contre l’orpaillage illégal: des parlementaires sensibilisés aux enjeux de la professionnalisation de l’EMAPE
content:
Yamoussoukro, 22 sept 2026 (AIP) – Des parlementaires ivoiriens ont entamé, mardi 22 septembre 2026 à Yamoussoukro, un atelier de sensibilisation consacré aux enjeux de la structuration et de la professionnalisation de l’exploitation minière artisanale et à petite échelle (EMAPE), ainsi qu’aux dispositions du Code minier qui encadrent cette activité.
Organisé avec l’appui de l’ONG COGINTA, à travers le projet SECORCI 2, cet atelier vise notamment à renforcer la compréhension des parlementaires sur les dispositions du Code minier relatives à l’EMAPE et sur les enjeux liés à l’orpaillage illégal. Les travaux portent également sur les différentes étapes d’instruction des demandes d’autorisation d’exploitation, conformément aux procédures et à la plateforme e-cadastre.
Ouvrant les travaux, le préfet de région, préfet du département de Yamoussoukro, Coulibaly Gando, a souligné la nécessité de distinguer l’exploitation minière artisanale légale de l’orpaillage illégal, relevant que les activités autorisées par l’Etat doivent être exercées dans le respect des règles et sous l’encadrement des services compétents du ministère chargé des Mines.
Il a estimé que les parlementaires, en tant que représentants des populations et législateurs, doivent mieux comprendre les réalités du secteur afin d’apprécier les réponses à apporter aux préoccupations des communautés.
Pour le représentant pays de COGINTA et chef du projet SECORCI 2, Hypolite Sy, l’EMAPE constitue une source de revenus et de moyens de subsistance pour de nombreuses populations, mais reste confrontée à des défis en matière de réglementation, de professionnalisation, de protection de l’environnement et de gouvernance.
Il a indiqué que les trois journées de travaux permettront notamment de présenter les principales dispositions du Code minier relatives à l’EMAPE, les conséquences de l’orpaillage illégal et les actions engagées par le projet SECORCI 2 pour structurer et professionnaliser la filière aurifère artisanale, protéger l’environnement et renforcer la gouvernance locale.
La présidente de la Commission de l’évaluation des politiques publiques de l’Assemblée nationale, Dr Flore Kouassi, a, pour sa part, relevé que le rôle du parlementaire ne se limite pas au vote des lois, mais comprend également le contrôle de l’action de l’exécutif et l’évaluation des politiques publiques. Elle a appelé à un renforcement des capacités des parlementaires sur les questions liées à la gouvernance minière, à la traçabilité de l’or, aux obligations des exploitants et aux procédures d’autorisation.
L’atelier aborde également les préoccupations environnementales et sécuritaires liées à l’orpaillage illégal, notamment la dégradation des terres et des ressources en eau, ainsi que les enjeux de gouvernance du secteur.
Les échanges doivent déboucher sur des pistes de réflexion et des recommandations visant à améliorer la gouvernance de l’EMAPE et l’efficacité des interventions publiques.
(AIP)

title: Koosin/Madouba : Une dynamique de reprise des activités pédagogiques au compte de l’année scolaire 2026-2027
content:
BURKINA-KOOSIN-EDUCATION-REOUVERTURE
Koosin/Madouba : Une dynamique de reprise des activités pédagogiques au compte de l’année scolaire 2026-2027
Djibasso, 17 sept. 2026 (AIB)-Le Président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de la commune de Madouba, Kouka Désiré Kiemdé, a présidé ce jeudi 17 septembre 2026 à la Circonscription d’éducation de base (CEB) de Madouba délocalisée à Djibasso, une rencontre consacrée à la continuité des activités pédagogiques dans la commune au titre de l’année scolaire 2026-2027.
La rencontre consacrée à la continuité des activités pédagogiques dans la commune de Madouba au titre de l’année scolaire 2026-2027, intervient après une première rencontre tenue le 15 septembre 2026 au cours de laquelle la question de la réouverture des écoles de Madouba avait été abordée.
Le Président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de la commune de Madouba, Kouka Désiré Kiemdé, a ainsi fait la restitution des échanges aux différents acteurs.
Il a rappelé les préoccupations des parents d’élèves concernant la reprise des cours, en indiquant que : « Chacun est mieux chez soi ».
Le Chef de la CEB de Madouba, Vincent De Paul Millogo, a indiqué qu’à l’issue des échanges avec le directeur provincial, trois sites ont été retenus pour regrouper les écoles de la commune dont Madouba, Touba et Yourouna.
Selon lui, cette réorganisation prévoit à la fois des relocalisations et des réouvertures.
Ainsi, les écoles de Pia n°2 et de Bamkoumani, fermées depuis 2023, doivent reprendre leurs activités à Madouba à compter de cette rentrée scolaire.
Au niveau du secondaire, le proviseur du lycée départemental de Madouba, Boukary Porgo, a exposé plusieurs besoins, notamment le déblayage du domaine du lycée, l’accès à l’eau potable, la réhabilitation des logements, l’insuffisance de professeurs, le renforcement de la sécurité de proximité et la mise en place de convois sécurisés pour faciliter les déplacements des agents.
Il a également annoncé l’ouverture des classes de 6e et de 5e et par la même occasion, il a invité les parents d’élèves à accompagner la reprise des activités scolaires.
Pour sa part, le directeur de l’école de Yourouna a proposé une inspection des salles de classe afin de vérifier leur état après les opérations de déguerpissement, en raison de traces d’individus constatées dans certaines classes.
Le président du conseil d’école primaire de Madouba, Laurent Dabou, a, quant à lui, plaidé pour la réparation des toitures de certaines salles de classe, tandis que le directeur de l’établissement, Pié Karim Traoré, a insisté sur la nécessité d’un contrôle rigoureux des passagers aux alentours des établissements scolaires.
Le directeur du Centre d’éducation pour l’intégration (CEI) a également fait le point sur la situation de son établissement. Il a notamment sollicité du matériel nécessaire aux apprentissages pratiques, notamment une machine à coudre usagée, du fil à coudre et des outils de mécanique.
« Tout don sera le bienvenu », a-t-il déclaré, appelant les bonnes volontés à soutenir le centre en attendant une éventuelle dotation.
Le vice-président de la délégation spéciale, Ezékiel Diarra, a estimé que le retour des élèves constitue une satisfaction pour l’ensemble de la population.
Il a invité les populations à mieux s’impliquer dans les actions nécessaires à la reprise effective des activités, sans attendre uniquement une aide extérieure.
Au terme des échanges, le PDS de Madouba a présenté des solutions relevant de ses compétences pour répondre aux différentes préoccupations soulevées.
Il a remercié les participants pour leur mobilisation et invité les partenaires à renforcer leur collaboration avec les acteurs de l’éducation.
Camarade Kiemdé a enfin appelé les parents à assurer le suivi des élèves à domicile afin d’accompagner la reprise des activités pédagogiques.

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/ La communication hospitalière au service de la qualité des soins à Lakota
content:
Lakota, 21 sept 2026 (AIP) – L’amélioration de l’environnement hospitalier et de l’offre des soins à l’hôpital général de Lakota s’améliorent grâce à une dynamique soutenue par le service de communication de cet Etablissement public hospitalier départemental (EPHD) dirigé par Guina Joël, a constaté l’AIP.
En service à Lakota depuis mai 2023, M. Guina, rencontré sur son lieu de travail, a animé un plateau improvisé destiné aux plateformes WhatsApp et au profil Facebook de l’EPHD de Lakota. À cette occasion,
il a conduit un entretien face caméra avec le point focal Qualité de l’établissement, le technicien biologique Klai Koutou Élysée, autour de la question de la qualité de l’accueil et des soins.
Selon lui, la diffusion de messages clairs sur les services, les procédures et les droits des patients permet de réduire les malentendus et de renforcer l’adhésion aux traitements. Les campagnes de sensibilisation qu’il pilote, axées sur la prévention et l’hygiène, contribuent à améliorer la santé publique et à diminuer la pression sur les services hospitaliers. En outre, ces actions renforcent la confiance de la communauté envers l’établissement.
M. Guina a souligné que la qualité ne se limite pas à l’aspect technique mais englobe aussi la dimension humaine, avec une communication transparente envers les patients, le respect de leur dignité, l’implication des familles et l’instauration d’un climat de confiance. Il estime que la valorisation du travail des soignants
accroît leur motivation, tandis qu’une communication ouverte avec la société et les partenaires renforce la crédibilité de l’hôpital.
Lors de la 4è édition de la Semaine des communicateurs en santé (SCOM-2025), tenue du 27 au 29 novembre 2025 à Yamoussoukro, Guina Joël a été distingué 2è meilleur chargé de communication national des hôpitaux généraux et centres hospitaliers régionaux de Côte d’Ivoire, une reconnaissance de son engagement en faveur d’une communication hospitalière au service de la qualité des soins.

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/ Fodjo Kadjo Abo, un magistrat au long parcours à la tête du Conseil supérieur de la magistrature (Portrait)
content:
Abidjan, 24 sept 2026 (AIP) – Magistrat hors hiérarchie du groupe A, Fodjo Kadjo Abo a été nommé, mercredi 23 septembre 2026, président du Conseil supérieur de la magistrature (CSM), après avoir consacré plus de quatre décennies à la magistrature et occupé plusieurs hautes fonctions au sein de l’administration judiciaire et sécuritaire ivoirienne.
Né en 1959 à Adoumkrom, dans la sous-préfecture d’Appimandoum, département de Bondoukou (Nord-Est ivoirien, région du Gontougo), Fodjo Kadjo Abo effectue ses premières études dans son village natal avant de poursuivre sa scolarité au Lycée moderne de Bondoukou, où il obtient son baccalauréat en 1978.
Il entreprend ensuite des études de droit à la Faculté de droit de l’Université d’Abidjan, puis intègre, en 1982, la section internationale de l’École nationale de la magistrature de France. Diplômé en 1984, il commence la même année sa carrière dans la magistrature.
Il exerce d’abord comme substitut du procureur de la République près le Tribunal de première instance d’Abidjan, avant d’être nommé juge d’instruction au même tribunal. Il est ensuite juge aux sections de tribunal de Sassandra puis de Soubré.
Son parcours l’amène également à exercer plusieurs responsabilités au ministère de la Sécurité. Il est notamment directeur de cabinet de ministres chargés de la Sécurité intérieure et de la Sécurité entre 1992 et 1996, puis de nouveau en 2000.
De 1996 à 1999, il occupe les fonctions de sous-directeur de la Législation au ministère de la Justice. Après un premier passage à l’Inspection des Services judiciaires et pénitentiaires en 2002, il est nommé procureur général près la Cour d’appel de Bouaké en janvier 2004, fonction qu’il exerce jusqu’en juin 2011.
Fodjo Kadjo Abo retrouve ensuite les fonctions de directeur de cabinet au ministère de la Justice à plusieurs reprises entre 2011 et 2014, avant d’être nommé inspecteur général des Services judiciaires et pénitentiaires, fonction qu’il exerce depuis mars 2014.
À ce titre, il a également présidé plusieurs instances disciplinaires et administratives, notamment la Commission administrative paritaire des greffiers depuis 2017, le Conseil de discipline des services pénitentiaires depuis 2017 et le Conseil de discipline des greffiers depuis 2018.
Son parcours professionnel s’est aussi enrichi d’activités de formation et de participation à diverses structures. Il a notamment été formateur à l’École de la magistrature et des professions judiciaires d’Abidjan, membre de la Commission supérieure des recours auprès de l’Organisation africaine de la propriété intellectuelle (OAPI), ainsi que président du Conseil d’administration du Bureau ivoirien du droit d’auteur (BURIDA).
Au-delà de la magistrature, Fodjo Kadjo Abo est également connu pour son activité littéraire. Il est l’auteur de 14 ouvrages publiés aux éditions L’Harmattan, parmi lesquels Pour un véritable réflexe patriotique en Afrique (2002), Que reste-t-il de l’autorité en Afrique ? (2008), Au nom de la Politique (2016), Mon grand-père me disait (2021), L’Apocalypse n’a pas eu lieu (2023) et Ma grand-mère me disait… (2025).
Il est également l’auteur d’une soixantaine d’articles publiés sur son blog et co-auteur de l’ouvrage collectif Penser la réconciliation pour panser la Côte d’Ivoire, paru en 2015.
Son parcours lui a valu plusieurs distinctions, dont les grades de commandeur de l’Ordre du mérite de la Justice et de l’Ordre du mérite de la Fonction publique, ainsi que celui d’officier de l’Ordre national et de chevalier de l’Ordre du mérite culturel.
Lauréat de plusieurs prix littéraires, il a notamment reçu le Prix Haut de Gamme pour la littérature en 2008 et le deuxième Prix d’Excellence pour la littérature en 2017.
Chef de son village natal d’Adoumkrom, Fodjo Kadjo Abo est marié et père de six enfants.
Avec sa nomination à la présidence du Conseil supérieur de la magistrature, il est appelé à mettre à profit cette longue expérience de magistrat, de responsable administratif et d’acteur de la justice ivoirienne au sein de l’instance constitutionnelle chargée notamment des questions relatives à la carrière et à la discipline des magistrats.
(AIP)

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/Des acteurs sociaux renforcent leurs capacités sur les droits à la santé sexuelle, reproductive et mentale à Doropo
content:
Doropo, 19 sept 2026 (AIP) – Des acteurs sociaux ont bénéficié d’un renforcement de capacités sur les droits à la santé sexuelle et reproductive (DSSR), la prévention de l’exploitation des abus sexuels (PSEA) et la santé mentale, lors d’un atelier régional organisé par l’ONG l’Etoile du Bounkani (EBONI), en partenariat avec Médecins du Monde (MdM), avec l’appui financier de l’Union Européenne (ECHO).
Cet atelier, organisé du 15 au 17 septembre 2026, à la préfecture de Doropo s’inscrit dans le cadre du projet « Réponse d’urgence pour l’accès aux soins de santé essentiels et renforcement des capacités de réponses aux chocs pour les populations affectées par la crise sahélienne dans le Nord-est de la Côte d’Ivoire »
Il vise à améliorer l’offre de services de santé et renforcer les mécanismes communautaires de résilience.
Lors de cette session de formation, les participants ont vu leurs compétences renforcées sur les droits à la santé sexuelle et reproductive (DSSR), la détection des signes d’alerte en matière de santé mentale, la conduite à tenir ainsi que leurs responsabilités dans la prise en charge des personnes présentant des risques de santé mentale.
La santé mentale repose sur les principes de dignité, de non-discrimination, de confidentialité, de consentement et de respect de la personne. L’atelier a également donné lieu à la gestion de cas pratiques de santé mentale, regroupant des leaders communautaires, guides religieux, travailleurs sociaux, les humanitaires et enseignants.
Selon les formateurs, les acteurs communautaires doivent être à l’écoute, dans le présent, respecter et adopter une attitude de non-jugement, éviter de projeter ses opinions, croyances et valeurs, savoir poser des questions et accepter ses limites, faire enfin preuve d’empathie.
Le directeur exécutif de l’ONG initiatrice de cet atelier, Dah Ollo Toussaint, a, pour sa part, rappelé que le contexte sécuritaire actuel de la région nécessitait d’accompagner les travailleurs sociaux et para-sociaux qui donnent chaque jour des soins, de leur temps dans l’accompagnement des populations impactées.
Ainsi, a-t-il invité les participants à prendre soin de leur santé mentale et à référer urgemment tout cas suspect pour une meilleure prise en charge.
(AIP)

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/ Le projet de résilience côtière restaure 53 hectares de mangroves pour protéger les zones lagunaires
content:
Abidjan, 18 sept 2026 (AIP) – Le Projet d’amélioration de la résilience des communautés côtières en Côte d’Ivoire et au Ghana a permis de restaurer 53 hectares de mangroves entre Grand-Bassam et Jacqueville, afin notamment de sécuriser les bordures de la lagune et de stabiliser les sols, a annoncé jeudi 17 septembre 2026 à Abidjan son coordonnateur régional pour le compte d’ONU-Habitat, Mouhamadou Diéné.
« En termes d’avancées, je pense qu’on a pu contractualiser avec des partenaires de mise en œuvre, dont Habitat for Humanity, qui est en charge de la restauration de plusieurs hectares de mangroves », a déclaré M. Diéné lors de la troisième session du comité de pilotage du projet.
« Aujourd’hui, on est à peu près à 53 hectares cumulativement entre Grand-Bassam et Jacqueville, qui ont été restaurés, où on a planté des palétuviers pour sécuriser les bordures de la lagune, mais aussi stabiliser le sol », a-t-il précisé.
La troisième session du comité de pilotage visait à présenter les résultats des discussions du comité technique sur l’état d’avancement des activités des différentes composantes du projet au cours du semestre, ainsi qu’à recueillir les avis et recommandations des membres pour la prochaine période de mise en œuvre.
M.Diéné a insisté sur l’implication des populations locales dans les activités de restauration des mangroves, estimant qu’il s’agit de l’une des conditions de réussite du programme.
« Ce sont elles-mêmes, ces populations, qui plantent avec nous, qui sont chargées de la sécurisation, de l’arrosage et de la préservation de ces zones-là, pour qu’on puisse avoir un taux de réussite assez important des palétuviers qui sont plantés dans les communautés », a-t-il expliqué.
Le coordonnateur régional a également souligné la collaboration avec le ministère de l’Environnement et de la Transition écologique ainsi qu’avec les directions régionales des Eaux et Forêts de Grand-Bassam et de Jacqueville.
Le projet prévoit également la mise en place de bassins d’infiltration et de rétention destinés à réduire les risques d’inondation dans les communautés, ainsi que des zones de drainage végétalisées.
« Ce sont des bassins de rétention qui vont éviter que les communautés soient inondées lorsqu’il pleut. Il y a ce qu’on appelle des zones de drainage également. Au lieu d’avoir des drains qui sont faits en béton et en ciment, on a des zones végétalisées qui peuvent permettre de drainer les eaux en excès », a expliqué M. Diéné.
Pour sa part, le partenaire du projet, Dr Luc Boerboom, de l’Université de Twente, aux Pays-Bas, a relevé que les activités économiques et les investissements sont fortement concentrés dans les zones côtières, particulièrement exposées aux risques.
« Nous avons découvert qu’il y a un corridor secondaire qui, par la nature, est déjà en train de se développer. Personne ne le connaît, mais nous le voyons maintenant. Et nous pouvons utiliser ce corridor secondaire pour enlever la pression du corridor primaire », a-t-il indiqué.
Le président du comité de pilotage, Pr Kouadio George, conseiller technique et coordonnateur du programme Ozone au ministère de l’Environnement et de la Transition écologique, a déclaré que le gouvernement a été interpellé afin de trouver des solutions urgentes pour réduire l’impact du changement climatique sur les populations, notamment celles des zones côtières fortement touchées par l’érosion et l’élévation du niveau de la mer.
La troisième session du comité de pilotage a été organisée par ONU-Habitat et le Fonds d’adaptation, en partenariat avec l’Université de Twente, le Bureau national d’études techniques et de développement (BNET), l’ONG Habitat for Humanity et la Convention d’Abidjan.
Le Projet d’amélioration de la résilience des communautés côtières en Côte d’Ivoire et au Ghana vise à réduire la vulnérabilité des petites et moyennes localités côtières face aux effets du changement climatique.
Il repose notamment sur le renforcement de la coordination régionale et de la planification stratégique à travers une stratégie transfrontalière de développement côtier et le partage de bonnes pratiques, ainsi que sur le renforcement des capacités locales d’adaptation.
Le projet, qui a débuté en 2024 et qui prend fin en 2026, s’articule autour de trois composantes à savoir le renforcement de la planification spatiale pour l’adaptation au changement climatique côtier à différentes échelles géographiques, le développement, la mise en œuvre et la gestion d’interventions concrètes destinées à renforcer les capacités d’adaptation des communautés côtières et le renforcement de la coordination et de la coopération entre la Côte d’Ivoire et le Ghana.
A terme, le projet doit contribuer à renforcer la protection des communautés côtières, les capacités des institutions locales et la diffusion de solutions d’adaptation reproductibles à l’échelle régionale.
Les participants à cette session, au nombre de 19, sont principalement des représentants du secteur public et des partenaires techniques engagés dans le renforcement de la résilience des communautés côtières en Côte d’Ivoire.
(AIP)

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/ Bondoukou: la joie renaît chez les commerçants sinistrés après les annonces du gouvernement
content:
Bondoukou, 21 sept 2026 (AIP)- La joie et le soulagement étaient perceptibles, dimanche 20 septembre 2026, chez les commerçants sinistrés de l’incendie du grand marché de Bondoukou, après l’annonce de mesures gouvernementales destinées à les accompagner dans la reprise de leurs activités.
Réunis à la mairie de Bondoukou à l’occasion d’une cérémonie de compassion du gouvernement, les victimes ont accueilli avec émotion l’annonce d’un appui de 32,5 millions de francs CFA en leur faveur, ainsi que les perspectives d’accompagnement annoncées pour les femmes et les jeunes ayant perdu leurs activités dans le sinistre.
Ces annonces ont ravivé l’espoir des commerçants, dont les marchandises, équipements et fonds de commerce avaient été détruits par les flammes dans la nuit du 12 au 13 juillet.
« Aujourd’hui, nous savons vraiment que nous ne sommes pas des laissés. Nous avons des gens qui nous soutiennent », s’est réjouie la présidente des commerçants du marché de Bondoukou, Ouattara Korotoum, exprimant sa gratitude au gouvernement et à l’ensemble des autorités mobilisées depuis l’incendie.
« Tous les commerçants disent merci. Merci à l’Etat de Côte d’Ivoire », a-t-elle ajouté, traduisant le sentiment de reconnaissance des victimes face aux différents soutiens reçus depuis le sinistre.
Pour les victimes, cette cérémonie marque une nouvelle étape dans leur parcours de relèvement, après plusieurs semaines de désolation, avec l’espoir de retrouver progressivement leurs activités et leurs moyens de subsistance.
Le ministre du Commerce, de l’Industrie et de l’Artisanat, Ibrahim Kalil Konaté, a assuré que le gouvernement entendait prendre en compte la réhabilitation des marchés affectés par les incendies.
Au-delà de cette assistance, le ministre a annoncé des mesures visant à améliorer la gestion des espaces commerciaux, notamment un projet de loi relatif à la gestion des marchés de gros et de détail. Il a évoqué la création d’une société de gestion des marchés, ainsi que la mise en place d’une carte de commerçant de Côte d’Ivoire destinée à faciliter l’identification des acteurs et leur accès à différents services.
Un programme de construction de 155 marchés de proximité, piloté par l’Office d’aide à la Commercialisation des Produits Vivriers (OCPV), ainsi que des projets de marchés de gros à Abidjan, Abengourou et Daloa, figurent également parmi les initiatives annoncées.
Pour les jeunes sinistrés, le ministre de la Jeunesse, Mamadou Touré, a évoqué la constitution d’une équipe chargée de les identifier, d’évaluer leurs besoins et d’examiner les possibilités de financement pour reconstituer leurs fonds de commerce. Une enveloppe pouvant atteindre 500 millions FCFA a été évoquée, sous réserve de l’évaluation des besoins et de la mise en place du dispositif approprié.
La ministre de la Cohésion nationale, de la Solidarité et de la Lutte contre la pauvreté, Myss Belmonde Dogo, a, pour sa part, invité les commerçantes bénéficiaires de prêts du Fonds d’appui aux femmes de Côte d’Ivoire (FAFCI) à se faire enregistrer auprès de la mairie, afin que leurs dossiers puissent être transmis au cabinet de la Première Dame pour un éventuel accompagnement.
Cette mobilisation s’inscrit dans une série d’actions engagées au profit des commerçants sinistrés depuis les premiers jours qui ont suivi l’incendie.
Dès le 18 juillet, le ministère de la Cohésion nationale avait procédé, à la mairie de Bondoukou, à la remise officielle d’une aide alimentaire composée de 10 tonnes de riz et de 50 cartons de dattes.
Le 29 juillet, le président du Parti Pro-Côte d’Ivoire pour la Démocratie, la Prospérité et la Souveraineté (PROCI-DPS), Kévin Fieni, avait, à son tour, apporté un appui évalué à 14,495 millions FCFA en vivres, en numéraire et en aide exceptionnelle.
Le maire de Bondoukou, Ouattara Anzoumana, a encouragé les commerçants à garder confiance en l’avenir, soulignant que l’incendie avait détruit des biens matériels, mais pas leur courage, leur dignité ni leur capacité à se relever.
